div.head: VALUE OF INTERNATIONAL GO-OPERATION.
div.p: VALUE OF INTERNATIONAL GO-OPERATION.
L
Solve Social Problems.
Local instances of excessive prices being

demanded for land required for municipal and industrial purposes were given at a meeting held at Dalton Bank on Friday. Mr. G. Walker presided, and Mr. Crosfield, Mr. Thomas Ternent (Rochdale), and Mr. J. Jarman addressed the large gathering.
How the _Workingmen of the World will

The first round in the Warrington Land Campaign, which lasted continuously for over a fort night, came to a conclusion on AVednesday with a largely at tended meeting at Bridge Foot. Great success has attended the series of meetings, and the town has now a fair foundation upon which to work respecting the chief plank of the Liberal platform at the next election. Land has been discussed in all its phases, but other subjects have been handled. Nothing has been more important than the hint Mr. Crosfield gave as to the probable outcome of the work of the Inter- national Labour Association, of which he is a member. When the civilised nations have been brought into line in industrial matters, and working men have really joined hands, they will see that an end is put to excessive expenditure by their Governments upon arms that helps largely to drain the life-blood of the peoples. In the first place—and the last—the better understanding that will prevail will make arms largely unnecessary.

shall contribute its quota to social needs, has added enormously to the revenue of our country, which has now reached the stupendous sum of 200 millions sterling per annum. Let me say, ' parathetically, that I by no means rejoice in the raising by additional taxation of that vast sum from any mere spiteful motive. Ido not think that as a general rule--though there are some exceptions to it—taxation for the sake of taxation is a good thing at all, but I do rejOice with all my heart in the fact that we are able to raise this vast revenue just because, ' with a large part of it, we are able to carry out so splendid and so truly patriotic a policy. (Cheers.) And so, friends, now that we are raising an annual revenue which would have staggered Mr. Gladstone had he been alive— (hear, hear)—let us at least see to it that, as far as possible, the money is well spent. (Hear, hear.) When I was in the House of Commons (A Voice: "You'll go there again," and very much for or Ikitnhdalynksumgygefsrtijeonnc,lsantldierle hope heir that one of these days it may be my good for- tune to return to the " Mother of Parlia- ments." While I was there I voted for every penny of necessary expenditure on. the Navy, and Army, atd Territorial Forces, and I did it with my eyes POen because there are times and seasons for reform, and in view of the Anglo- German rivalry which prevailed at that time it did not strike me that, all things considered, the cause of International Peace and reduction of armaments would be advanced if at that juncture we seemed to flinch from the cost of keeping our end up. (Hear, hear.) But now I feel most strongly that that time and season for far-reaching reform, and for a reduction on a vast scale of this colossal and wicked expendi- ture on the destructive forces of the nations— I do feel convinced that the time for this is approaching. I hold that it is the duty of good citizens to further the cause of sane inter- nationalism in the interests of humanity, of science, and of civilisation—(hear, hear)—and as time goes on I look to see the artisans of Europe exercising an ever-increasing influence in helping on that same great and beneficent international cause. Trade Unionism, a great and invaluable force in England,i will, I hope, be better developed in France. It badly needs development there, just as democratic govern- ment needs to become more of a reality than it is to-day in Germany. (Hear, hear.) We have to a very great extent made it a reality in England, and we are going to put the finishing touch to it very shortly when we pass the Plural Voting Bill, and, with the help of the demo- cracy, deal with the reform of the Second Cham- ber. Well, as in matter of science and educa- tion, we may often with advantage take a leaf out of Germany's book, in other matters she may learn a useful lesson from us; and so in the future one looks to see a development aria im- provement in democratic government in Ger- many. That, and the strengthening of trade unionism in France, will all give added strength to the cause of wise, international co-operation. It is for the people themselves in these great countries to say, "We will not permit this frightful waste of national resources to go on." (Applause.) It is fearful to think that expen- diture on the Navy is fast approaching fifty millions sterling a year. (Hear, hear.) I do not intend to detain you by discussing at any length to-night questions of foreign politics, but I may remind you that the one great fundamental difficulty in the Europedn situation, and the root, therefore, of untold mis- chief and wasteful expenditure, is the question of Alsace and Lorraine. It is undoubtedly a formidable and difficult question, but I have good reason for believing that it is not one that presents insuperable difficulties, and that it is not a question fundamentally incapable of ad- justment. If ever it were adjusted and you had a central alliance formed between England, Germany and France, that expenditure of fifty millions per annum on the Navy might at once be cut down by one-half. Next year we are going to celebrate a great and grand event, memorable for all time as a landmark in his- tory—l mean the Centenary of the Peace, which has existed unbroken for the last hundred years between Great Britain and the United States of America. (Cheers.) Yes, that is a fact we can dwell upon with heart-felt satisfaction. (Hear, hear.) Peace maintained between these two great branches of the Anglo-Saxon race, and never again to be broken; yes, friends, and that without one single fort to preserve it along all the thousands of miles of frontier between the United States and Canada. How signifi- cant! What an earnest of progress in the same direction which is bound to follow! (Hear, hear.)

div.head: LOCAL TAX ON INDUSTRY.
div.p: A LOCAL TAX ON INDUSTRY.

The CHAIRMAN said that otBoo and £l,OOO per acre had been asked for land required for school purposes in that ward. The land in Liverpool- road, previous to the erection of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works, was agricultural land, with a very low price on it. By skill and by the business capacity of Mr. Monks, large works employing a large number of hands had been erected, and the groun l rent for the land was £BOO, yet the lanclewm_ did not contribute any- thing to the rates of Warrington. (A Voice: "Shame.") Such co-ditions were going to be altered; it was going to be done by supporting the Liberal party in their campaign. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. JARMAN AND LAND VALUES.
div.p: MR. JARMAN AND LAND VALUES.
A Sunday Closing Lesson for the Member.

Mr. JARMAN, referring to current politics, said that a few weeks ago he was thinking of Harold Smith. It was not often Mr. Smith troubled his (the speaker's) thoughts, but on this pavticular occasion he thought about him pretty consider- ably. On a certain Sunday evening he was pass- ing the last public-house in the London area, and noticed a lot of children outside, who were waiting for their parents, who were crowded inside. When the place closed about eleven o'clock the people were turned, out. One woman had evidently made up her mind to let all the neighbours know her troubles, for she was screaming them at the top of her voice for a quarter of an hour afterwards. He only wished that Harold Smith had had the privilege of standing behind that public-house bar, not in front of it, during the hours of that Sunday afternoon and night, for he would then have different notions in regard to Sunday Closing. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: ASTOUNDING PRICES FOR LAND.
div.p: ASTOUNDING PRICES FOR LAND.

There were evidences in Warrington that something needed doing very urgently in regard to the land question. High prices were charged for land, not simply because the land was worth the money, but because the public wanted it. He had been astounded at some of the prices asked for land in Warrington which one would hardly think worth giving to the people. A price of I'2oo per acre was not an extraordinary charge, because such land as was charged for could hardly be reckoned worth anything. The Town Council would not consent to a Town Planning scheme because some of the men on the Council who were against it were owners of land, and they thought they would not get such a good price for it. They were doomed by the Town Council to a continuation of overcrowded areas which existed at the present time. They could not have a worse condition of overcrowding than existed in Winwick-road houses. At the rear of the houses there were vast stretches of waste ground doing nothing and paying ilothing. The land campaign was going to abolisli such a con- dition of things. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S METHOD FOR CHECKING TAXATION.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S METHOD FOR CHECKING TAXATION.

After referring to the time, 20 or 30 years ago, when they were talking about ploughing the sand, and had what they would describe in Lancashire as "a pretty dree ' time of it" politically, Mr. CROSFIELD said: We have now come into our own, and if my friend, Mr. Walker, casts his memory back to those early days when times were not so bright for Liberalism as they are to-day, I am sure, in thinking of the con- trast, he must feel a very great pride in taking the active part he does to help on, not one or two good causes, but the whole mass of really splendid progressive work which many of us have had the privilege of backing up in the course of the last eight years. (Applause.) I am not going to try to give you even briefly an entire summary of all the work that has been done, but it is enormous. (Hear, hear.) You know the old saying that a prophet is not with- out honour save in his own country. You might similarly say that the full value of pro- gressive reform is not wholly realised by the generation which paSses it. I do not mean to say that we are unappreciative of the work that has been done for the people of England have shown pretty well at three General Elections what they think of it. (Cheers.) Ido not think many, years will pass, however, before people will be looking with even greater admira- tion than we .Progressives regard it to-day, at tire great constructive edifice that is being erected by the present Government with your help. (Hear, hear.) That piece of constructive work will be a monumental record for all time.

PROGRESSIVE WORK FOR YOUNG AND OLD. It is hard to say what they have not done. Mr. Herbert Samuel, who does not perhaps have as much of the limelight upon him as some people, but who is one of the ablest in that wonderfully able band of men at the head of political affairs at the present time—Alr. Samuel passed the Children's Bill, and so we are look- ing after these little kiddies who have mustered in force and support us so enthusiastically to- night. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) We all know, and it will never be forgotten, what has been done in our time for the old folk. We never had a finer piece of work carried by a British Parliament than that Old-Age Pensions Act—(cheers)—and we have had another piece of work every bit as fine, every bit as valuable, in the provision made against sickness, disable- ment and affliction—against the rainy day of adversity, if it overtakes any of our people. (Renewed cheers) I say emphatically it is to the eternal shame of our opponents. that they ever descended so low as to try and use that Insurance Act for political purposes against the other party. (Hear, hear.) In a very short we shall be asking how ,on earth our t along without stich an Act, how it was possible for millions of our people to face ctoimunetry go the risk of going unprovieled without this k Iss'ohicelioifsttl°guard them as it 1e worst afflictions to-daydsloleiesld d buck e against m , I oy- hich ever overtake mankind. Yes, friends, qualified individualism and graduated taxation, of which I have spoken to you time and again these last 20 or 30 years, are now realities in old England. (Cheers.)
INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION WILL BRING SANITY. Lloyd George, by the taxation of luxuries and O! great wealth, and by instituting for the first time the principle that wealth socially created

div.head: NTERNATIONAL WORKERS WILL CHECK
div.p: NTERNATIONAL WORKERS WILL CHECK

ARMAMENTS. "I am not arguing," continued Mr. Crosfield, "that the Milleniurn is at hand, or that we should take any rash step and weaken ourselves by premature, isolated action. That I would not support. What We Want is collective action. We are faced with the fact that the chief civilised powers of Europe are arming, not so much against less civilised powers, or so as to check and keep in order some of the coloured races of the world, should they at one time or another become a menace to order, but that these great powers are arming mainly against each other. It is to get rid of that we need collective action, just as combined effort afikong People of different nationalities has enabled us 'to bring about industrial reforms of far-reaching importance, as, for instance, when we practically got rid of night 3n ork for women, and abolished the use of white phos- phorous in the manufacture of matches, so sav- ing thousands and thousands of workers from the horrible disease called " Phossy Jaw." (Hear, hear, and cheers.) We have now set on foot an agitation for the entire abolition of the twelve-hour shift in all industries where work is carried on continuously day and night. We shall not rest till throughout those indus- tries the eight-hour shift is established by law. (Cheers.) That will be a measure of enormous importance in itself, and it will have an im- mense effect in helping to further the introduc- tion of more civilised and scientific conditions of employment—(hear, hear)—and I say it is by the same kind of international cc-operation, and by that alone, we shall be enabled to curtail this terrible wasteful expenditura on arma- ments. (Hear, hear.) While that is the out- look let us, to say the least, avoid making matters worse by further swelling this expen- diture on armaments. EXCESSIVE

MILITARISM MEANS RE-ACTION. Never listen to the gospel of excessive mili- tarism which has been preached far too much already in this town. That way, friends, lies re-action. (Applause.) It will not do. We claim, and we are justified in claiming what the Prime Minister has defined as an "Unchal- lenged and unchallengable supremacy on the water," and we have got it. Yes, and we are entitled to it, for us it is a matter of necessity; but if in addition to this we are going to make ourselves a "Nation in Arms," why, then, with our vast mercantile marine and the Navy to protect it, we should be able to land a fight- ing force amounting to many hundreds of thous- ands of men in any direction we chose. And that is what the National Service Leaguers are after. They speak of Home Defence, but they are after an adventurous policy on the Con-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914

tinent. And, of course, if they got their way our Continental neighbours would realise fast enough what was in the wind, and Britain, which now stands for European Peace, would seem to menace powerful neighbours of ours on the Continent with war. You would make it more difficult to develop and strengthen friendly relations between Gerraany and England. (Hear, hear.) You would create suspicion in- stead—(hear, hear)—and, I repeat, that way lies re-action. I give all credit to the members of the National Service League for high patriotic motives, but I hold that they are mistaken, and their policy insidious and dangerous, and I intend, before the year is out, on other plat- forms in Warrington, to go further into this question. (Hear, hear.) While there is not time for me to do so to-night, I do put in a word of caution and of warning to any members of the Progressive party who have been tempted to coquette with this gospel of excessive mili- tarism, and I utter the same warning to those fellow-townsmen of mine who are on the borer line, so to speak,' which separates the party of progress from the party of re-action.

div.head: PROTECTION, CONSCRIPTION, AND SLAVERY.
div.p: PROTECTION, CONSCRIPTION, AND SLAVERY.

At a meeting recently held in Warrington I saw it was stated that the Prime Minister, who a sliort time before had received a deputation from the National Service League, had said in effect that the National Service League was I doing, very good work, and should go on and prepare the way in the country. Now I want at once to, warn all members of the Progressive party that that statement; although doubtless made in all good faith, is none the less abso- lutely inaccurate. I first read the report of the interview which the deputation of the National Service League had with Mr. Asquith in the "Manchester Guardian "—a splendid journal, of which I am a pretty constant reader. The report was evidently abbreviated and summarised, and so I thought it best to write at once direct to the Prime Minister and inquire if this report were correct. I promptly received in reply an assurance that the report , was entirely contrary to the fact, and in proof of this I received a verbatim, or, at least, a very full report of the conference that had taken place. Therefore, friends, do not let it be thought that the Prime Minister's nitrite and authority can be quoted in favour of this dan- geroue doctrine of Conscription. (Hear, hear.) There is no foundation, ladies and gentlemen,. for such a statement, or insinuation, and I beg you to remember that the Chief Whip of our party himself not long since came down to Manchester and said that the whole massed forces of thel Progressive army would be used to withstand this insidious attempt to fasten Conscription upon our people. (Cheers.) I have quoted before now what John Burns said not long since. He spoke of the "Jingo Rake's Progress—Protection, Conscription, and Slav- ery."_ That was soon after the time when

_ forced Chinese labour was imported into South Africa. Well, the massed forces of the Progres- sive party have been strong enough effectually and finally to put a stop to that ill-omened attempt to establish quasi-slavery under the British flag; and I think we have pretty well done for Protection, which is certainly in a very sick way just now. (Laughter.) And so in the same way the massed forces of those who believe in human progress will be able to resist this not less dangerous, not less pernicious doc- trine which is being preached to us where these efforts are so constantly made to induce us— with our eyes open—to saddle ourselves with a system, hated on the Continent, a tremendous handicap for and a drag upon our Continental neighbours, and which is only tolerated by them as a melancholy necessity. The proposal to introduce such a system into England is noth- ing less than preposterous, and I think it is the duty of good democrats to join, as I now ask you, friends, to join, in a vigorous and determined effort to defeat it. (Loud cheers.)

div.head: OUR NEXT MEMBER. The Barriers in the Way of Progress Swept Away.
div.p: OUR NEXT MEMBER. The Barriers in the Way of Progress Swept Away.

Mr. TERNENT expressed the hope that the people of Warrington would return Mr. Cros- field to Parliament, for lie was full of sym- pathies for the people. (Applause.) The barriers which had previously been against the Liberal party had been broken down, and now they' were going forward they had plenty of items in their 'programme, one of which was the great land campaign. After giving a lengthy historical review of the land question and dealing with the way in which landlords had rid themselves of their responsi- bilities, the speaker dealt with the effect the raising of the minimum wage for the agricul- tural labourer and all the attendant improve- ments would have on the towns. The farmer would be secure, and the labourer would have a fair reward for his labours; and such a state of affairs could not but tend to improve the con- dition of those in the towns who were unfairly competed against for their labour by the lab- ourers in the country, who came to the towns because the wages were slightly higher than in the country. They wanted every agricultural labourer in the country to feel a spirit of inde- pendence; that was the essence of Liberalism— independence for the democracy of the country. (Applause.) A comprehensive vote of thanks was accorded the speakers and Chairman, on the proposition of Councillor LOCKER.

div.head: F. E. hMITH.
div.p: F. E. hMITH.
Mr. Crosiield on Unionism that Preaches Disunion.
REAL SELF-GOVERNMENT.

Despite the inclemency of the weather there was a very large attendance at Bridge Foot on Monday evening, when Mr. W. H. Sherburn presided, and Councillor Grindle, of Manches- ter, and Mr. Crosfield delivered inspiring and instructive addresses.

div.head: THINGS OF WHICH WE ARE NOT PROUD.
div.p: THINGS OF WHICH WE ARE NOT PROUD.

The CHAIRMAN said they were proud of many things connected with the Empire, but there were one or two things of which they were not proud, but wanted to Mend. One of these was that a vast number of people were either going to other lands from the country districts, or migrating into the towns and cities. (Hear, hear.) They were also not proud of the slums in the towns and cities. They,were not proud that so many people were rich and so many poor. Many thought that something was radically wrong. One of the causes of such undesirable conditions in the country was the monopoly of land. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party—proposed by tackling that question to right many of the wrongs that existed at the present time. (Applause.)

div.head: WHERE WE. MIGHT IMITATE
div.p: WHERE WE. MIGHT IMITATE
GERMAN

Councillor GRINDLE remarked that as a magis- trate he had had white gloves presented to him that morning. He thought that when the Liberal reforms were accomplished there would be less crime and ,therefore more white gloves would be presented. There would be less incen- tive to do wrong and more incentive to do right; (Hear, hear.) Deprecating the idea that we should not take any hints from the foreigner, Councillor Grindle referred to a recent visit which he had paid to Germany, and said in ,regard to housing and town planning and other reforms connected with land we might very well take hints worth copying. We were not going to copy Conscrip- tion or Tariff Reform—(hear, hear)—but those things by which we would benefit. They must not despise the foreigner in what he did that was good simply because they were behind in England- (Hear, hear.)

RELEASE THE LABOURER FROM SERFDOM. After giving typical examples of where Liberal legislation had benefited large masses of the people, the speaker dealt with the land pro- posals; commencing by stating that ,they were going to release the agricultural labourer from comparative serfdom. They could only remove those awful conditions by giving the agricul- tural labourer decent wages and a good home. A man who lived in a model lodging-house in the town and paid threepence per night , need not fear losing his home if he went on strike, but if the agricultural labourer did that he was given his notice in many cases. (Hear, hear.) They were going to follow the maxim that the best countries in the world were those who paid best wages. If the lowest wages meant prosperity, then Russia would be the most prosperous nation in the world. (Hear, hear.) It was the country which paid the highest wages that was the most prosperous.

SECURITY OF TENURE. They were going to give the farmer security of tenure, which would be another very good thing, for the farmer would be protected against the bad landlord. He would be able to claim through the Special Court for the value of im- provements which he had effected on the land. Industry would also be relieved of the tax put upon it by the land monopoly; the shopkeeper would not be penalised for making his premises attractive, and municipalities would have more scope and a freer hand in carrying out local improvements for the good of the people. (Ap- plause.) In conclusion, the Councillor referred to the Home Rule question and said he • bought those who had been against it were getting into a more collected state of mind and were cooling off their energies by walking about and practising gym- nastics. (Laughter.) Some people said the Home Rule question was religious, but he could tell them it was no more a religious question than Tariff Reform or Free Trade. ll•sar, hear.) Ireland would shortly be more contentad, pros- perous and peaceful. (Applause.)

div.head: F. E. SMITH AND THE TORY GAME I WARRINGTON TO COUNT IN ULSTER.
div.p: F. E. SMITH AND THE TORY GAME I WARRINGTON TO COUNT IN ULSTER.
Home Rule Advocacy for 30 Years.

Mr. CROSFIELD, who had a hearty reception, said that just before he came to that meeting he read a speech delivered by Mr. F. E. Smith. (Laughter.) He had got it there. (A Voice: "Where was Harold?") Well, Harold was not there. They would hope he was more pleasantly employed. Xaughter.) First of all, " F.E.," speak'ng of vc hat was going on in Ulster, said: "Let, there- fore, no one be so foolish as to suppose that the party which of all ethers in the State stood to gain by the maintenance of law and ciyic stability, had, lightly or inconsiderately, advanced to their present posit, aa." No one did suppose that. (Hear, near: They knew what they were about, and knew the game they were playing. (Hear, hear.) He could answer P. E. Smith out of his own mouth, for it was he who gave the whole show away in London, when he said they set great store by the Ulster ques- tion, for it was such an admirable means of ' enabling them to break the Parliament Act. tHear, hear.) Continuing, " F.E." said: "The Home Rule question was shirked by every Cabinet Minister and every Liberal candidate at the last election." Well, F. E. Smith spent a little of his time in Warrington at the last General Election, and he ought to remember well enough that there was no shirking of the Home Rule question in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) There had been no shirking of that question on any of their platforms, not only at the last election, but for 30 years past. It was mere mockery to pretend that everybody with his eyes open and ears to hear in the town did not know that the Home Rule question was one of the foremost questions of the day that was to be decided at the last election. All over the country it was placarded on every hoarding. , (Hear, hear.)

UNIONIST PREACHER OF DISUNION. Then Mr. Smith said: "The Government would never settle the question of Irish Gov- ernment until they had consented to the un- limited exclusion of Ulster." (Laughter.) Well, that was a nice sort of sentiment to come from a man who called himself a Unionist—a Union- ist preaching the disunion of Ireland. (Hear, hear.) They were a contradictory party all through. The party of law and order, as they used to call themselves, ought to be called the party of lawless disorder. They called them- selves the Constitutional party, but they had not hesitated to play any trick they could with the Constitution. It would be nothing less than a disaster of a most grievous kind if all these "Constitutionalists" got their own way. He did not say they had not persuaded themselves into a semi-serious frame of mind over the Ulster question. But at the root of it all was what Mr. F. E. Smith was driving at—the destruction of the Parliament Act. (Hear, hear.) The efforts of the Die-hards were all the more desperate as they felt this Was their last chance to resist the rising tide of democracy. (A Voice: "The last kick in the last ditch.") Yes, and the Die-hards would be left flounder- ing there. But what a policy it was, this at- tempt to fan the flame 3 of religious bitterness, which for years past had been gradually sub- ; this violent and reckless effort to work upon bigotry and prejudice and passion, in the Lope that party capital might be made out of it. ("Shame," "Hear, hear," and cheers.)

CONCESSION—BUT HOME RULE, Concession they had offered and were still pre- pared to offer, but the policy of Home Rule had triumphed. The advantages of self-government were going to be given to a vast majority of the Irish people, and those counties which were foolish enough to stand out of it for a time, if any of them did, would not stand out for long. He was convinced that even if the option to stand out was extended beyond the proposed six years, no county would act on it permanently. The forces tending the other way would inevit- ably make themselves felt and would be too strong for bigotry and intolerance in the long run, all the more so as the absolute necessity of a Federal system in the future became the more apparent. (Hear, hear.) The self-govern- ment would be a reality, and they would have the great advantage of relieving their own over- worked and overloaded Parliament, and shift- ing some of the local business on to the Parliament in Ireland, and afterwards on to the Parliament in Scotland, and another assembly in Wales. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The time had long passed for religious bigotry, but when they heard of parsons in the north-east corner of Ulster offering up a prayer of thankfulness • for the weather and wind which had wafted to their shores arms imported into Ulster to form an unlawful Army there, with the certain con- sequence of spurring on the Nationalists to do the same, they could not but recognise bnce more the spirit of religious bigotry which permitted this kind of thing, and, like their fathers before them, in the interests of true progress, set their faces against the doctrine of religious intolerance and ascendancy.

After dealing with the land and denouncing Tariff Reform, Conscription, and excessive naval expenditure, Mr. Crosfield appealed to the audi- ence to support the present Government in all they were doing for the general welfare of the whole community.

div.head: In the Carrying Out of Coming
div.p: In the Carrying Out of Coming
Reforms.
"THE BREEZE" RISES.

A meeting that the Chairman, Mr. C. E. Parker, described as a fitting termination to the fortnight's land campaign was held at Bridge Foot on Wednesday evening, when an exceptionally large audience assembled, and ,Councillor Grindle (Manchester) and Mr. Thomas Worthington (Wigan) dealt in racy fashion with our land law anomalies.

div.head: IMPORTANCE OF CONCENTRATION How the Land Question Touches all Classes.
div.p: IMPORTANCE OF CONCENTRATION How the Land Question Touches all Classes.

The CHAIRMAN said it was a good thing to concentrate on one subject, whether in business or anything else. They could only, get things done by unity and concentration on one thing, and that was what they had had in regard to the important question of land. There were many other subjects which would have to engage the attention of the Liberal party, when the ques- tion of land was seirtled, but a settlement of the land question was long overdue because it. touched everyone of them a great deal closer than many imagined. Some of them might think the latd question was all right for the people who owned land, or those who wanted it and could afford to pay for it. But they might ask, "What has it to do with me, having no land at all?" It touched everyone of them, because they all lived on the land. We were land animals. We came from the land and we should go back to the land. We had houses on the land, worked on the land, and had to pay rents for those houses on the land. That Was where it touched everyone, for that un- controlled private property in land had to be oaid for by those who lived on the land. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: SERIOUS EFFECT UPON LAND.
div.p: SERIOUS EFFECT UPON LAND.

It affected the rents a great deal more than many of them thought. He was of the opinion that on an average in Warrington for working- class houses the working people were paying in the rent ninepence or one shilling for the land, upon which the house was built, for site values. It was wrapt up in the rent and not separated. If land had been kept as it ought to have been by the State as the common possession for them all, the rents would be ninepence or one shilling less than they were to-day. (Hear, hear.) He did not mean to say that they were paying that amount for site values, although in some cases the charge for site values was more, but he wanted to point out that everything that went to make up houses was made dearer from the fact that there was private property in land. If they took bricks, for instance, the land from which the bricks were taken had to be paid for; the clay had to be paid for; so had the roads on which the bricks travelled. These were dearer, because of the price that had been paid for the land upon which the roads and railways were made. If they followed that line out they would find that everything that went to make a house was made dearer because of the uncon- trolled private possession of land. They had to take all those things into consideration, and, consequently, the land question was very im- portant.

div.head: WAY OUT.
div.p: THE WAY OUT.

It was a mixed-up -question, and they had to suffer from the confusion of the past. It would not be fair to take away from the present possessor of land that which he had because it was likely that that land had changed hands, perhaps half a dozen times, and probably the original owner had gone off with the "swag." (Laughter.) What they were going to do was to make the site values bear more of the bur- dens, and the increase that came of such great aggregate work of the whole population should come back in a large measure to those who made thoseiralues. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: NOTHING MORE VALUABLE THAN
div.p: NOTHING MORE VALUABLE THAN
"OUR FOLK."

Mr. WORTHINGTON said that land was a very complex question and they were going to bring about refoyms that were needed in regard to it when they were returned, as they would be, at the next election. There had been an inquiry into the land question, and it had been found that agricultural labour was a diminishing quantity. There was nothing more valuable in the country than the folk, and they should get them to stay here instead of going abroad. The agricultural industry was not only the oldest industry, but it was one that was most necessary. Whatever crippled industry and prevented the development of man was a crime against man and a sin against God. (Hear, hear.) Such was the monopoly in land. Large numbers of agricultural labourers had left the country because their conditions of living became intolerable, and they saw no prospect for themselves but the workhouse. They wanted to keep those people in the country and build up the grand old industry again. The landlords were, in a large nreasire, responsible for the emigration of the agriculturists. Those landownets, in many cases, were ignorant of farming, and all that they could do properly and with satisfaction was to put a penny stamp on the receipt for rent. The Liberal party said that the agricultural industry was very ae2o„ sary, and as such ought to be inade .to pay a living wage. If that could not be paid, then they must either change the circumstarces or the management. They were going to enact another minimum wage for farm labourers. lifear, hear.)

A REAL "MERRIE ENGLAND." They had got to know from the landowners at what price they valued their land, and that was the price they would pay when they bought the land on which to build. houses for the workers of the country. These would be let at such a rent that the people would be able to pay comfortably. A man would not be living on charity, but would be able to pay his way, for his wages would be increased and his rent would be reduced. He wouid have the ladder at his feet, and it would be his own fault if he did not get to the top. Every man should have the opportunity of de•.eloping and helping to contribute to the prosperity of the nation. (Hear, hear.) They proposed to change the whole country-side and make a real "Merrie England," not merely a thing written about in books. (Applause.) The country was under-cultivated and under- manned, but they were intent on getting abso- lutely the most and the best out of the land. The farmer would have security of tenure so that if he looked after the farm properly and paid his rent, neither saint, angel, nor the Devil could put him out. He would be a free man in a free country, so that he could do his best for the benefit of the nation. They would lessen their dependence on other countries for good and find employment and houses for their own people. (Applause.)

PETER RYLANDS'S PROPHECY. He urged them to keep their weather eye open, and see that it was to their interests, and to the interests of the community at large, that they Voted for the Liberal candidate. With a wide eye, deep conviction and independence of spirit they would aim a blow at that monopoly. (Hear, hear.) Speaking in 1874, Peter Rylands said, "You know the next breeze will be the land breeze." The wind had now begun to blow and would blow a great deal stronger as time went on, until next summer it would be half a gale and sweep all before it. Those people who are down would come out of their prison houses and exercise their heads and limbs and send back a Government that would put those land proposals on the Statute Book, and a series of laws that the people would rejoice that they had assisted in their initiation and enactment. They would be able to tell their children and grandchildren how slow the pro- gress was, but how sure had been the victory. (Applause.)

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.
THE NEW MICHELIN GUIDE FOR 1914.

When you take up your copy of the new Michelin Guide, now being issued for 1914, you will realise in a few minutes that here is a strik- ing example of excellence made more excellent. The first facts revealed by a cursory glance through the book are that there are 36 more pages and some fifty or sirty additional town plans. To be exact, there are .fifty new plans. But, turning the leaves with greater care, you will observe at once that careful revision has been devoted to the 748 pages contained, and that, in the geographical -section, a complete series of references to the Michelin Map of the British Isles, of which several of the 32 sections have already been published, gives the tourist just that connecting link between publications which binds them into the most informative and most readily accessible encyclopeedia ever placed before the motoring and motor cycling public of Great Britain. There is literally nothing omitted which can be of nse to the traveller or of interest to the sportsman: The Guide now contains no less than 330 town plans with all principal streets and exits plainly marked together with the positions of the hotels recommended—of which the Guide mentions 2,soo—Stockists premises, public buildings, &c. Full details of hotdl accommodation and prices, for car and occupants, are given in the town descriptions, which also contain a wealth of local information ,en ,repairers, car agencies, garages which are -open all night and on Sun- days, with a special mention of those which supply benzole. ' There are also SI separate detailed excursions of interest from various towns and a complete sectional atlas of the British Isles.

All important 'towns without exception are connected up by beautifully complete itiner- aries, and the roads to the smaller towns are also finely described, the turnings, gradients, quality of road surface, dangerous hills, and places of interest being dealt with, with that minute accuracy Tor which this Michelin work has become so famous. Take Of links, for in- stance; not only islhe'fact announced that there are links in the neighbourhood, but the direc- tion in which they lie from the town is given, together with the number of holes they possess, and, if you look la `the Michelin Map you will find them marked out in admirable detail.
England's toll-gates being a distinct feature, a complete list of 'them is given together with their fees; and all the ferries have also been listed.

Coming down to the seaport towns the reader will find a further fund of information in the full details given of steamship and railway com- munication time-tales, fares, freightage rates, &c., and for him who has decided to take his car abroad, there is a chapter on the Customs form- alities, rates, Sze., of foreign countries, their rules of the road and other distinctive features of travel that can only be of the greatest help. And the page on foreign coinage equivalents will be found by no means the least useful. "The Law on Motoring:" again is a chapter dealing with licences, registration and identifi- cation plates and o'ther administrative formali- ties and conditions, which must be complied with; while points on legal procedure, action in cases of accident, speed limits, and so forth are also included. , This excellent publication is to be obtained free of charge from any Michelin Stockist or post free for 1/3 from Michelin Tyre Co., Ltd., 81, Fulham-road, London, S:W., and in view of the fact that it is naturally in tremendous de- mand, I strongly advise every reader of the fore- going notes to write to his local Stockist, or, if he has not got one, to send his modest one and threepence to the Michelin Tyre Company not to-morrow morning, but to-day—now—this very moment—and so avoid disappointment. '

div.head: EXAMINERS SATURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINERS SATURDAY,
FARM AND GARDEN.

FRUIT CROPS. Severe Damage by Frost and Drought. Two spells of frost which occurred in May, assisted by harsh winds and drought, have suc- ceeded in making the fruit crop of the country, which was so promising at the end of April, a ruinous failure.

Rarely, if ever, says "The Times," had there been a better all-round prospect for fruit than there was up to the evening of May I. Nearly all varieties of plums, pears and cherries had blossomed profusely, and apples had an equally liberal display. Gooseberries and black cur- rants promised at least an average yield, straw- berries in the earliest districts were wall covered with blossoms or buds, and raspberries were satisfactory. Red currants alone among the principal fruit crops were somewhat below the mark.

Early in the morning of May 2,, however, without any warning, frost of exceptional severity for the time of year occurred through- out a great portion of the country. The results were disastrous, but curiouay partial. Much harm was done by north-east winds-during much of the second half of May. It remained, how- ever, for the frosts of the last week dm the month to inflict the worst of the disasters. While they swept away most of the plums 'and pears, which had escaped on May 2, they annihilated much of the strawberry crop where they were in full severity. Fortunately, Kent, usually a great sufferer when frosts are prevalent, 'again escaped lightly. As Kent is the greatest supplier of strawberries and cherries, the shortness of these crops will be less serious than -might 'be sup- posed if sufficient rain falls Bunn enough. This is particularly the case with cherries, and local reports are still hopeful for this crop. The fruit harvest will be 'one of great ,in- equality for different growers. 'Those who have escaped frost damage will' rea-p the 'benefit of the high prices resulting fromgeneral'deflciency, while it is to be feared that many 'small growers will be ruined. The partiality tufo the frosts was extraordinary, some orchards in even the most badly injured 'districts having suffered very little damage. Similar variation is noticeable in the attacks of insect and fungous pests. On the whole the season of 1914 will 'be placed on record as one of the mast unfortunate ever experienced by fruit-growers. In Cheshire, says "Farm ;and home;" the frost is reported to have been the keenest .ex- perienced during May for years past. Many acres of potatoes in the district have 'been .ad- versely affected. The ;,damage :done to fruit trees and crops, particularly potatoes, was enormous. Even in the warm Isle of Wight the potato crop was much damaged. Reports from Dublin state that the early potato crop suffered severely. In Ulster, where more fruit is grown for marketing purposes than in ,any part of Ire- land, apple and pear trees have suffered so severely that in some cases only half the usual yield is expected. The flax crop and peas and beans have also been damaged. In North-east Warwickshire acres of potatoes have been cut down, and kidney beans have 'suffered .exten- sively.

div.head: WHY DEVONSHIRE CREAM JS BEST.
div.p: WHY DEVONSHIRE CREAM JS BEST.
- At the recent Dairy Conference in Devon- shire, Mr. R. Ernest Cocks wad a paper on Devonshire cream. _

Although, he told the visitors, you may regard my next point as being prejudicekl, coming as it does from a Devonshire man, yet truth Will stand. I must be honest with you.. so, .despite what perhaps you may allow me to term your prejudice in thinking it to be universally true that we never see ourselves as others see us, I claim that scalded cream obtained from milk produced beyond lovely Devon is not of so high quality as that produced within its charming valleys. The cream of the West Country excels that of the busy North; the fact is plain, what- ever may be the cause of it. Now let me assume my usual modest vein. Not for a single moment would I venture even to hint that the patent fact is due to any superiority in the methods and management of our sturdy Deven yeomen. Far be it from me to harbour such a suspicion. I believe the cause of the admitted excellence is to be found in two factors, namely, the nature of the climate, which, though humid, is salu- brious, and the breed of the cattle, the far- famed South Devons. You will readily admit that the influence of the climate we are unable to transfer to you who come from afar, despite our proverbial generosity, and that the breed of the cattle is within your reach whenever you care to appeal to the true business instinct of the typical Devon cattle breeder; and, in pass- ing, let me emphasise the fact that for young and old the best tonic that has ever been or ever will be found is the famous Devonshire "junket and cream."

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

SHRUBS IN POTS. Very frequently shrubs in pots are employed for standing on balconies, terraces, or similar positions. To keep them .in good condition they need at this season a reasonable share of attention. In the first place, they must be well supplied with water; nest, it is very probable that the soil will be more or less exhausted. In this case the plants will be greatly benefited by an occasional dose of one of the many plant foods now on the market.—" Agricultural Economist." .

div.head: HOLLYHOCKS FROM SEEDS.
div.p: HOLLYHOCKS FROM SEEDS.

Formerly it was the practice-i.;;;;Opagate hollyhocks by division, grafting or cuttings, but the deadly fungus created so much havoc among the named sorts that the great majority of holly- hocks grown in our gardens are now raised from seeds. These plants, having plenty of vigour, are less susceptible to the fungus. To secure strong plants for flowering next summer, seeds of single and double flowered hollyhocks should be sown during May or June. Sow either in the open ground or in a cold frame. In due course prick off the seedlings in shallow boxes, and later plant them out in the open border. Seed- ling hollyhocks may be raised in many pleasing shades of colour, including crimson, red, deep rose, pink, orange yellow, sulphur and white. Hollyhocks vary from 6 feet to 10 feet in height, and flower from June to September.-4` The Garden."

div.head: ART OF HEDGE PRUNING.
div.p: ART OF HEDGE PRUNING.

Hedge pruning, like fruit pruning, is some- what of an art, though not such a difficult one as might be supposed from the bad condition of most of our fences. The main point to bear in mind is to attend very carefully to the top. This, with due attention to the sides, which are of less importance, will prevent the bottom from being gappy—a simple remedy for .a very common and bad complaint. Needless to say, the drip caused by want of attention to this simple point is largely responsible for the trOuble so often met with. Sometimes, though rarely, the opposite extreme is seen, and over- bushy sides and stunted top testify to want of judgment in regulating top growth. Summer should be carefully avoided for the operation with most hedge plants, but box is a somewhat curious exception; and August is said to be the best month for this work, and also, strange to say, for moving the roots.—" Agricultural Economist."
CHESHIRE CHEESE—continued.

div.head: JUNE 13, 1914.
div.p: CHESHIRE CHEESE
Remarkable Test Case at Local Police Court.
FIXING A STANDARD.

The question of what is and what is not Cheshire cheese was raised in an important case heard at Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday, in which Ernest Samuel CoHinson, grocer, Church-street, Frodsham, was Sum- moned that he being the seller or consignor in pursuance of a contract to sell and deliver Che- shire cheese to the Guardians of the poor for the Runcorn Union at Dutton Workhouse, unlaw- fully did, through his servant, George Wrench, sell and deliver to the Guardians and to their prejudice, cheese which was not Cheshire cheese, inasmuch as it was deficient in milk fat to the extent of 29 per cent., and was not of the nature, substance and quality of the article of food agreed to be sold and delivered. The defendant was represented by Mr. H. M. Linaker, -Runcorn, whilst Mr. W. E. Hough represented the Cheshire County Council, who prosecuted. Mr. Hough said that on February 12, Mr. Hal- lard, inspector of weights and measures under the County Council, happened to be at Dutton Workhouse when the cheese in question was being delivered by Mr. Collinson's man. The Inspector took a sample of the cheese, one por- tion of which was sent to the county analyst, whose certificate stated that the constituents of the cheese were : Water, 51.8 per cent. Milk fat, 17.0 per cent. Casein,Mine Mineral 1 24.9 matter, per 3.9 per cent. cent.

_ Lactose, 2.4 per cent. 0, This," the analyst's certificate stated, "was not a genuine sample of Cheshire cheese, inas- much as it was deficient in milk fat to the ex- tent of 29 per cent. That opinion was based upon the fact that genuine Cheshire cheese con- tained at least 24 per cent, of milk fat, whereas the sample contained only 17 per cent. of milk fat." "CHESHIRE." lf ,mconigitiisntruai the t to consider what was continuing, , said it would be neces- sary Cheshire cheese, and whether any article in the form of cheese could be sold as " Cheshire." sa Hough, From the evidence he would submit he would ask their Worships to say that a cheese con- taining only 17 per cent, of milk fat could not possibly be Cheshire cheese; the Bench had authority to fix a standard of that kind. The Board of Agriculture had not fixed any standard obviously on the ground of expense, because, he thought, they preferred each county to take steps to protect the producers in their own areas. However, in a report issued by the Board during the present year, it was stated the evidence obtained appeared to justify the conclusion that Cheshire, as well as Lancashire and some other cheeses, should be made from whole milk, except in cases, which it was stated might arise towards the end of the season, in which the milk was too rich and part of the cream could be removed in order that the cheese could have a uniform constituency. Answering a question by the Chairman (Mr. C. H.Burder), Mr. Hough said the cheese con- taining 17 per cent. of fat could be sold, but the objection was against the designation "Che- shire cheese." The prosecution was in the in- terests of the cheese producers in the county. William Hallard, inspector of weights and measures under the Cheshire County Council, said that on February 12 he went to the Dutton Workhouse and saw the .defendant's cart in charge of George Wrench, who was delivering cheese to the Workhouse. Witness took a sample of the cheese—about threequarters of a pound—and divided it into three parts, one of which was :given to Mr. Wrench, and another portion was sent to the public analyst. On re- ceiving the certificate already read he visited the defendant on March 3rd, told him that the sample was not genuine Cheshire cheese, and asked him for an explanation. He did not say any more than that "you know what you have to do in business, and that prices have gone up." Defendant further said that when he went to buy it he was not particular what kind lie bought, if the price suited lise bought it. By Mr. Linaker:: Defendant did not mention Cheshire cheese when witness interviewed him.

div.head: WHEN CHESHIRE CHEESE IS NOT CHESHIRE CHEESE.
div.p: WHEN CHESHIRE CHEESE IS NOT CHESHIRE CHEESE.

_ William Henry Hobson, Gonsley Farm, Blakenhall, said he had had 25 years' experience in the making of that particular class of cheese, and had probably won more prizes than any man in the world. Cheshire cheese, in his opinion, was made from whole milk. The per- centage of butter fat varied according to the time of the year. Samples taken in October, when milk was supposed to be at its ricltest, came out at about 36 per cent. In April, when milk was supposed to be poorest, 29 per cent. was about the lowest. He would call cheese with only 17 per cent, of butter fat half-meat or skimmed milk cheese. Although a cheese was made in Cheshire from Cheshire milk, it would not be called Cheshire cheese if it contained only 17 per cent. of fat. Jane Forster, principal of the Worleston Dairy Institute, said she had held the position for 19 years, and during that time had trained some -2,000 dairymaids. The lowest percentage of fat in analyses of cheese from the Institute had been 28. Cheshire cheese should be made from whole milk. She would call the cheeses contain- ing 17 per cent, of fat partially skimmed milk cheese. The Clerk: What percentage of fat would you expect to find in cheese contracted fcr as " fine Cheshire at 7d. per lb."?—From 28 to 34 per cent. William Dutton, Brindley Hall Farm, Nant- wich, who said he. had had 30 years' experience in the making of Cheshire cheese, stated that c the lowest percentage of fat found in his cheeses, which had been analysed, was 30.16. Cheshire cheese was twhaespmraacdtieeef rtoamtak some fat away in the whole milk. autumn, because the milk was then exceedingly rich. That was done to make the cheese the right constituency, but the amount that was taken away would not reduce the fat to a very great extent. FIXING A STANDARD. After an argument between the Chairman and Mr. Hough, the latter said that in the first place he was there to prosecute on the ground that defendant supplied cheese not according to con- tract. The contract was to supply Cheshire cheese, and he did not do so. It was, however, necessary to fix some standard for the purpose of this case only. Unless the Bench did so they could not say what was Cheshire cheese and what was not. The Chairman: I can say most distinctly what is not. Mr. Trough: My evidence will be adduced for the purpose of showing you that 24 per cent, of butter fat is a reasonable standard. Samuel Ernest Melling, analyst for the county of Chester, said that in 19 samples he had ana- lysed during the quarter ended March 31st, he Thefound thpalet theg he averagefat butter fat was 30.29. was 37.66 per cent, and the lowest 24.01 per cent. The cheese the subject s highest in of the -charge was not Cheshire cheese. From his experience be fixed a fair standard of fat at 24 per cent.—but that was below the average. The Chairman asked if the Board of Agricul- ture had fixed a standard for any other cheese in England. Mr. Melling: No, there is-no—standard at all. The only standard is with regard to foreign fat. They bring forward several suggestions as to why they do not fix a standard. One, which I think could be overcome, is that they say the water content of cheese, not only Cheshire, but Cheddar and several „others, varies from 35 per cent, to as high as 45 per cent., or even more. Further, the fat percentage varies accoraineto the amount of moisture. The more dry the cheese and the higher the fat. That could be got over by calculating the fat on the moisture for each sample. Judged on the dry sample the cheese in question could not be regarded as „genuine Cheshire cheese. TIER DEFENCE.

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
London to make Motor 'Buses Pay for the Roads.
VARIABLE GEARS.

The " Cycle Trader" gives some interesting particulars with reference to a novel competition that was recently held in France. The event was confined to cycles of the touring type, but all had to be fitted with variable gears. The total distance to be covered was 621 miles, com- prising 24 miles on the level 24 uphill and 181 downhill. Five hours was allowed for the whole distance. There were forty-four entrants, of which twenty-eight were fitted with three-speed gears, nine with four-speeds, three with two- speeds, three with six, and a tandem with nine. An interesting feature was that nearly one-half of the machines were fitted with gears on the multi-sproket and shifting chain type. This form of gear is almost unknown in this coun- try, but is very popular in France. Eighteen riders succeeded in completing the whole course in the time allowed, the first home being Chris- toplie on 'a Pengeot machine fitted with a Brit- ish gear. The venue of the race was a 10 kilo- metre circuit near Paris, and this had to be , circled ten times.

Do You Answer Advertisements? I have been thinking lately that it is about time that strong action was taken to put a stop to the bogus advertisement. The number of papers that carry advertisements to the effect that individuals have second-hand cycles for disposal is very great. lam not suggesting that every small advertisement offering these machines is bogus, but I do know for a fact that a considerable proportion are not legitim- ate. Hundreds of machines are turned out every year by shoddy manufacturers at a figure in the neighbourhood of 305., complete with tyres. The value of such machines can be deter- mined in the first hour of riding, but this is re- servedifor the seller, who then has a mount for sale showing signs of wear, which he plants on the first simple-minded purchaser_he can locate. My advice to buyers has always been to invest in a new cycle, even if they have to wait a little longer before they come into possession of their desire. It is only the experienced who can tell Whether a machine is a genuine second-hand article, and not a contraption built specially to cheat the public. I suggest that amateurs should always purchase their mounts from re- liable firms.

The Popularity of the Tandem. I have been impressed with the fact recently that there is evidently a coming boom with the tandem. For many years past this type of cycle has been unpopular, hut there is every indi- cation that the number of riders is increasing rapidly. One has only to take a spin along any of the main roads to note at once the fact there are three or four times as many double machines to-day as was the case a couple of years ago. For myself I cannot understand the liking that many have for the tandem. I likb to have my companion, whether male or female, by my side rather than in front or behind. One ad- vantage I can see, however, namely, that such a machine levels up the relative speed of both riders. In some instances, where single machines are used, the pace must either suit the slowest member of the party or there will be considerable lagging behing. It is equally im- portant in this case to have a suitable gear, as when single machines are considered, and I be- lieve that 64 will be found very convenient where a variable gear is not fitted.

Benzole a Commercial Proposition. One day last summer I had the pleasure of visiting some large works in Cumberland where unrefined benzoic is set free' as a by-product. Even in this crude state the spirit is bought at a low price by local motorists and used with moderate success in both cars and motor cycles. So far so good, but if benzole is to be a genuine commercial proposition. it must be more than a b. y-product. For this reason I am particularly interested in the latest process for the produc- tion of fuel oil, Szc., by the distillation of cannel oil, shale, Fee., at a low temperature. The lOw temperature is the important part of it, as other processes have all required great heat. For the proper development of the new Del Monte process, so called after its inventor, a commercial plant has been erected at Chiswick, and the motoring world may now expect tangible results in the near future. One distinct advantage is the almost inexhaustible supply of raw material available in the British Isles. Experts estim- ate the cannel reserve at 14,000,000,t0ns and oil shales at 190,000,000 tons. These represent no less than three thousand six hundred million
gallons of petrol! Another advantage of the Del Monte process is the complete utility of all by- products, thus eliminating any loss in manu- facture.

div.head: Motor 'Buses to Pay.
div.p: Motor 'Buses to Pay.

The Middlesex County Council have come to a wise conclusion in deciding to make the 'bus companies pay for every mile they run on the new road that is to be constructed between Chis- wick and the Bath-road. The road is to be five miles in length, and will cost about half a mil- lion of money. Everyone must be willing to grant that motor 'buses do a considerable amount of damage to the roads over which they travel, and, therefore, the charge of j of a penny per mile that is to be made in the future is not an outrageous figure. This is the same as is oharged in the case of trackless trolley vehicles. The committee of the County Council have the right to inspect all books belonging to the com- pany and the money will be paid every three months. The charge, moreover, will be deemed a debt due to the committee and recoverable from the company. The same charge will be levied on motor and other 'buses. The new road will fill a long-felt want and will be used largely by the 'bus company; therefore the amount that will be contributed by them will total a con- siderable sum each year.

Advertising and the Motor Industry. The past few weeks must have been excep- tionally good for all those connected with the art of advertising. I had occasion three weeks ago to say something with reference to the very successful light car trials that were held in the early part of May in Yorkshire. If one can believe all that one reads in the advertisements in the technical and daily Press one must come to the conclusion that success was mainly due, not to the special cars themselves, but to the fact that certain proprietary articles were used. We read to-day of someone's tyres, another's lubricating oil, and the special motor spirit of &third. I suppose that it is only natural that makers of these various commodities should take every opportunity of advertising their goods, but one certainly does grow just a little weary of the claims that are made by them. I think , it is a pity that the sporting element does not enter a little more into these contests. They would then make a greater appeal to the average person.

div.head: CYCLISTS' NOTE BOCK.
div.p: THE CYCLISTS' NOTE BOCK.
Some Modern Pleasantries That Are to be Avoided.
CHESHIRE REST HOUSES.-15.

Mrs. PoHitt's, Rose Cottage, Knolls Green, Mobberley.—Mobberley is one of the most pictur- esque villages in all,Cheshire, as it owns some big hills, some awful cobbles and setts, some beautiful houses and gardens, and can tie its roads in a knot almost as well as Dolgelley or Knaresborough. The direct road to Knolls Green is through Knutsford, Cross Town and Mobberley Village, but a much easier way is to take the Chelford road to about a quarter of a mile past the Duncow Inn. At the 011erton cross roads turn left as if towards Wilmslow. Another left turn at Brook Farm takes us to Warford House, where a third turn to the left brings us in less than a mile to Rose Cottage and tea. The cottage is surrounded by a flower and fruit garden, and is covered with roses and laburnum and barberry. All the roses sold add to the contents of .the missionary box, a worthy object in these days of unfair criticism. Twenty members of the Warrington Wesleyan Cycling Club raided this beautiful spot on \ Saturday, arriving by the above route at half-past four. Tea was served in the big wooden tent, and the attack was altogether a success. The tea was brought in in one of those big teapots with three handles; one behind as usual, one for the lid as usual, and one in front for the other hand to hold. Such a machine gets the young fellows to work, and needs more muscle to work it than turning- a tea-urn tap. The return journey was , taken round Tatton Park, by Ashley Station, Bollington, and 'Lymm, thus making a com- plete circuit of this, the largest of all the Che- shire parks. It may be of interest to know that a cyclist who takes the shortest road round Tatton Park, without trespassing, will have made a ride of eleven miles. Even Knowsley. the next in size of local parks, can lie circled by less than a ten-mile ride.

The danger is not from the conveyance itself, for as a rule the drivers are the most careful men on the road. But I would advise all cyclists, and especially men, and more espe- cially men who are riding in clubs, to give them a wide berth, particularly on Saturday nights. The half-intoxicated man who sits at the off-side is the danger. Suddenly jumping up and lean- ing over the rail he will grab at a passing cyclist's cap. This is merely his fun, for he will drop it in the road half a dozen yards fur- ther on; but if his fist, travelling 15 miles an hour, comes in contact with the other man's face, travelling eight in the other direction, the effect will be something akin to that on a man leaning out of a train and catching a bridge with his head. Of course: the law can be invoked, but the principle holds good here, "Prevention is better than cure."

div.head: DING-DONG TINKLES.
div.p: DING-DONG TINKLES.

What? Not heard of the cyclist who was bom- ' barded with cheeses? Well, here it is. Wyle Cop, one of the most hilly streets in Shrewsbury, was the scene of an amusing inci- dent yesterday. A lurry laden with cheeses was being driven up the cop when a number of the cheeses fell off, and, careering down the hill, ran into a cyclist, who was promptly knocked off his machine. He was injured ao the result of the fall.—" Daily News," Wednesday, June 10.

In answer to W.K.F.—The unpaced record from Land's End to John o' Groats is held by H. Green, who rode it on a Raleigh feather- weight fitted with a Sturmey-Archer tricoaster. The ride of 837; miles was completed at 1.50 a.m. on July 30th, 1908, having taken 2 days 19 hours 50 minutes. This was 2 hours 50 minutes lower ' than the previous record. I remember the Raleigh people issued a pretty booklet about this splendid ride. You might ask for it at an agent's.

div.head: TAR SPLASHES AND THEIR REMOVAL.
div.p: TAR SPLASHES AND THEIR REMOVAL.

Road construction being what it is, motorists at this time of the year are usually faced with two alternatives—clouds of dust or the evil aris- ing from freshly-sprayed tar. The second is, perhaps, to be preferred, but where insufficient care has been taken to cover the dust destroyer with a layer of granite chippings the coachwork , of one's car is liable to considerable damage. The removal of tar splashings should be taken in hand as soon as possible since tar quickly hardens and then cannot be removed without detriment to the varnish. There is no better agent than butter, which disscilves the tar very well. It should be applied carefully on a piece of rag with a slow, circular motion, as coach- work easily scratches. If one application is in- sufficient another rag and more butter will generally bring about the desired result. When properly applied, this simple method should remove all traces of splashings, without leaving the slighest mark or stain on the most delicate varnish. Of course, in such places as the inside of mudguards, where appearance is of secondary importance, there is no need to go to any such trouble. A knife or other sharp instrument soon removes the offending tar, and, if necessary, a coat of quick-drying enamel can easily be applied.

them with their locality fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, or even ten years ago, and You will understand how the army that goes in search of renewed health and strength has grown Tastes in holidays differ, like tastes in all things mundane. One man prefers to rush off to a big town by the sea, where all is life, gaiety and hustle; another prefers to get away to the country and hide himself for a spell in loneli- ness that brings the complete cl-fange and rest for which he has longed during the preceding 11 months; a third takes a middle coarse, and enters upon the delights of one of the many smaller seaside places which combine the quali- ties of restfulness and the advantages of the seaside town.

There are those who prefer the country, and especially the hilly country, for their annual jaunt. But whatever we desire or require in the way of holiday accommodation, we are now in the fortunate position of having a whole world conspiring to make us happy, so far as the giv- ing of facilities for enjoyment can make us happy.

div.head: HOME oR ABROAD?
div.p: HOME oR ABROAD?

One of the earliest matters to be settled is: Shall the holiday be taken in our own land or shall we go afield—because the nations of the earth are practically at our feet? It is, perhaps, a good plan, apart from the question of mere patriotism, to make sure of seeing most of what there is to be seen and en- joyed at home before entering upon the more ambitious foreign journeys. An argument against this is that you may never get abroad in such conditions, because there is so much at home that equals or surpasses anything that can be discovered overseas, that life is too short to ex- haust our native stores.
OUR UNRIVALLED CITIES. . Assuming that we are oat for sight-seeing,

in the list of places to visit. An American, singing the praises of a world-wide tour, thirty or forty years ago, had much to say of Dublin. " Moreover," he said, "this [Sackville-streeti is the great promenade of Dublin, and it has often been stated that nowhere can there be seen more beautiful women than one may meet here on a pleasant afternoon. For if a ' real old Irish gentleman' is one of the most agreeable of acquaintances and one of the truest and warm- est of friends, so Irish ladies are not only charming in form and feature, but remarkably attractive from a rare sembination they exhibit of high breeding and dignity, together with a quick sympathy and warm-hearted impulsive- ness, which no mere uvering of conventionality can ever quite concegr"

Paris .with its Boulevardes, its monuments of revolutions, its military triumphs and humilia- tions, is at our doors. But shall we to Paris before we have explored that greater and, from our standpoint, more enchanting city of London, in which, all our national and imperial life centres and has its source? There are in Lon- don more Roman Catholics than in Rome 7 more Scotsmen than in Edinburgh, more Irishmen than in Dublin. Here are towns within a town almost without number, and the most wonderful collection of buildings in the world—either from ' an historic, governmental, ecclesiastical, com- mercial, or any other point of view. The domain of Dickens has a charm that English- men and Englishwomen are quite unable to resist.

Edinburgh, which is often compared with Athens—and even then the compliment is held to lie on the side of Athens—has all the attrac- tions that the tourist or pleasure or health seeker can hope to find concentrated in its noble self. Arthur's seat, Holyrood, are here with buildings which make us live over again the pages of history or the scenes described by the great writer whose monument, " Scott's Monu- ment," stands singular among all such tributes to genius by his people in the middle of Princes street, the finest thoroughfare in Europe. Dublin, another of our great cities, ranks high

div.head: PLEASURE NEAR HOME.
div.p: PLEASURE NEAR HOME.
If our towns and cities can provide us with rivals to the best the world has to offer, our countryside, our picturesque scenery, our "spas', and our seaside resorts know no superior.

Do we want historic ;;;-ciations that take us down the ages, as far as we need go for any practical or sentimental reason, with attractive modern environment? We have them at our very doors. Chester, the ancient city on the Dee, that sheltered Csar's legions, and gives us proof of the fact to this very day, is only twenty miles away. Americans cross the Atlantic to "do" Europe, and make Chester their first call- ing place. We do not think quite so much of Chester—it is too close at hand! Do we want to go farther afield? Meeting this desire and still near enough to be reached in a few minutes or hours, we have the equivalent of almost every celebrafed place on the earth. The man who pines for Switzerland and cannot afford the time or the means should betake him- self to the beauties of Derbyshire, or if the

Rope and bar play a great part in the apparatus used. In golf too, the arms are the chief centres of muscular activity. The legs, which are the limbs most naturally exercised in the ordinary circum. stances of life, can perform much work with- out fatigue, because they possess powerful muscular masses, in the swing they must co- operate with the muscles of the spine and pelvis to maintain equilibrium. Not only the vertebral column, but shoul- ders, neck, head, and hands are active, and the general increase of exertion is involunt- arily preceded by increased irOalation—na- ture providing a largeer supply of oxygen to substitute that which is used up by the mus- cular contraction. Exercise inducing re- spiration, the general circulation and the quality of the blood improve, so that the i brain n its turn becomes better nourished, an4l its power of action enlarged. The inti- mate relation between brain and muscle, and their co-ordination by the will, whose facul- ty is of a psychic order, is often forgotten. SKILL NEEDED BEFORE STRENGTH. Over-exertion with its resultant fatigue, can produce nervous exhaustion, but if many trained and pofessional athletes are stupid it is because they make no efforts towards mental cultivation, and not because exercise lessens their powers in this direction. We call those difficult gymnastics which need rather a clever co-ordination of muscles than a vast quantity of physical force. They usually require attitudes to which one is un- accustomed; new movements which the limbs have never before practised. Needing very Ad good example is the jump of clown who has to measure great precision of movement they involve ra- ther an intellectual operation in their ma- teriale; athned a action.cersotbi estimate an at e distance and forc and in whose performance sensibility and judgment. are dominant factors. Golf is essentially an exercise of skill and applied strength,' rather than of muscular force. Whatever a man's strength is, he will not succeed at first. All the energy he throws into muscular efforts cannot make up for the want of practice, be- cause skill is more needed than strength. Automatism is not possible in this game al- though perfect play is described by the golf scribe as machine-like and mechanical. The which correct attitudes and successful effort of will and work of muscular co-ordina- tion,

the game, and even if he never attains to great heignts, aria never carries on any ceps, he will have found health and pleasure on the links. In most cases he will find himself growing so keen on his game that there will be no trouble about getting the prescribed daily amount of exercise, that which was merely a bore when represented by an object- less walk. being now eagerly welcomed. The opinion is often expressed, and doubt. less widely held, that golf is an expecsive form of recreation, but this is not the case evazywhere. In many country c:ubs the membership and entry fee are extremely mo- derate, while the cost of clubs and balls with the service of a caddie do not reach any very high figure. Systems of physical develop.. ment are not learnt for nothing, and there are appliances to be bought too, so that if it comes to money, the real question to be de- cided is in what way it shall be spent, and surely if one style of spending can be coupled with keen pleasure, that is the best way.

AN INVALUABLE NERVE TONIC. Many people who live lonely lives suffer a good aeal from nervous disorders and such people if they consult a physician are almost invariably to.d to engage in some form of ex- ercise which will call the muscles into play, and take the mind off the nerves which have grown to insist upon more attention than they are entitled to. FOr such golf is really an invaluable tonic; it will provide exercise for every muscle of the body, calling into play one after the other, but never over- straining any, and better than all it will pro- vide distraction for the mental faculties. While pl.aying all worries and self-conscious- ness engendered by loneliness are put aside; there is no past, there is no future, only the healthful, invigorating present. 'Nor does the beneficial effect of the game pass entire- ly awcaayllson forleathvingallthtehelipnokwsers of the mind, The effort of from worry or unstrung by overwork. play judgment, coolmess, restraint, dedibeaatdon and perseverance, and this very effort, con- stantly good effect o n ad, c the n which r o t ist sbaufierhina;:e om a In taking exercise in most ordinary forms the lonely man is unable to get away from his loneliness, in other words his mind still continues to occupy itself with the cares and worries of business, but let him once take up golf and he will find that he has no difficulty in detaching himself from his troublesome companions; his whole attention will be given to the game, and this whether he is a good ylayer. or the veriest duffer. The gains over lie will come fresh to his work.
