div.head: OUR ANNUAL REST.
div.p: OUR ANNUAL REST.
Continued from Page 4.

wished for change, men to whom custom has indeed been second Nature, and have come almost to love each brick and stone that formed the narrow boundaries of their daily walks; even they with the hand 9f death upon them have been known to yearn at last for one short glimpse of Nature's face; and, carried far from the scenes of their old wins and pleasures, have seemed to pass at once into a new state of being. . . . The memories which peaceful country scenes call up are not of this wurld, nor of its thoughts or hopes." How can we conjure up a more inviting picture of an enduringly profitable holiday than reflecting upon a visit to Buckingham- shire, standing in the village churchyard of Stoke Poges, where Gray heard the curfew toll the knell of parting day, and was inspired to write the immortal lines—
Beneath those rugged elms, that yew-tree's shade, Where heaves the turf in many a moulder- ing heap, . Each in his narrow cell for ever laid, The rude forefather's of the hamlet sleep.
Perhaps in this neglected spot is laid Some heart once pregnant with celestial fire; Hands that the rod of Empire might have swayed, Or waked to. ecstacy the living lyre.

What 'better than visit Stratford-on-Avon, which gave us Immortal Shakespeare, who " exhausted worlds and then imagined new," and left such an impression upon his people and his neighbourhood that Warwickshire is often described as Shakespeareshire? It is no use pining for fresh air and the sweet fields on the eve of death; let us take them and enjoy them while it is yet day. • On the other hand, the man or woman whose life is cast in quiet places should see the other side of the picture of life as it can only be seen in populous places.

div.head: ALONE, OR IN COMPANY?
div.p: ALONE, OR IN COMPANY?

Circumstances and inclination rule here as in other directions. The family man who sees all too little of his family during the year will take a delight in having the whole circle round him for awhile; those who are always together may find it congenial to take separate holidays. Those who, with or without family, having a liking for loneliness, will go upon their way rejoicing; those who prefer company will admit sharers in their experiences.

div.head: AN IMPORTANT POINT TO ALL
div.p: AN IMPORTANT POINT TO ALL

Whether an intending traveller expects to go far or near in his (or her) pursuit of relaxation and pleasure; whether he goes alone or with battalions; whether he goes to the city, the seaside, or the country, he will in one respect be on common ground with all the rest of his holiday-making fellows. He (and especially she) must be equipped in every way consistent with the resources available. The outfit should be carefully considered before the journey starts. To look smart personally—in dress and all its accessories—on holiday when we really live for ourselves and not for others, as Charles Lamb said, when he retired on a pension and found his time really his, is necessary if we are to have full benefit and enjoyment for our journeyings. But this side of the question does not, by any means, exhaust it. For example, the cyclist has many little needs that are better foreseen, and the amateur photographer requires reserves that are unnecessary when within reach of his dealer. These are only a few hints, but they will direct the reader's mind towards an all-important department of preparing for the holidays, a department to which the many advertisers in " The Examiner" to-day call special and tempting attention. W.

div.head: "TILE BEAUTIFUL WORLD I GAVE
div.p: "TILE BEAUTIFUL WORLD I GAVE
YOU."

Some years ago, in the heart of the Rocky Mountains, a gentleman encountered a French priest, his locks completely white with age. travelling apparently for pleasure. Astonished at the sight, he ventured to inquire what had induced him, at his time of life, to go so far from home.

"'Tis very easily exnlained," replied the priest; "six months ago I was apparently about to die. One night I dreamed that I was already in God's presence, and that He spoke to me these words: My child, how did von like the beautiful world I gave you to dwell in?' I an- swered nothing; in fact, I was too mortified to answer. For think of it I, who had preached for fifty years continually of a 'better world,' had never examined this at all. Awaking from my dream, I made a vow to God, that if He gave me back my health, I would devote some months at least to seeing and admiring His works. So here I am, making a tour of the world."
IR, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914.

div.head: GOLF GYMNASTICS.

Gymnastics are usually understood to mean a systematised exercise for develop- ment of the inuscles. Any bodily movement is exercise, and a oystematic gymnastic ac- tion is found more or less in all athletic ex- ercises and games. The hygienic value of ex- ercise is no longer. questioned. Experience has proved its good effect on the lungs, blood, digestive and locomotive organs. Thc nervous system and the mind are influenced through it, and the surgeon and "beauty " doctor alike pl3scribe muscular movement to produce health, strength and loveliness !

WORK FOR ALL THE MUSCLES. In golf nearly al: the muscles of the body are brought into play. The muscles of the arms are stretched forward, sideways, and backward in the swing. There are lateral trunk movements, and those of the shoulder blades, head, neck and legs. civilised rich class ought to be foremost in seeking to cure it." In the light of the cl6ar-defined issues that are raised by the -workers, and on their behalf by the Liberal party, the specifics of the Tory party are revealed in all their glaring quackery. Their 'principal and only, " cure" for uplifting the working-classes is Tariff Reform. That is, they would make the food and the clothing of the work- ing-classes dearer in order to raise wages! But would they raise wages? These , is as - much 'muddle-headed thinking on this subject as upon that of taxing unlimited wealth in private hands. When commodities are dear demand drops away, a short demand means less work, less work means fewer workmen employed, and the fewer the men needed the smaller the wages they can command. That is the " a.b.c. of econbmics. The pro- tected manufacturer might get his wages raised, but that is another ques- tion. We are indebted to LORD WILLOUGHBY DE BROKE for a thorough- going definition of the policy of his side. Mr. BONAR I_,AIAT has said that Tariff Reformers are not Protectionists and also that food taxes are "off." But LORD WILLOUGHBY, addressing the Women's Tariff Reform Association last month, moved a resolution expres- sing "unswerving adherence to Fiscal Reform as the first constructive work of the Unionist party." and said "At the next election . . . it would be a choice between Cobdenism, on the one side, and what he would call Protection on the other side. Theft leaders must be given a free hand to deal with the fiscal system in whatever way they thought proper but it did not seem to him that a one-sided one- legged policy of Tariff Reform would be much good, andsif they intended to frame a tariff that attempted to exclude agriculture from its scope, they might save themselves the trouble, because it would not wash." The Tariff Reforming ladies raised "loud cheers," which was natural., We always thought Tariff Reform [without food taxes • would be a one-legged sort of arrangement, and that pretences to the contrary won't wash. We are glad of corroboration in high places. Tariff Reform is impossible with the agricultural interests left out ; it is also , impossible with those interests left in. The Tories are in the same hopeless mess regarding Ireland. They speak in the name of Ulster when they know that more than half of Ulster is Nationalist. Not only' so, but we have such declarations as Mr. F. E. SMITH'S that "Ulster is armed, and purposes to resist by force of arms the passage of this Home Rule Bill unless and until it receive the support of the people of England." That is, "Unionists " who deny the' right of self-government to Ireland, but are willing to separate Ulster from the rest of the' country claim that England must be allowed to veto the desires of Ireland. If the Tory party require the "support of the people of England "at the next election they will have to come out of the clouds and tell the people what they really mean.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914.

OUR BEFOGGED OPPONENTS. - It is a question whether we ever had in history such a befogged party as the Tory party of the present day. We recently had the spectacle of Mr. JOYNSON-HICKS saying that the Budget proposals would make him repair one of his motor cars this year instead of buying a new one. This, he argued, would hit the worker, as the money spent on car-building would be with- drawn to the extent of his economies ; upon luxuries. He forgot the material point that the taxes he pays on his wealth will go in paying for the neces- saries of those in a lower grade than his own luxurious class, and will be the cause of making far more work for the people than his new car would have done. Then we have LORD ESHER drawing attention to the loss the retainers of the rich may sustain under Lloyd Georgian methods, and entering a plea for the gardeners, servants and other poor persons who share the „wealth of their employers. This is a kind of special pleading which, like the new motor car, is quite beside the mark. No sane CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, would aim at gratuitously and needlessly upsetting any arrange- ment without finding more than even compensation for the disturbance. Mr. LLOYD GEOHGE is beginning that re-Organisation of conditions that will regenerate our whole social system, and the nation as a whole will gain by the slight displacements that may take place, if any. -For our part we believe that Mr. JOYNSON-HICKS'S new car and LORD ESHER'S Servants will be quite safe, in spite of the exertions of Mr. LLOYD GEORGE"- on behalf of those legions who can scarcely afford to breathe in a land that can we!l afford Motor cars and servants. If our friends could Only under- stand the trend of the times in which they live they would recognise the necessity of lending a helping hand M the task suggested by the Progres- sives of the country—or a similar task. " The process," as "The Westminster „ Gazette " succintly points out, "has been in the main one of diversion from the luxuries , fund to the necessaries fund, and if it has entailed some cur- , tailment in expenditure on gardens ' and 'pleasure-houses it. has meant increased expenditure on food, cloth- ing, 'and medical aid for the poor. Fifty years ago the State was content to sweep up after its rich people and . captains of industry. They went their way, employed whom they would and how they. would, and the State came - on the scene afterwards with the work- house, the infirmary, or the out-relief dole, for those who had gone under or had been used for half a week 'and left to shift for themselves the other half, at the convenience of their employers. That was Said to be it was the State need i do or ought:to do, f t was not to inter- Sere with the laws of Nature. In these days we have a new conception of an on-lered and organised State in which all classes are called upon to co-operate according to their means. We have learnt th-at the piling-up of wreckage, and leaving it to chance or fate, is a clarigerthis as well as a discreditable condition. An educated working- class will not be reconciled to it; and a . '

TOWN PLANNING. There was a most curious discussion at the Town Council on Tuesday evening. Since the Town Planning Act was passed there has been a great deal of plunging in the dark by our local administrators, and the Street Improve- ment Committee, who have the matter in hand, recommended that Alderman Bennett, their chairman, and Councillor Pemberton, accom- panied by two officials, should be a deputation to interview the Local Government Board, "with regard to the scheme and as to the posi- tion of the Corporation Under the Town Plan- ning Act." They also reported that they had resolved to give notice that any persons build- ing houses in excess of 20 to the acre pending the adoption of the scheme would "do so at their own risk, having regard to section 58 of the Town Planning Act." These were fairly well specified subjects, but under each head the merits of the Act were discussed, with the re- sult that there was much stray and irrelevant talk. The proposed deputation was described as one-sided, though it is difficult to see how people could be one-sided in the seeking of information of this kind. A stand was, made lagainst the proposal to limit the number of houses to 20 to the acre, but, as Councillor Haw- thorn pointed out, that means 100 persons to the acre, and anything more dense would mean the deliberate perpetuation of sltimdom. Coun- cillor Wilkinson' stated that houses could not be built upon this scale with land costing £BOO or £9OO an acre. We want fewer houses per acre, that is clear. Cheaper land to make it possible is wanted, that is also clear. , The land reform that will give these cheaper facilities is on the way—that has been made clear at the campaign of the last three weeks.

CERTAIN TO COME. A suggestion was made that there could be no interference if the Act were not adopted locally, but Alderman Bennett assured the Council that Mr. Herbert Samuel, the new President of the Local Government Board, was very keen on tthoismyquoefricstioen; and would probably make the application of the Act compulsory. "I come Mr. Samuel recently said, "with the profound conVietion that there is no work being done in England at this time which is of greater importance than that which provides for the future development of our towns." He looks with admiration upon the state of things that exists in our few garden cities, and exclaims what a different outlook upon life the people generally would have could they only live in such conditions. So that the substitu- tion of Samuel for Burns will only make town

div.head: WORKING MEN AND TIIE INFIRMARY.
div.p: WORKING MEN AND TIIE INFIRMARY.

The Working Men's Infirmary Committee have been passing through difficult tithes, but perseverance in 'a good cause has carried them through. At a well-attended meeting of the committee on Wellnesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. George Walker, it was re- 'ported that the deadlock at Pearson and Knowles' had ended„ and that subscriptions would be forthcoming in the future almost as in the past. The committee are engaged for the moment on arranging for the two open-air musical festivals that are to be given this sum- mer in Bank Park, and the excellence of tbe programmes to he submitted by the Musical Society and the town choirs should ensure large attendances and bumper takings. Next Satur- day the Mayor will be "at home" at the Town hull to the members and their lady friends, a public recognition that will establish a worthy precedent. Ale. Chairman of the Committee, Alderman Burton, who attended during the later stages of the meeting, was aceorded quite an ovation in honour of his recent celebration of his golden wedding and in appreciation of his long-standing services to the 'committee.

div.head: CHESHIRE SOCIETY IN LONDON.
div.p: CHESHIRE SOCIETY IN LONDON.

The formation of a society to be a centre for Cheshiremen in London has been successfully carried through, and an. inaugural meeting for the election of officers for the year Will be held at the Holborn Restaurant, W.C., on Monday, June 22nd.‘ Mr. Yerburgh, M.P. for Chester, whose association with the county dates from 1886, will be one of the speakers; and the Duke of Westminster will be elected the first president of the society. There is a long list of represen- tative Cheshire names among those who have joined the society, including Brocklehurst, Dixon, Groves, Greenall, Latham, Newton, Potts, Smale, Sykes, Verdin, and there are many others who, like Mr. Yerburgh, have been adopted by the shire of 1116 "chief of men." Tickets for admission to the meeting may be obtained from Mr. C. W. Hill, 53, Riffel-road, Cricklewood, NAV., the hon. secretary.

• INSURANCE COMMITTEEMEN'S HALF- CHOWN. "Much ado about nothing is probably the way Shakespeare would have described the agitation displayed by the Warrington Insur- ance Committee over the proposal of the Insur- ance Commissioners to pay 2s. 6d: for attending meeting to .each member who resides two miles frem the 'meeting-place. .The original idea which emanated from Warrington was 7s. per meeting, although One member " tipped " the most likely' rate at 25.. ed., and he has Proved a reliable tipster. What seems to be in the minds of the Commissioners is that the half-crown should not be actual pay for work, and on that point we hardly think the members of the' Warrington Insurance Committee. are out for hard cash, but an allowance for travel- ling jexpenses, although they unfortunately used the word remuneration. If our reading is correct, 2s. Gd. is not a bad allowance for travelling expenses. The printed resolution to be sent to the Commissioners may have the effect of clearing up the difficulty. We cannot believe that the Insurance Committee are out for pay, or that they are so worked that pay is necessary. Many members of the Council, between Council and .committee meetings, put in more service on behalf of the public, and they have not even had the chance to discuss a proffered half-crown.

div.head: TANNERS' STRIKE.
div.p: TANNERS' STRIKE.
800 Men "Down Tools "in Com- plicated Dispute.
SOME MISUNDERSTANDINGS.

With dramatic suddenness about 800 tanners in the Warrington district "downed tools" on Tuesday, with the result that at present the majOrity of the yards are practically idle. A large mass meeting was held the same after- noon, but in an interview with Mr. Edward Ormsby, the general secretary of the Liverpool Branch of the Tanners' Union, "The Examiner" representative could only ascertain that the strike was unofficial. On Wednesday it was stated that the men were discontented with the agreement drawn Up last September, but it was said that the trouble had been brought to a head by the action of the masters regarding the South American hides. The men contend that when the settlement was arrived at an assurance was given that there should be no reductions of ex- isting prices, but they now claim that some of the masters had tried to find ways of enforcing reductions. The men object to the South Ameri- can hides being placed in the same category as Continentals for that meant a reduction of id. per hide. On Wednesday afternoon tbe Co-operative Hay was again filled for a mass meeting, over which Mr. IL' Harrison, organising secretary of the Tanners' Union, presided. Mr. E. Ormsby spoke.

The Chairman intimated that the strike could practically be said to be officially recognised, although the sanction of the Executive Com- mittee had to be obtained, but they could see no difficulty in that, as six of the members were concerned in the dispute. The Secretary said that the employers had been making preparations for a strike, for at various yards in Warrington they had ceased putting hides in last week, and even in some cases .a fortnight ago. He was not surprised that the-men had taken the reins in their own hands, for the agreement said that no distinc- tion should be made between unionists and non- unionists.

The men decided to demand full recognition of the union and increases in wages to all grades of tannery workers. This programme has been submitted to the Executive Committee. Pickets have been stationed at various yards and the men have marched in a body to the works of other tanning firms to persuade the workers to join the ranks of those now out on strike.

div.head: AN UNAUTHORISED STRIKE.
div.p: AN UNAUTHORISED STRIKE.
Can the Parties Come Together to Settle?

The unfortunate feature of this dispute, so far as it has gone, is the unauthorised nature of the strike, inasmuch as the men had already ; consented in an agreement to a fortnight's notice on either side. In their own interests men who are striving for what they consider to be their,rights should see that they stand-on The strongest possible ground. Here they struck without, co-operating with their union,, and so deprived themselves of that moral and material support to which they are entitled. We have heard that a letter has been received by the Secretary of the Tanners' Federation from the Secretary of the Tanners' Union 'lntl- mating that his committee had condemned the men's action in coming out without notice, and stating that they offered their good offices to bring about a settlement. This appears to contradict the rumour that the union has made the strike official, and in- tendS' to give strike pay to unionists and non- unionists alike. The next few days will prob- ably clear up this apparent contradiction. It is to be hoped that both sides will direct their best endeavours towards a settlement. Haring made extensive inquiries it appears to us that there are misunderstandings on both sides that could be rectified under the machinery that is set up by the agreement that already exists between the parties. It is because of' these Palpable misunderstandings that we re- frain from going into the questions at issue. They are technical trade points which cannot be discussed in an esparto manner. On the other hand they seem capable of adjustment if the parties go to work in the right way and , : ' •,;e.

div.head: JUNE 13, 1914.
div.p: NOT FIVEPENCE AN HOURILOCAL WEDDINGS.
Insurance Committee and the Pay
Offered to the Members.
MAYOR'S SCATHING COMMENT.

Scathing comments about the niggardly re- muneration offered to members of Insurance Committees by the Commissioners administer- ing the Insurance Act were made at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Insurance Com- mittee in the Town Hall on Thursday evening. Dr. Joseph presided. The scheme of Lie local committee was 7s. 6cl. per meeting, bi.,; now the Commissioners have presented a model scheme under which the re- muneration is fixed under several restrictions at 2s. 6d. To earn this. the members, it was said, had to work eight hours on committee business, and must reside at least two miles away from the place of meeting.
" INQUISITORIAL AND VEXATIOUS." The minutes of the Finance Sub-committee stated:—

" The Commissioners" model scheme with re- spect to payment to members of the committee of subsistence allowance and compensation for loss of remunerative time' was considered, and after some discussion it was resolved: - " That the Clerk write the Commissioners, pointing out that the remuneration named in the model scheme is totally inadequate, and the restrictions and ,conditions laid down are un- necessarily inquisitorial and vexatious.' " Councillor Dr. Joseph was asked to put this view before the Executive Council of the National Association of Insurance Committees at the first opportunity."
The Mayor, THE MAYOR INDIGNANT. moving the confirmation of the minutes, said think the model scheme sug-

-- gested by the CommissionerS is nothing but an insult to any intelligent person 1,1.ri0 operates on the committees. To offer anyone, however menial, 2s. 6d. for any absence from home up to eight hours is degrading in the extreme. To shy the least, the Commissioners ought to under- stand we do not get people from the workhouse to attend on these important committees. The subject is a debatable one, but in any case we ought to reject, with all the emphasis in our power, such an insulting scheme. (Hear, hear.) In their model scheme, the Commissioners state that subsistence should not be paid to anyone whose place of residence is within two miles of the meeting-place. Therefore, I take it that unless we purposely go out to the country to hold our meetings we, in Warrington, would not receive this magnificent salary. I think Dr. Joseph will be very emphatic in his remarks upon this point when it comes before the execu- tive. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Wadsworth seconded and agreed entirely with what the Mayor said.

THE 7/6 SALARY. Mr. Brocklehurst, while agreeing with the vexatious nature of the proposals, thought the way was still left open for the Commissioners to reconsider the matter. He did not think any- one on that committee anticipated that they would get the 7s. 6d. or 10s. per meeting, and if they would remember, he said at the time that 2s. 6d. would be as much as they would get. He thought the Clerk should write to the Commis- sioners pointing out that the remuneration was inadequate, and the restrictions vexatious, and that they should re-Consider the matter. The Chairman According to the terms I do not think the scheme applies to any member of this committee, as no member lives two miles away from our meeting-place. The Mayor: We could arrange for the com- mittee meetings to be held at Dutton 'Work- house. (Laughter.) - Mr. Delaney thought if ever there was a good case for the total abolition of the Commis- sioners it was to be found in that scheme. Mr. Brocklehnrst moved that Fite matter be referred back to the Finance Sub-committee for further consideration.

div.head: NOT A LIVING WAGE.
div.p: NOT A LIVING WAGE.

-.-- - - - - Alderman Bennett did not think the resolu- tion shut the door on future re-consideration. The remuneration was less than sd. an hour, and yet they heard a lot about a living wage. Alderman James Evans: The Commissioners evidently consider it a fair wage question. (Laughter.) Alderman Bennett said he sometimes thought that those who governed them from London had neither eyes to see nor ears to hear, judging from the way their requests were ignored. Unless they got the governing power out of the hands of these people in London, England would never be properly governed. (Hear, hear.) Finally Mr. Brocklehurst withdrew his amendment, and the Mayor gave notice that the whole matter be re-considered at the next meeting. The minutes were then unanimously adopted. MATERNITY BENEFIT. •

The meeting discussed a proposal to be raised at the meeting of the Association of Insurance Committees that the administration of the maternity benefit should be transferred to the Public Health Authorities. The Mayor said they as an Insurance Com- mittee could not agree to any other authority taking the work out of their hands. If the work was to be taken from the approved societies it should pass on to the Insurance Committees. Mr. Bibby feared if the administration of the maternity benefit was taken out of the hands of approvedlisocieties it would lead to delay in pay- ing the benefit., _ _ _
Dr. JosePli—;nid he would Ntatch the matter closely at the conference to be held by the Association.

div.head: BOWLERS' GOLOSHES.
div.p: BOWLERS' GOLOSHES.
Players Object to the Charges.

There was a brief yet pointed discussion at the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday on the question of the charges for goloshes, which bowlers have to wear upon the municipal bowl- ing greens. The matter came up on the follow- ing minute of the Parks Committee : " A petition from users of the Municipal Bowl- ing Green, Liverpool-road, protesting against the charge for use of goloshes, was read.—Re- solved That the Committee cannot see their way to reduce the charge already fixed." Councillor BROADHURST thought one reason for the Committee's decision not to abolish the charges was because they had no knowledge of what even a half- penny meant to a working man. He thought the first charge of 21d. was too much for a working man to pay, and a halfpenny was too high a charge for the use of a pair of goloshes. on public-house greens men could play a whole day for a charge of threepence, yet the Council charged 2id. for the .first hour and lid. for the next. He thought the Parks Com- mittee should modify the charges. He moved that the matter be sent back for further con- , sideration.

Councillor WILSON seconded, and thought the restriction in regard to wearing goloshes should be abolished. Dr. Josßpi; supported the amendment, although he did not think it would be wise to abolish the use of goloshes, as the greens were damaged by hob-nailed boots and acids from the boots of iron and chemical workers. Councillor Gonna said the greenkeepers at present had hard work in keeping the greens in order, and they should not put obstacles in the greenkeepers way. Councillor PEMBERTON thought no charge should be made for the goloshes. Councillor DiciaNsox said the goloshes cost £4O, and they ran about 3s. per pair. The com- mittee were not seeking a profit out of them. If the bowlers bought their own goloshes they would have nothing to pay. (Laughter.) The amendment was defeated by 11 votes to two.

div.head: CRAMPTON-FLETCHER.
div.p: CRAMPTON-FLETCHER.

A very pretty wedding took place at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Thursday afternoon, when Miss Mabel Crampton, only daughter of Mr. Thomas Crampton, of Victoria-road, Grap- penhall, became the wife of Mr. Charles Eric Longsdon Fletcher, son of Mr. William H. Fletcher, of London. The bridegroom, a Bachelor of Arts of London University, is a member .of H.M. Customs and Excise Office staff, London. . _ _

_ The bride, who entered the church leaning on the arm of her father, looked charming in a dress of ivory satin charmeuse, trimmed with chiffon and lace, with a Court train; her'Veil was of embroidered Brussels net, with orange blossom. She carried a magnificent sheaf of lilies, the gift of the bridegroom. _ .

Mr'. W. 11. Payton presided -at the organ, and "The voice that breathed o'er' Eden" having been sung by the large assembly, the ceremony was conducted in impressive manner by the Revs. J. Yonge and T. T. James. The bride was given away by her father. The bridesmaids were Misses Dora Roberts and Ethel Crampton (cousins of the bride), and were becomingly dressed in ivory chiffon taffeta, with lace hats. They carried bouquets of pale pink roses, and wore gold bracelets, the gift of the bridegroom. The duties of best man .`were perforMed by Mr. R. A. Petzsche, of Lon- don; whilst Mr. Percy Crampton, brother of the bride, and Mr. Lynn Whitehouse acted as groomsmen. The guests wore orchids, kindly presented by Alderman W. Bolton. The Wedding March resounded through the church as the happy couple departed for the Winmarleigh Cafe, where a reception was held, about 35 being present. The bride and bride- groom afterwards left for London, en route for , Devon, where the honeymoon is to be spent. The bride's travelling costume was of navy serge, and she wore a white aeroplane hat, trimmed with pink roses. Many handsome presents were received.

div.head: MOUNFIELI)-lIUDSON.
div.p: MOUNFIELI)-lIUDSON.

At Friars' Green Independent Methodist Chapel on Wednesday afternoon, the wedding was solemnised of Miss Amy Gibson Mounfield, daughter of Mrs. John Mounfield and the late Mr. John Mounfield, of Walton-road, Stockton Heath, and Mr. William Hudson, son of Mr. and Mrs. James Hudson, of '` Maythorne," Latchford Without. The ceremony was very pretty. Councillor Henshall, minister to the Connexion, 'officiated, and Mr. Ernest Wilkes played the Wedding March from "Lohengrin," and the hymn, "The voice that breathed o'er Eden" was sung. The bride, who was given away by her uncle, Mr. William Mounfield, wore a lovely •dress of cream mousseline satin, draped with pearl dew-drop net, and trimmed with Maltese lace. She carried a bouquet ‘of white roses and lilies of the valley. Her present from the bridegroom was a handsome gold brooch, set with pearls and sapphire.

The bridesmaids were the Misses Mounfield and Phyllis Brough, and Master Stuart Fell was page. Miss Mountield was dressed in pale blue satin, with over-dress of embroidered ninon. Her bouquet was composed of pink carnations. Miss Brough's dress was of embroidered muslin, and her bouquet was of sweet peas. Both bridesmaids were presented with gold bangles, by the bridegroom, whilst Master Pell received a tie-pin, set with turquoise. Mr. John W. Hudson (cousin of the bride- groom) performed the duties of best man, and the reception was held in the schoolroom attached to the chapel. Congratulatory telegrams were received from Macclesfield, Dundee, and Hamburg. After the reception the happy couple left for Beaumaris, where the honeymoon is to be spent. The bride's travelling costume was of navy serge, with hat to match.
11ir: and Mr;. lluds—o'n--.were the recipients of many beautiful and useful presents.

div.head: WORTHY BAPTIST CAUSE.
div.p: WORTHY BAPTIST CAUSE.
The Golborne-street Sale of
Work.

An enthusiastic assembly held a 'sale of work in the Golborne-street Baptist Sunday Schools on Thursday, with the object of assisting in wiping out the debts incurred by the erection of new premises adjoining the chapel. As the announcement made on the posters—" Dainty Teas: Pleasing Music: Interesting Competi- tions "—was not at all exaggerated, the pro- ceedings passed off in a very pleasant manner. The sale was opened by the Mayor (Councillor Peter Peacock), Councillor R. Henshall occupy- ing the chair. There were also present on the platform the Mayoress and the Rev. H. Ogden. The Rev. H. OGDEN made a statement, which he prefaced by an expression of gratification at the presence of the Mayor and Mayoress. They had a £l,OOO mortgage upon that building, and it had been necessary to contract the debt. Still, they "did not rush into the battle like an unthinking horse," and since the school had been built there were more scholars on the books than ever there had been before in the school's history. He hoped the visitors would be as sympathetic and generous as possible. (Applause.) In introducing the Mayor, the CHAIRMAN said that most folk in Warrington would soon have seen "His Worship," or it would be their own fault. Of all the Mayors they had had, there had never been one more anxious to associate with the people. He had just paid a visit to the Continent, all the expenses of which came out of his own pocket; so that if the rates, went up a penny in the st—and Ile hoped they would not—it would not be the Mayor's fault. (Laugh- ter.)
The Mayor was then presented with a button- hole by Olive Balmford, Phyllis Michael hand- ing one each to the Mayoress and Councillor Henshall.

div.head: "NEAR TO A BAPTIST."
div.p: "NEAR TO A BAPTIST."

"I, was something near to a Baptist," said the MAYOR, "in the days when I was a very good boy !" , Therefore, he continued, he had extreme pleasure in attending the sale. He had not a stock of stories like Councillor Hen- shall—he had never had time to attend to them —but he would say that when he went to Ger- many the Corporation trusted him to take the Mayoral chain, and that afternoon they had sent' a man with it! (Laughter.) In declaring the sale open, the Mayor thought that every man who took up the duties of Mayor should help every denomination' in the town. (Bear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: BEST OF MAYORS..
div.p: BEST OF MAYORS..

Mr. E. W N-NE Tio;E;3, in proposing a vote of thanks ,to the Mayor, Councillor Henshall, and also to the Mayoress for their presence that afternoon, believed that Mr. Peacock was the best Mayor they had ever had in Warrington; many, people had been surprised at what a good Mayor he had made. If Councillor Henshall was called upon to be Mayor some day—and he hoped he would—he would make a splendid Mayor. (11?ar, hear.) Mr. BEN Psw seconded the motion and it was carried, whereupon the MAYOR replied on behalf of all three.

Miss Annie Bate played the piano at the open- ing ceremony. Tile officials of the sale were: The Rey. H. Ogden, chairman of committee; Mr. H. Buckly, secretary; and Mr. D. Michael, treasurer. There were Congregational, Young.Ladies', Sunday School, Pound, Refreshment and Flower Stalls, the work of which was undertaken by the various sections of the church and Sunday Schools. A museum attracted considerable attention.
The receipts were 1:63, and the Minister and officers wish to express, through "The Examiner," their gratitude to the public for their generous support.

div.head: Medical Officer's Report.
div.p: Medical Officer's Report.

At a meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil on Tuesday it was decided to hold a special meeting on 24th June to discuss the Medical Officer's report. Alderman James Evans described the report as one of the most impor- tant ever presented.

Warrington Market. The market prices for Wednesday were Wheat, ss. per 7011).; oats, 25..94d. to 2s. 101 d. per 4511).; wheat straw, 275. 6d. per ton; oat straw, 275. to 28s. per ton; XX flour, 235. 3d. per 2401 b.; bran, Is. Id. per 20Ib. Wheat firm on the market, oats slightly easier, fair sup- plies offered.

Seeing By Telephone. Mr. James Mills, 9, Gladstone-street, War- rington, is engaged upon an invention by means of which persons speaking by telephone will be able to see each ' other or "receive " .photo- graphs instead bf messages. He has been successful in getting an image at one end of the instrument, rather blurred, but quite recog- nisable. He has received official encouragement sent day.

Bensey-road Telephones. Alderman Bennett, at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday, drew attention to the erection of overhead telephone wires in the residential part of Bewsey-road.—Alderman Tinnion said it was a case of "Hobson's choice," as the Post Office had more power in the matter than the old Telephone Company. The local l'ost Office engineers were endeavouring to make the wires as unsightly as possible, and were endeavouring to meet the Council's wishes in the matter.

Warrington Leaflier Trade. Trade wag very quiet last week (says the "Leather Trades Review ") and although the holiday was restricted to Monday locally there was very little life in business until towards the end of the week, when a few moderate orders came through, and the presence of a few buyers helped to improve matters. The quan- tity of leather turned over was naturally below the weekly average, but factors who visited this district last week reported that leather was going into use steadily, and anticipating that a steady run of business was likely to follow.

div.head: Progress at the Bridge. _
div.p: Progress at the Bridge. _

- - Alderman Smethurst informed the Council, at the monthly meeting on Tuesday, that rapid being made with the erection That day the last of the of frotghrie progress new rr-asb iridivge b.e T foundations had been put in. All the trouble had been in the foundations, and now he thought the bridge would rise with mushroom- like growth. He hoped the public would be able to use the bridge by Christmas, if not before then.—The Mayor was pleased to hear that the bridge wotild be finished during his term of office.—Conncillor Gough objected to the Council having to pay £2OO extra for the removal of the stones in the bed of the river.—The Mayor said that work was outside the terms of the con- tract.

div.head: Mersey-Street Widening.
div.p: Mersey-Street Widening.

At the meeting of the Council on Tuesday the Street Improvement Committee reported that the Town Clerk produced an agreement with Messrs. W. Reynolds and Co., Ltd. dated 31st December, 1839, for the setting back of their premises in Mersey-street. The Town Clerk was instructed to negotiate with the corn- for the further setting back to the pre- scribed line.—Councillor Gough asked for infor- mation as to what the cost of setting hack was likely to be.—The. Mayor: The Town Clerk is negotiating for a price and particulars will be submitted to the committee when obtained.— Councillor Gough: Before this is sanctioned I understand the members of the Council will get to know what the price is.—The Mayor: That is so.
Tramway Men's Wages.

. Dr. Joseph announced to the Council on Tues- day that the tramway ,men's wages had been increased by the Tramways Committee by a half-penny per hour. That made the Warring- ton men about the beset paid men in Lancashire and they were better paid per hour than were the members of the Insurance Committee under the Insurance Commissioners' scheme. (Laugh- ter.)—Councillor Gough aSked if the motor 'buses paid anything to the upkeep of the roads which they 'damaged.—Councillor Hawthorn said the department contributed .t 2,500 a year to the relief of the rates, and that helped to maintain the roads. They paid more than would be spent on the roads in a year.—Dr. Joseph said in addition to that the 'buses paid rates And taxes.

Monday—Progressive Labour League, Bridge Foot, 8. Wednesday—Messrs. A. H. Clive and Co.'s Property Sale, Blue 'Bell Inn, 5 p.m. Thursday—Maytr's "At Home," Town Hall,

Wesleyan Methodism in AVarrinitton. The w aqsu ahretledr at meeting Stockton Heathoftli e Wesleyann Thursday ,l i Cir- cuit evening. A large number- of friends sat rd.0"13. -11 to tea before the meeting began for the trans- action of business: The Rev. W. A. Beckett presided. Great regret was expressed that Messrs. Withinshaw and Meldrum were unable to be. present, and Messrs. Weaver and Harris were requested to act as their substitutes. The erection of the primary schoolroom at Latch- ford curtailed an expenditure of £825, of which ,R,815 was defrayed by Miss Hartley. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to the donor for her munificent gift. Sincere sympaily was ex- pressed with the Rev. J. H. Pawlyn in his ill- ness. The numerical statement showed the membership to be about the same as last quarter, but showed considerable increase dur- ing the last three years. The financial income was about equal to the expenditure.—The Revs. W. A. Beckett, E. Morgan and H. Middlewood close their term of triennial service next Con- ference and they were all very cordially thanked for their excellent service's. The circuit con- tributions to Connexional Funds indicated a good advance on the previous year. The total this year was ,t492.—The following gentlemen were nominated and elected members of the Foreign Missionary Committee: Messrs. Within- shaw, Meldrum; Upson, G. Guest, Wheatley, Harris, G. Weaver, Mellor, Sherlock and Llewellyn.—The financial proceeds of harvest festival services are to be divided between cir- cuit funds and local interests. It was resolved that the whole of the Deficiency Fund collection (not the half as hitherto) be devoted to circuit funds, and that .R 2 10s. be allowed to each place for the provision of the quarterly tea meeting.—While the committee on the Winwick Chapel case recommended trying it as an experi- ment for one year, the quarterly meeting was in favour of its immediate acceptance. The con- sideration of the Norris-street scheme was post- poned until next March, when a special meeting will be held.—The date . and arrangements for Class Leaders' Convention are to be left in the hands of Messa.s. Hall and Wheatley. The next The Rev. W. eetingis th be held at Padg suc- ceed Thompson Derry (Bury) will the Rev. W. A. Beckett, and the Rev. A. J. Morton (Grimsby) will follow tthe Rev. E. Morgan. The Rev. Hugh Williamson continues for a fourth year at Bold-street.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914.
Increased Scarlet Fever Cases.
There were 85 cases of scarlet fever in the Warrington Hospital last week. Fourteen new cases had been reported.
Detective Officer Praised.

During the hearing of a betting case at the local Police, Court on Thursday, dlr. Harry Backhouse, the defending solicitor, of Black- burn, paid a tribute to Detective-Sergeant Holland, one of the officers who made the raid. He said: "I have met him before and I can pay him a high compliment of being a sound officer."

Mayor Calls Out Fire Brigade. Last night the first of the series of false alarms to be given by members of the Fire Engine Committee to test the efficiency of the brigade was given by the Mayor and Councillor Chrimes. The alarm came from Walker's Brewery, and in less than seven minutes the brigade arrived on the scene with a full com- plement. Water tests made in the yard for some time were deemed quite satisfactory.

The Perambulator Came. • Mr. Wilfrid Rowland, 'Guild of Help secre- tary, writes: "Referring to my letter last week, I am glad to say that I have had two offers of perambulators for the family concerned. The first was promptly and thankfully accepted. I should still like to hear, however, from anyone who would care to give financial assistance. An epidemic has broken out in the home since last week, and there is need for special nourish- ment."

A Marriage Presentation. The marriage of Mr. S. Pinney, of Newlands, Latchford, who is employed by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, to Miss:Whitley, of Stretton, took place at Stretton Parish Church on Tuesday morning, and a number of the bridegroom's brother employes attended to give the happy couple a hearty send-off upon the honeymoon.— On Monday afternoon the employes at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles gave a suitable present to Mr. 'Finney,

The Week's Accidents. The three following accidents have occurred during the week, and are receiving attention at the Warrington Infirmary: Herbert Carter, ago 22, of 41, Forster-street, admitted yesterday, cut head, contusions and shock, condition satis- factory; Gilbert James Harvey, age, 23, of 30, Sharp-street, admitted Thursday, scalds on both arms, progressing satisfactorily; John Wood, age 33, of 12, Crown-street, Earlestown, ad- mitted Wednesday, fracture of spine, condition critical. The number of admissions for the week is 31, whilst the number of patients in the Infirmary is 45.

Citizens' Guild of Help. Captain Crosfield on Saturday gave a garden party to the workers of the Guild of Help at Tower House. A most enjoyable afternoon was spent in the beautiful grounds, Jnost of the guests taking a hand at bowls or running potato races. About 50 people were present. Tea was served in a marquee, and afterwards a hearty vote of thanks, moved by the Rev. W. Bracecamp and seconded by Dr. Langdale, was accorded to the host. Captain Crosfield, in replying, expressed the belief that organised personal service was never more needed than to-day. Mr. Boothroyd's band greatly added to the pleasure of the afternoon. The catering was undertaken by the Winmarleigh Cafe.

Fire Brigade Re-organisation. Alderman Burton, as chairman of the Fire Brigade Committee, submitted a new scheme, whereby one man will be always on duty at the Station, to the meeting of the Warringon Town Council on Tuesday, and he congratulated the brigade on the way they handled' the large fire which recently occurred at Bridge Foot. The motor engine had justified its purchase.—Coun- cillor Broadhurst thought they should have an experienced motor mechanic in charge of that engine, and not be dependent upon the use of the tramways mechanic. Under the present , system the motor engine was not running faster than five miles an hour.—The Mayor defended the present system and said they had now got one of the finest brigades in Lancashire, and hoped to make it, through the new scheme, still much better. It would be unnecessary and un- wise to increase the staff when they had the tramways mechanic at their disposal.—The scheme for re-organisation was unanimously adopted.

div.head: Motor Cyclists' Test.
div.p: Motor Cyclists' Test.

The Warrington motor cyclists held a 60-miles reliability test on Saturday, starting out from Stockton Heath, and proceeding through Mere- corner, Knutsford, Holmes Chapel, Congleton, Dunibers' Hill, Allgreave, Burbage, Cat-and- Fiddle, and Macclesfield, finishing up at the Dun Cow, Allerton, near Knutsford, at which about 30 members had tea. Mr. H. Jackson, whose cycle is a "Zenith Green," and Mr. W. Young, or a "21 Douglas," tied for the first place, whilst Mr. Foster finished third. The whole of the competitors seemed free from trouble, except one, whose side-car outfit had a bad burst, causing him to retire shortly after the start.

"Scottish Wedding." The wife who thought 'terse-if a widow end went through a form of introduetery marriage in Scotland with William Speed, C3rporation tram driver, 35, Wash-lane, Knutsiord-road, got no further satisfaction at the Police Court yesterday, when the summons for persistent cruelty wag dismissed.—Mr. Swallow, on behalf of Mr. Browne, appeared for Sarah Speed or Platt, 96, Knutsford-road, and Mr. Steel called two witnesses, who swore they had seen Platt in blebden Bridge six years ago, one of the wit- nesses stating that Platt had stayed at his hotel. —Mr. Swallow said there would be a summous of another nature.

The P.S.A. Great Campaign. The first Warrington meeting in connection with the P.S.A. National Campaign was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings on Thursday night. Although the number present was com- paratively small, the enthusiasm evidenced was unbounded, which augurs well for the forth- coming effort. The Rev. T. T. James occupied the chair, the address being delivered by the Rev. J. G. Gascoigne, of Manchester; the Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's, was also on the platform. Mr. Gascoigne expressed Plea- sure at seeing a Warrington vicar upon the plat- form as well as a representative of the Free Churches. The Church of England had agreed to work alongside the campaigners, and only their periodical mission had prevented the Roman Catholics doing more than wishing them God-speed. The following committee to make arrangements was appointed: Revs. T. T. James and W. Bracecamp, Mr. B. Farrar, (Wycliffe P.S.A.), Mr. W. Clegg (Watrington P.S.A.), Mr. F. Fox (Adult Schools), -Mr. J. Thorniley (Brick-street Independent Metho- dist), and ;qrs. Moores (Working Alen's Mis- sion).

div.head: Working Men and lhe N.S.P.C.C.
div.p: Working Men and lhe N.S.P.C.C.

The newly-constituted Working Men's Com- mittee of the Warrington and District Vranch of the N.S.P.C.C., of which Mr. T. Kendrick is chairman, and Mr. H. Taylor hon. secretary, is gradually adding to its representation, the desire being to embrace every organisation in the area. The formation of these committees in all parts of the country has done much to make the work of the society known and to bring to light many cases of child neglect and ill-treatment. At a recent meeting held at the 'Town • Hall it was reported that during the month of May 20 cases of.. neglect and cruelty were dealt with by the Inspector, affecting the welfare of 49 children and involving 22 offenders. Eighteen of the cases came under the head of "neglect and starvation" and two "ill-treat- ment." In two instances proceedings were taken in the Police Court, and in all 18 warn- ings were served upon the parents. Of the 20 cases, 18 were reported by the general public. In addition to these cases the officer made 131 visits of supervision and four inquiries for various branches in the country. A feature of the report was the sample cases quoted, showing the pitiable condition under which some of the children were found,. and the wonderful im- provement effected as a result of the Inspector's visit.

div.head: Fusion of Local Societies.
div.p: Fusion of Local Societies.

A second meeting; of the General Committee to consider the federation of local societies was held in the Museum Lecture Room on Wednes- day night. Mr, liade/ey presided, and there were represented the following societies: Arts and Crafts, Warrington, Literary and Philo- sophical, Philomathic, Field Club, Musical, Photographic, Municipal Officers' Association, Shakespearean, Esperanto, Caledonian, Welsh National, and the Workers' Educational Asso- ciation. The scheme as originally drawn up was slightly amended, and it was decided that it should then be forwarded to all local societies and that they should be asked to give it their best support. Those societies which support it will be asked to send two members to a meeting of the Council to be called early in the Winter Session. The amended constitution is as follows: (1) To form a federation of societies, interested in art, literature, science and philo- sophy, or any allied subject; (2) that a Council be formed, consisting of two members of each constituent society; (3) that the object of federation be to co-ordinate and stimulate the activities of various societies interested in all or any of these subjects; (4) each society to contribute to the expenses of the general feder- ation pro rata; (5) to provide, if possible, a common place of meeting, with suitable equip- ment; (6) that the federation should arrange for the publication of a handbook of Warring- ton societies 4

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. –
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. -
A SERNION-PLAY AT THE ROYAL COURT.

The interest of the Royal Court Theatre patrons has this week been concentrated upon the drama, "Mary Latimer—Nun," which is Presented in splendid fashion by Mr. W. H. Glaze's company. The beneficent woman whose name conStitutes the title of the piece, imme- diately captures the affection of the audience by her timely interventions and kind deeds. Chief of these is the transference of her fortune t "r t adre kYb Stubbs, a girl endowed with Con- s little money, in order that she may become the .wife of the 'Hon. Alfred Pierpoint; who has ever remained true to her, despite the innumerable obstacles wMch con- siderable Sy, u have been set in his path. The chief character is portrayed in masterly manner by Miss Laura Walker, and leaves nothing. to be desired in humility and unworldliness. Miss Kathleen Magee excels as "Larky," whose husband is well presented by Mr. Charles A. Baker. Humorous interludes are provided by Sam and Dicky Stubbs (Mr. Edward de Vere and Mr. Will Glaze), whilst Mr. E. H. Burton and Miss Millicent Maynard depict John and Crate Dayton very well. • "A Fool in Paradise" Next Week.-

The special attraction next week at the Royal Court Theatre will he the famous passion drama, -" A Fool in -Paradise." It will be pre- sented by Dora Eastlake and her original corn. pany, including the great emotional actor, Cecil Gray.

div.head: FINE HIPPODROME PROGRAMME.
div.p: FINE HIPPODROME PROGRAMME.

The programme provided this week by the management of the Hippodrome does it credit. Albert Weston and Nellie Lynch's American comedy skit is attended by signal success, the acting of both being Quite spirited. The Four Durhams provide high-class music with the aid of a variety of instruments, concluding with a novel march, played upon concealed instruments. The quick-change characters in " Bonnie Prince Charlie" are presented in ex- citing and finished style" by• Gertrude Bibby; and the areo-pantomimical humorists, , the Three Bros. Huxter, perform marvellous acro- batic feats in "Languid Energy," one of the company excelling in his affected languor. Some clever dancing is included in the "Electrician" comedy, given by the Haytors; whilst Nellie ' Babble and "Just a Baritone's" appearance is , greeted with well-deserved applause. The Three Siddons perform thrilling balancing feats; and Archie Glen humorously describes the days when he was a Boy Scout. All-Star Programme Next Week. The all-star programme, which will doubtless attract large audiences next week at the Hippo- drome, includes the Four Diving NorMs, in which Olga Norin, said "to have the most per- fect figure of any lady who has yet appeared on the stage," appears; Bay and Zack, juvenile comedy duo; Will Sullivan, character comedian and patterer; Chas. Santon, male soprano and double-voiced vocalist; Sinclair and Whiteford, in their new sketch, " Kitty's Hero"; the Mums Comedy Four, male vocalists, in seena, "Burglars in Harmony"; Lilly Denville, come- dienne and expert wooden shoe dancer; and the Perfection Pictures.

div.head: STAR KINEMA ATTRACTIONS.
div.p: STAR KINEMA ATTRACTIONS.
Excellent pictures at the Star Kinema House. Church-street, include "The Golden Pathway" and " The Devil's Eyes,'' first and last three days respectively of next week. '

div.head: PROTECT THE CHILDREN. To the Editor.
div.p: PROTECT THE CHILDREN. To the Editor.

- - Sir,—Will you grant _us the favour of a few lines to make an earnest appeal to the indus- trial, social and religious leaders of our town in order that the newly-formed Working Men's Committee of the Warrington Branch of the N.S.P.C.C. may be in every sense a representa- tive body? Until we came in immediate con- tact with the work we had no idea of the extent of child neglect in our midst, and certainly no knowledge of the needless suffering these help- less little ones are called upon to bear. Non- political and unsectarian, this work appeals to all, and for that reason we desire to include representatives of every section on the com- mittee. By making the objects of the Society better known and rousing the public conscience on this question of child neglect, we feel the committee is making a substantial contribution to the happiness and well-being of hundreds of little ones in our midst. We shall be pleased' to answer any inquiries. J. KENDRICK, Chairman, H. TAYLOR, Hon. Secretary. 15, Bold-street Warrington.

WATER POLO. WARRINGTO,N.'S, FINE WIN OVER WI.D,N.E.S In the Liverpool and District League,. War- rington are making themselves felt. On Tues- day evening, they won a glorious victory aver Widnes at Widnes Baths by nine goals to six. There was, a Large attendance, but a rother "scrappy" game was witnessed., Warrington were short of H. Sisson, whose place was taken by his brother Willie. C. Turner, the Warring- ton skipper., scored the first goal with a beautiful shot and he quickly added another, as also did J. Graham, R. pepper and Ince. Fairclough scored for Widnes before the interval. Pitt then scored for Widnes and Laverick and Fair- dough netted two each. Warrington's score was made up to nine by goals from L. Graham (2), and Ince (2). WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS. St. Helens were the first team to defeat War- rington this season, for at St. Helens they won by four goals to two. Warrington won the toss and defended the deep end, but were soon in trouble, Lomax scoring two goals in quick suc- cession for Coronation. Then J. Graham added one for the visitors. The game was very open, and half-time arrived with the home teem lead- ing by two goals to one. On restarting C. Turner received from S. Inoe, and soon reduced the lead. From this stage the visitors were outplayed through IT. Sisson leav- ing the water through cramp, and Walker scored two goals, the final being: St. Helens Corona- tion,four goals; Warrington, two goals.

div.head: Opposition in the Council Leads to "Scenes,"
div.p: Opposition in the Council Leads to "Scenes,"
A SUGGESTED DEPUTATION.
'lnformation that is Needed to Stop

div.head: Floundering.
div.p: Floundering.
There was a somewhat heated discussion at the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday over a deputation which proposed to go to London to interview the Local Government Board on town planning.
This deputation was to have been made up of Alderman Bennett and Councillor Pember- ton. Several members objected to their going, as they were of the one opinion.
Others contended that both sides of opinion should be represented. Still other members thought a deputation was unnecessary until the scheme had been submitted to the Council and approved.

Councillor Pemberton said that he did not want to go to London, as he could do more for the ratepayers by staying at home. He withdrew his name, but the suggestion of the Street Improvement Committee to send a deputation was carried by three votes.
There was ancther heated debate over a pro- posal that warning, be given to builders that not more than 20 houses must be erected per acre. If any built, more they did so at their own risk.
Members alleged that this was an attempt to stop building, to- frighten builders, and was really holding a pistol at their heads,
This was denied by Alderman Bennett, and it was stated that one builder had flouted the Council and threatened to build as many houses as he liked. The proposal was carried by a majcrity of one vote.

The discussion, over the deputation arose Upon the following_ from the minutes of the Street Improvement Committee: That the Chairman (Alderman Bennett), with the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor, be appointed to interview the Local. Government Board with regard to the scheme and as to the position of the Corporation under the Town Planning!Ael; that Mr. Councillor Pemberton be added to the deputation to wait upon the Local Government Board re Town Planning Scheme." INFORMATION WANTED.

Councillor lIEssuALL thought they should have some information about this deputation. Alderman BENNETT said that in a matter of such great importance as town planning they were at present more or less feeling their way towards the best solution. They felt there were various points on which the Local Govern- ment Board could give them help, ancL tiiew were anxious to do the best they could, with fairness to all the interests concerned. Councillor IlmisnALL said he would have to move that the matter be referred back. They must have more particulars as to the specific question the deputation were going to put before the Local Government Board. Ile thought they should first prepare and approve of their scheme before going to London. Many mem- bers of the Council felt very keenly on some aspects of the town planning scheme, and it was only right that when a deputation was sent it should represent those who held views on both sides of the question. It was much better to know what they wanted when they went to see the Local Government Board than to go with an open mind as that deputation seemed to be going. Councillor WILKINSON seconded.

"THE AUDACITY." Councillor GOUGH supported the amendment. He could not understand how the committee came to fix upon 20 houses to the acre, or how they had the audacity to suggest such a one- sided deputation as that proposed. All points 'of view ought to be fairly represented. There was a dearth of cottage property in the town— there were 10 applicants for each house that became empty—but if the Council imposed the stringent measures which had been attempted ! it would be impossible to get builders to specu- late in such property. It was really an attempt to stop the building of cottage property. (Hear; hear.). He thought the committee would be well advised to take the proposal back. Alderman TisNioN thought the committee ! should have said what the deputation were to do in London, and certainly the deputation should have been more representative. They knew the opinions of Alderman Bennett and Councillor Pemberton, and it was advisable the Council should know for what they were going to London. There were different opinions and the difference of opinions should be represented on the deputation. Would it not be advisable to send someone like Councillor Henshall, with an open mind? (Laughter.) Councillor Hen- shall had a mind sufficiently open to retain all that he wanted and to allow the remainder to pass through. (Laughter.) Alderman Bennett ought to see the justice of allowing someone else to have a cheap trip to London and enjoy themselves. (Laughter.)

SOUNCILLOR PEMBERTON WITHDRAWS. Councillor PEMBERTON : I withdraw my name from the deputation. Alderxuan TINNION : You are not on it yet. Councillor PEMBERTON : I refuse to go. You !cannot send me if I do not want to go. The MAYOR You can refuse to go. Councillor PEMBERTON : I shall. I have no ,wiot to gp, to London: have plefity to do here. But when I do go to London, I always attend :to, Corporation business—not like some people who look after their own pleasure. A MEMBER: Knock your name out.

Councillor PEDIRERTON said if some members took more interest in the Corporation work and in what the committee did it would be better for the town and the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) They required information, as only two schemes in the whole country had as yet been carried thaw* all their stages. There were much more important matters than the limitation of houses Oer acre—such as the construction of roads and the choice of situations for works. He, however, ventured to say, without fear of contradiction, that no builder who went into the cost would be hindered from erecting houses by the restriction of the number to 20 per acre. What actually had stopped his building operations.was the Finance Act of 1909. It had stopped hundreds of others and had ruined some. The deputation to the Local Govern- ment Board would not be complete without the inclusion of Councillors Wilkinson and Hen- shall. Councillor WILKINSON: I would not go. • think you should be put on the deputation.

ALDERMAN BENNETT REPLIES. Alderman BENNETT, in reply, expressed his great surprise at some of the remarks. It seemed hardly courteous for members not only to wish to reject such a moderate and business- like proposal, but to couple with their attempt unnecessary taunts about cheap trips to Lon- don.

"Whatever may be said about other people," he said, "I cannot be accused of having many trips to London at the expense of the Corpora- tion. Probably some of the gentlemen who 'indulge in these taunts go half a dozen times to my once." They did not want to go blindly blundering along, not knowing what they were doing or whither they were going. They therefore pro- posed to consult the experts at the Local,Gov- ernment Board, and not wait until they had prepared a scheme and then find some of it out of court. There was no thought of one-sided-
ness ih the deputation and the inclusion of the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor should surely be sufficient safeguard against any undue zeal. which the others might display in any direction.

It was one of the great puzzles of his public life that any member of the Council should oppose the principle of town planning, and especially Councillor Gough, who took the chair at meetings where one of the great cries was "Room to live" and "Give the people a decent chance of. housing." (Laughter.) Councillor GOUGH : I shall claim the right to reply if he goes on like that. (Laughter.) Alderman BENNETT : My philanthropic friend, Councillor Henshall, as Lord Beaconsfield once put it, makes use of sublime sentiments—l had almost said for the furtherance of sinister ends. At any rate, the source of some of this opposi- tion has surprised and disheartened me. No scheme can so vitally affect the happiness, wel- fare and economic prosperity of the town as a properly considered scheme for regulating its development. I hope the scheme will not be rejected, and that you will not debar this com- mittee, which is responsible for work of enor- mous importance, from getting the necessary information from the fountain head. (Hear, hear.) THE MAYOR'S SUPPORT. The MAYoe said he voted, for the resolution , on the committee on the ground: that the coin- mittee had been floundering for ,the last two or three years. They had wasted meeting after meeting in discussing the subject, and when they got a .scheme which they thought desir- able, it was referred back. It was therefore thought desirable that there should be aninter- change of views with the Local Government Board. That was the only reason for the depu- tation. They would get ideas which they could Put *to use on the committee. It was because of Councillor Pemberton's knowledge of the subject that he was put on the deputation. Alderman TINNION said they knew exactly the position Alderman Bennett and Counefilor Pem- berton would take up, and it was because of that he suggested that Councillor Henshall should be put on the deputation. Councillor Gocou : I also suggest Alderman James Evans.

Councillor DICKENSON was surprised to find that two men with the same opinions were to constitute the deputation. That made it look as if there was something behind the deputa- tion. He expected someone else would have gone.
- The MAYOR: You may take it Councillor Pem berton will not go.
Councillor PESI;ERTON : I would ask the Chair- man to withdraw the resolution.

The MAYOR: You refuse to-g-o—,-s.o it is the same thing. QUESTION OF DETAILS. Alderman BENNETT : There is not the slightest objection to any other member of the Council going—Alderman Tinnion or Alderman James Evans. It is purely a question of details. The MAYOR: A question of knowledge. Alderman JAMES EVANS said the committee had promised to get out a scheme to put before the Local Government Board and had not. Meanwhile building was going on, and the builders were doing so at their own risk, accord- ing to Section 58 of the Act. He did not see why a deputation should go to London about that section.
The MArott: They are going for information.
THE VOTING.
Finally a vote was taken, and it resulted as follows:

For the Amendment: Aldermen Tinnion, Smethurst, Burton and James Evans, Council- lors Dr. Joseph, Henshall, Shaw, Wilkinson, Dickenson, Gough-10. Against: The Mayor, Aldermen Forsham and Bennett, Councillors Dr. Fox, Broadhurst, Lindley, Wilson, Hawthorn, Pemberton, Archer, Chrimes, Cminington, Lashford-13. The minutes were approved, and on Councillor Pemberton declining to serve, his name was taken off the deputation.

div.head: BUILDERS AVARNED. Stirring Debate Over Another Proposal
div.p: BUILDERS AVARNED. Stirring Debate Over Another Proposal

There was a stirring debate over this proposi- tion of the Street Improvement Committee : " That notice be given to all persons proposing to erect houses in excess of 20 to the acre that they will do so at their own risk, having regard to section 58 of the Town Planning Act." Alderman BERTON said if there was anything likely to starve building, it was such a proposal. Some of them knew little about town planning —(Councillor. Pemberton : "Shame I—and he had not even got a copy of the Act, hut he would like to know what risk a builder was likely to incur if he built more than 20 houses to the acre. Alderman BENNETT said if the scheme was adopted, and the houses exceeded 20 to the acre, the builder might receive an order from the Local Government Board to demolish the sur- plus houses. Councillor WILKINSON: If the Local Govern- ment Board dare? Alderman BENNETT said he was speaking of the law and the power of the Board. Alderman TINNION said the Town Clerk was not so definite upon that pesint, and said the Local Government Board would not interfere. Alderman BENNETT: The Town Clerk does not say so. lie says it is left to the Local Govern- ment Board's discretion. Councillor BaoAntmasv thought it was putting the threat on the builders. Alderman BENNETT said that was one of the points upon which the deputation would con- sult the Local Government Board.

"GOT SO WARM." Alderman JAMES EVANS said the question of whether ?.0 houses per acre or more should be allowed was a question of circumstances, and that was the point where he differed from Alder- man Bennett, and he was sorry Alderman Ben- nett got so warm about the difference. (Laugh- ter.) He thought the Town Clerk should ex- plain the point. The MAYOR did not think the Town Clerk should be asked to do so. The TOWN CLERK: I do not wish to be brought into it. Councillor Goren moved the resolution back. He thought such a resolution would ruin build- ing of cottage property. The committee were trying to intimidate the builders. Alderman BURTON seconded. Councillor PEMBERTON expressed surprise at the discussion, and more especially at some of the remarks from Councillor Gough. Really, the resolution was in the interests of the builders. It was a very kindly warning to them. You must remember, added Councillor Pem- berton, although you may think yourselves a very important body, that you are only the War- rington Town Council, and you are not above the Government. I venture to think that even the Local Government Board are above the War- rington Town Council, and you cannot over-rulethem. (Hear, hear.)
Alderman lINNION : They won't be if we don't adopt the Act.

CORTICiIIOE PEMBERTON' : But as Mr. Samuel says, the Government may make the Act com- pulsory, arid will take no notice of you as a Council. Councillor WILKINSON : Then what is the use of the deputation?
COUrieIUOT PEMBERTON : If you Were on the deputation you would probably go for a row on the Thames while the deputation is seeing the Local Government Board. (Laughter.)
FEAR OF-VVHAT?
Councillor WILKINSON: When L had finished the Corporation's business Z might go on the Thames at my own expense. (Laughter.) I WEIS
astounded when I read this resolution, which is going to put the fear of—l will not say what— on the builders. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON : Where are the -

builders? Councillor WILKINSON contended that ss. 6d. per week houses were required, but these could not, be erected if only 20 were to be built per acre. They were going to prevent the building of cottage property. Dr. JOSEPH (Deputy-Mayor) did not believe in any hard and fast rule. They might have better health where there were 25 houses to the acre than where thre were 20. It was a matter of circumstances.

ALDERMAN BENNETT HITS OUT. Alderman BENNETT expressed his amazement at what had, been said by some of hi 3 progressive and advanced friends. (Laughter.) He was surprised at the reactionary attitude of Council- lor Gough, who had never studied-: the question of town planning, had no imagination, and did not realise what the Act aimed at. (Laughter.) Yet it was only the other night Cotineillor Gough was on a land campaign platform asking for decent conditions and houses for the workers. (A Voice: "Rub it in !") In' regard to Coun- cillor Wilkinson—
• COUIICiiiOr WILKINSON: I will not stand the language he used to my friend, Conneillor Gough. I will resent it. (Voices: "Sit down.") Alderman BENNETT : The language I am going to use—

Councillor WILKINSON : Alderman Bennett had better reserve anyremarks he has to make about me. I can only say that shall not stand the language from him that my friend has stood. (Addressing Alderman Bennett): I won't have it. Don't you attempt to do it, sir. Councillor GO_7.GH: He wants crying down. Councillor WILKINSON: He must be respectful. Alderman BENNErr: I am going to use lan- guage which is perfectly justified. Councillor Goruri : You have been making a political speech.

Alderman BENNETT : I have long regarded Councillor Wilkinson as one of the most re- actionary members of this Council. He is prov- ing it by his attitude on this question. lie ought to be on the better side, helping us. Councillor WILKINSON : You don't know what you are talking about. Your speech is mislead- ing._ _

Alderman BENNETT thought the Local Govern- ment Board would not sanction more than 20 houses to the acre. He wanted Warrington to set a good example to other towns by adopting such a forward policy. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: BUILDERS' THREATS.
div.p: BUILDERS' THREATS.

The MAYOR said certain builders had sub- mitted plans and said if these were not passed they would still go on with the buildings. The committee, in their kindness of heart, thought they should give these people due warning of what was the law of the land. (Hear, hear.) Councillor TlAwrnonx was surprised at the dead set made by some members against town planning. The question of 20 houses to the acre was most important, for that meant 100 people would be living on a single acre. Surely they could not have healthy conditions with that number per acre, and to allow more houses per acre was to perpetuate slums, which they were seeking to destroy.

Councillor DICKENSON said that 20 houses per acre could not be provided to rent at less than Bs. to 10s. per week. No working man could pay' such a rent. Councillor WILSON objected to the Council being flouted by any body of builders.

div.head: VOTING.
div.p: THE VOTING.

The division resulted as follows : For the Amendment: Aldermen Smethurst, Forshaw, Burton, James Evans, Councillors Dr. Joseph Henshall, Wilkinson, Dickenson, Lind- ley, Gough-10. Against: The Mayor, Alderman Bennett, Councillors Broadhurst, Dr. Fox, Hawthorn, Wilson, Archer, Pemberton, Lashford, Chrimes, Chantler—ll. The MAYOR said the amendment was lost, and the resolution was carried.

div.head: HEART OF THE IRISH
div.p: THE HEART OF THE IRISH
- QUESTION.

A correspondent sends us the following state- ment for publication in the interests of peace, and in the hope of preventing that outbreak of civil war which he already sees looming over our devoted town. He proceeds as follows: My son, who is spending, a holiday in the Isle of Man, determined the other day to study the Irish question at first hand, and with that purpose in view took advantage of a special boat fitted up for the intention of carrying an intelligent company of Manxers to the Irish capital and back during the day with a sojourn of some four hours in the city. Arriving there, he at once began to study the problem at close quarters, with the result that a picture post card was forthwith purchased and the ominous words indited thereon, "Home Rule would not only be a blunder, but a crime." These fateful words, although soundhaig somewhat familiar, struck the present writer with dismal forebod- ing. For although never having seen Ireland except on the map, and even then closely asso- ciated with England, he had dared by his vote to endeavour to bring about that state of separ- ation between the two countries which happily as regards the immediate purposes of the local ballot the electors' intelligence had frustrated. And now behold a few short hours—or were they minutes?—had served to convince one who was on the spot of the awful nature of the crime. And that this opinion must be gener- ally held in Ireland who can doubt? for if further proof were needed it is only necessary to observe that the dreaded words are written on the front of the card, alongside the address, in such a way that they could not have escaped the observation of the intelligent Dublin Postal officials, who, instead of impounding it as a , scurrilous falsehood, did all in their power successfully to urge it on its course, and even ' boldly imprinted the postmark twice on the face of the card as a guarantee of good faith. And now I feel that, although my vote was die- annulled by an adverse majority, the only reparation I can hope to make is to ask you, Mr. Editor, to publish this startling and con elusive evidence of the unwisdom of granting 1. Home Rule to Ireland, in the earnest hope that ,it will serve to enlighten and convince ihass who, like myself, have never spent a couple of hours in the sister island studying at first-hand one of the most complex questions of the ,•re- sent day.

Territorials at Newton. A detachment of the South Lancashire Regi- ment, commanded by Major Crosfield, held an excellent turnout on Saturday, when they marched to Newton. About 80 of all ranks were present, and the band and drums accompanied them.
