div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
WOMEN'S FIERCE FIGHT.
Combatants Strip to the Waist.

What was described' as "a disgraceful scene in Dial-court" by the Chief Constable was con- sidered by the "Warrington magistrates on Tues- day, when two women appeared before Messrs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair), C. Jackson Holmes, and T. Locker. The first was Mary Ann Bowler, of Dial-court, and she was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Monday afternoon. A police- constable said he found her fighting with two other women. She was stripped to the waist to fight and was in a most disgusting condition. The remainder of her clothes was torn, and.. she was covered with blood. Defendant: I don't know anything about it. The Chief Constable: She has been in War- rington ,four months, and in that time she has been mixed up with a number of drunken brawls. When the police were making investi- gations recently she cleared out of the town, and we thought she had gone for good, but she came back. She is worse than a wild 'animal; in fact, a wild animal would not conduct itself as she does. She was stripped to the waist in order to fight the other women, and she was smothered in blood. The magistrates, in imposing a fine of ss. and costs, said they took an extremely lenient view of the-case:

ASSAULT ON THE POLICE. • Mary Fisher, Dolman's-lane, who was described by the Chief Constable as "one of the fighters," was charged with being drunk and disorderly and with assaulting a police officer on Monday evening. P.C. Harrison said that nearly three hours after "the fight" he found prisoner quarrelling with another woman in Dolman's-lane. He asked her to go into the house, but she refused, spat in his face, and kicked him all over the legs. Even with assistance he had great diffi- culty in getting her to the Police Station, as she kicked and struggled all the way. The Chief Constable said Fisher was one of the women engaged in the fight earlier in the day. She had been convicted 38 times previously for various offences and had received three months for assaulting the police. The Chairman: Another three months in prison.

THE THIRD COMBATANT. The third combatant, Catherine Clancy, of Dial-court, appeared before the magistrates on Wednesday on a similar charge. P.C. Turner said accused was one of the women who partici- pated in the fight on Monday. She was fighting. with her hair down, and when he saw her she was covered with blood. lie failed to secure her arrest until Tuesday afternoon. Defendant: I have no marks and was not fighting. I was trying to separate them and the police have a spite against me, and that is why I an here. • The Chief Constable said there was no doubt but that accused took part' in the fight. She had been 12 times previously convicnd. The Mayor, who presided, imposed a fine of .tl, which included costs, -with the option of 14 days in prison.

div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.
Before Mr. R. I'. -Ra-i-c-lo.u-g-1-1 (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion, and Messrs. J. Upson, A. _ _

, J. Jolley, and T. Pemberton. A Man of Mystery.—There was no prisoner in Court when the Chief Constable said they only had one case for trial. It was a man whose name was unknown, who was brought in at 12.30 that morning and who was observed to be peculiar in his mind. He was found lying asleep on a couch in Jolley's-yard at the rear of Brick-street by an officer. Whilst the officer was in the yard a woman put her head out of a window, and said that the man had been try- ing to get into the house by the ordinary man- ner of opening the door. The man was without money and was locked up on a charge of lodging out. That morning he had apparently had a fit', and the police surgeon, who had to be called, recommended the man's removal to the Work- house Infirmary. Five minutes before the Court sat the man had had another fit, and so far as the charge of lodging out was concerned he (the Chief Constable) asked to be allowed to with- draw it, and that the man be committed to the Workhouse on al4 days' order. The man was a sign writer, and it appeared that he desired to do some work in the police buildings, apparently for his keep.—The Chief Constable's suggestion was adopted.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

Before the Mayor (in the chair), Dr. Joseph, Aldermen J. Smethurst, Bolton and James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson, and Messrs. T. Locker, S. Wright, W. Roberts, W. Furness, and G. Pilling. The Home-coming.—Ernest Briggs, cab driver, 4, Halifax-street, Warrington, was charged with being drunk in charge of two horses and a wag- gonette in Buttermarket-street on Saturday. He was further charged with ill-treating a horse by flogging it with a whip.—Detective Clough said he saw accused in charge of two horses and a waggonette belonging to Mr. Maginn. There were in the vehicle about ten persons, who had been to a bowling match at Croft. The horses were driven in a loose way and several times they almost fell. At the end of Scotland-road one did fall. Briggs beat the horse in a very cruel manner with the whip.—Accused's defence was that the horse would lie down anywhere, and on the setts it was very bad. He did lash the animal two or three times, but whip would not knock a fly off—it was like a tape.—lnspector Wainwright corroborated the officer's statement, while Inspector Dee said there were traces of whip marks on the horse when he examined it.— Briggs was fined 10s., including costs.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Before Messrs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair), C. Jackson Holmes, and T. Locker. , Smart Detective Work.—Leo Worthington, Chapel-lane, Howick and Hutton, near Preston, was, in absence, fined 405., with £2 10s. Bd. costs, for travelling on the London and North- Western Railway from Preston to Warrington without paying his fare. He sent a letter admit- ting the offence.—Mr. A. Browne, for the com- pany, said on 4th May Worthington arrived at Over Wharton and said he had not time to book at Warrington. The station master asked if he had a platform ticket at Warrington, but he said he had not. This aroused the official's suspicion and he asked for accused's address, which he gave as "Rose Cottage, Newton Heath, Manchester." This was found to be incorrect. He was seen to tear up a ticket. The pieces were gathered, i put together, and it was found the ticket was from Horwich to Preston. By that means the company's detectives were able to trace Worthington, who admitted to the Detective-Inspector at Preston that he had travelled from Preston to Warrington without a ticket on 4th May.
WEDNESDAY. Before' the Mayor (in the chair), and Messrs. J. W. Hayward, H. Thornton, C. Jackson _

Holmes, and W. T. Williams. A Naughty Boy.—A boy of ten was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch-rod for stealing ss. of his father's money. This he spent in the purchase of toy pistols and sweets, which he distributed amongst other boys. He disappeared from home for three days after the theft, yet went regularly to school.

THURSDAY. Before Mr. A. J. Jolley (in the chair), Alder- man Tinnion, and Messrs. W. Roberts and W. T. Williams. A Betting Case Point.—John Gillibraml, 85, Ellesmere-street, Warrington, was charged with using a certain house, 25, Warburton-street, for the purposes of betting. The Chief Con- stable stated that on Saturday last Detective- Sergeant Holland and P.C. Skelton were con- cealed and kept observations on the defendant. At 12.30 they saw Gillibrand go to the back- yard of 25, Warburton-street, and between 12.30 and 1.40 they saw 32 persons enter the back- yard who were observed to hand to the de- fendant Slips of paper, some of which appar- ently contained Money. The officers raided the place, and when the defendant was searched it was. found that he had in his possession 49 betting slips relating to 149 bets on horses running the same day at Manchester and Lingfiehl Park-.—Detective-
Continued in preceding column.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,

STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

There are now some tidy gardens To be seen in different parts of the village. Have the Garden Society been speeding up The villagers as they threatened to do At the annual meeting, or has it been done voluntarily? The farmers have been crying out for rain. They got a little, but not quite enough. Such an array of the men of the law, as seen In the local Police Court on Tuesday, has not before Been assembled at the local Petty Sessions. Their number constituted a new record. It was all over the Cheshire cheese case. Mr. Dunlop, of the Warrington Museum, is quite A hero with the Stockton Heath school children.
He guided a number through an interesting ramble. The stories he told quite captivated the youngsters.

_ _ They are already looking forward to his next visit. The Heathens who wield the willow and throw the leather Were, greatly disappointed over the result Of the cricket match played with Bold-street Wesleyans. The local " Jessops " could only knock up 33 runs. Bold-street batted and beat them by only five runs. The Heathens had several "ducks," and that was , Perhaps due to Bold-street Wesleyan bowlers Playing "ducks and drakes" with their wickets. The Heathens have another cause to boast over Warrington. They have a system of town planning, while the borough has none. There is scarcely an acre to be found where There are more than 20 houses to the acre. In some cases there are not four to the acre. "Well, that is cheek !"'exclaimed the Heathen on the tram. He illustrated his meaning by pointing to a scene on the Canal. A fussy little tug was whistling for a big liner To get out of its way and give it a clear course. "It's like a mouse trying to drill an ele- phant," . Was the after comment of the tram passenger. The village clocks each have a " Greenwich " time of their own. Whether it is the weather or not, each per- sists In disagreeing with the rest to the mLtent of several minutes. Heathens are said to be careless about the time. Do the clocks represent our alleged tempera- ment?

Horse's Adventure.—A farmer's horse, taking fright in London-road, jumped over a low wall into a garden% and became fixed. The vehicle remained on the other side of the wall. The animal was extricated without injury.

On the Bench.—The magistrates at the Stock- ton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday were Messrs. H. C. Burder (in the chair), Roger C. Parr, F. A. Frost, G. Dakin, J. J. Whitley, C. Jackson Holmes, J. A. Ransome, and Captain H. G. Roberts.

Gun that was a Toy.—For having a gun in his possession at Walton and for oeing drunk, George Ernest Keates, of 2, Smith-street, Walton Inferior, , was fined 55. at the Stockton Heath Petty Sesiions on Tuesday.—Defendant said the gun was only a toy, for which he had paid 2s. 3d.

Searching for. Game.—Charged with trespass- ing on land at Keckwick, belonging to Sir Richard Brooke, John Miles, of no fixed abode, appeared at the Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday and was fined 405., with the alterna- tive of a month's imprisonment.—A gamekeeper said that when prisoner was asked for his name on the day of tne alleged offence, February 13, he ref used to give it.

Licensee's Danger.—At the Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday, John Wardle, Lower Walton, was charged with being drunk on licensed premises and refusing to quit the Stag Inn, Walton, when requested.—Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. Arthur Browne, who prose- cuted on behalf of Mr. Frederick George Hatton, the licensee, said that the defendant was a boatman and a respectable man. On Whit Thursday he went "on the spree," and when he asked for more drink, Mrs. Hatton refused. She had to ask the defendant several times to go away, and he eventually did so. It was for that fact that the case would not be pressed. The prosecution was principally instituted to pro- tect licensees from such men as the defendant, who were a danger to them.—Defennt was fined ss. •

Garden Society Juniors.—The members of the junior section of the Garden Society, under the leadership of Mr. G. A. Dunlop, had a delight- ful ramble to the "Denna" on Saturday. The afternoon was fine and the juniors took keen interest in all the beauties of Nature brought to their notice. The district abounds in inter- esting features, in the history of which Mr Dunlop. of the old "sea dog" at Bellsfield and the Italian is well versed, his entertaining stories Peet, who took his daily walk round Hill Cliff, being much enjoyed. In view of the annual picnic and competition, which is fixed for July 11th, prizes were not awarded on this ramble. The attendance of seniors and com- mittee. left much to be desired, and the same little band seems to keep this section together each year.

A Boy's Theft.--At the Stockton Heath Juvenile Occasional Court on Wednesday, before Messrs. F. A. Frost (in the chair) and Roger C. Parr, a boy aged 15, in the employ of a Stockton Heath butcher, was charged with stealing 15s. from the till of a shop occupied by Mr. T. R. Westbrook, Walton-road. It appeared that Miss J. Barton, housekeeper, went into the shop at 1 p.m., June 3rd, and pris- oner, who was standing there, asked for a pint of beer. After serving him, Miss Barton opened the till to put in the money, and discovering 15s. to be missing, called him back. The boy imme- diately handed over the stolen money, saying that he was very sorry and did not know what came over him to take it. The boy's employer and his father testified to his good and honest character, and he was accordingly warned, an4.l placed under the probation officer for six months.

Electric Light Scheme.—Progress is evidently being made to supply the district with electric light, as suggested at a recent meeting of the Parochial Committee. The matter, at the re- quest of the committee, has been taken up by the Warrington Town Council, who, at their monthly meeting on Tuesday, approved of the following minute of the Electricity Committee: "The Parish Council of Stockton Heath having agreed to support the application of the Cor- poration to the Board of Trade for a Provisional Order to supply that parish with electric cur- rent: Resolved, that the parishes of Latchford Without, Thelwoll, Grappenhall, Lower Walton, Higher Walton, and Appleton, be included in the application for a Provisional Order, and that the authority of each parish affected be re- quested to support the application." This probably means that a local inquiry will be held, but it cannot take place until the other parishes give their decision in the matter.

Church of England Men's Society.—The annual meeting of the above society was held in the school on Wednesday. The Vicar pre- sided. It was encouraging to see such a large number of members present, and the interest shown by the meeting as a whole would prove were it necessary, that the ideals of the society are still held well in view. The following 1 officers were unanimously re-elected Hon. secretary, Mr. R., H. Smith; hon. treasurer, Mr. 1 W. Webster; auditor, Mr. A. Stannard; com- mittee, Messrs. Partington, Woods, Collyer,` and Wightman; Federation delegates, Messrs. Par- tington and Heesom; while the Rev. J. Collins and the Rev. E. W. Clarke are again acting as president and vice-president respectively. Mr. John Hallows was again appointed Conference delegate for the London Conference in October. —Mr. Smith, secretary of the Branch's Mission Circle, gave an interesting report of the work done, and the progress made in connection with the Parochial Missionary Study Bands, as well as the Bible Study Circle, which have been formed. The subject of the latter is St. Mark's Gospel.—Mr. Janeway spoke briefly on the work of the Federation, and brought to notice a new and valuable work the C.E.M.S. is iindertaking in assisting with the Prisoners' Aid work.—A short account was also given by the Rev. E. W. Clarke of the Mission services held in the parish during Lent, adding that the decision had been arrived at for future work in this direction during the coming months.—The meet- ing closed with a hearty vote of thanks to the officers for their services during the past year.

Stockton Heath Petty What is an Agricultural Engine?—At the Henry Massey, of Little Leigh, was summoned for using a locomotive on the lighway for haul- ing purposes without having a haulage licence.— Sessions on Tuesday, Mr. Moss, of Northwich, defended, and pleaded n'ot guilty.!--Supt. Owen said defendant had several locomotives registered by the County Council. On April 17, whilst in London-road, Inspector Breeze saw a locomotive belonging to the defendant, which was drawing three wag- gons loaded with straw. From inquiries- made, it was ascertained that defendant held no licence for the locomotive for haulage purposes on the date in question. It might be pointed out that there was no necessity for a haulage licence, seeing that the locomotive was registered for agricultural purposes. In a case which had been decided, it was held that the hauling of wheat to a mill did not come within the term " agri- cultural purposes" in the Act under which the prosecution was taken.—Mr. Moss relied on the second definition in the Act—a locomotive em- ployed solely for the btirposes of a farm. Mr. Moss contended that the hauling of hay to be sold came within the scope of that definition. It was exceedingly difficult for a farmer to de- cide what was an agricultural engine.—The magistrates ruled against Mr. Moss, but con- sidering the offence was committed inadvertently the case Was dismissed on payment of costs. Without Reins.—At the Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday, George Acton, Moss House Farm, Grappenhall, was summoned for riding on a hirry Without reins attached to the horse.— Inspector Breeze proved the case, and defendant was fined 2s. 6d.

div.head: DARESBURY.
div.p: DARESBURY.

Rifle Shooting.—A match was shot on Saturday afternoon between the Daresbury and Appleton Rifle Clubs, eight men a-side shooting at the 25, 50 and 100 yards ranges, ten shots at each range. The respective teams were captained by Messrs. Charles Ryder and C. P. Day. A close contest ensued, Daresbury ultimately winning by nine points. The following were the scores :—Daresbury team: Messrs. S. Whit- low, 269 points out a 300; C. Ryder, 279; J. Ravenscroft, 285; G. Wallworth, 283; C. Green- halgh, 273; Albert Ryder, 282; Arthur Ryder, 267; Fred Speed, 268; total, 2,206. Appleton team: F. Tole, 291 out of 300; J. Hartley, 278; J. Towers, 273; F. Black, 260; R. W. Cook, 261; C. Shepley, 278; W. Hutchinson, 275; C. P. Day, 281; total, 2,197. At the close of the match tea was provided in the pavilion for the com- petitors.—On Monday a visit was paid to the range by the Whitecross Club (Warrington), who competed with Daresbury on the 25 and 50 yards ranges, with teams of six men, ten shots each. This resulted in a second win for Dares- bury by 45 points. The scores were :—Dares- bury, C. Ryder, 191 out of 200; G. Wallworth, 192; C. Greenhalgh, 186; Bert Ryder, 189; J. Ravenscroft, 183; Arthur Ryder, 186. White- cross : F. Tole, 194 out of 200; T. Morris, 174; L. Scargill, 171; J. Eckersley, 187; W. Sparks, 161; H. Baines, 185.

div.head: Nw WIN WICK.
div.p: Nw WIN WICK.

ASYLUM TEAM'S BAD PATCH. Winwick Asylum team have struck a bad patch, as was clearly shown on Saturday, when TYldesleY Wesleyans inflicted their fifth consecu- tive defeat by four wickets. Only two of the home team reached double figures—A. Simpson, who played in a much improved style before being given out lbw with 23 to his credit, and Dr. Stone (13). The total for Winwick was 81. The visitors knocked up 150 for the loss of six wickets.

Funeral of Mr. W. Britch.—The funeral took place at the Parish Church on Monday after- noon of Mr. William Britch, who died at the Warrington Infirmary as the result of an acci- dent sustained while, following" his employment as head fitter at the County Asylum, Winwick. All the outside male employes of the Asylum, other than attendants, were present at the funeral, lining the churchyard. The service was conducted throughout by Canon Penrhyn. The chief mourners were: Mrs. W. Britch (widow), Frank and Willie (sons), and Mrs..o lare (sisters), Nellie, Jennie and Florrie (daughters), Mrs. Jepson, St. Helens; Mrs. Berry, Padgate; Mrs. Toft, War- rington;Mrs. Oldfield, Huddersfield; Mrs. Tonge; Herefordshire; and Mrs. Woods, Warrington (sisters-in-law), Messrs. Tongs, Bone and Berry (nephews), Mrs. Bennett, Mrs. Bone and Mrs. Simms (nieces). The deceased was carried to the grave by Messrs. employes. Wreaths and floral R. Smith, W. Smith, J. Hodnett, H. Williams, B. Copple and T. Frodsham, all except the last two being fellow tributes were sent from: "Wife and family," Mr. and Mrs. Berry, "Sister . Hannah," " Nephew and niece," " Nephews and nieces, St. Helens," Mr. and Mrs. J. Britch, T. and E. Egerton, J. and E. Bennett, Mr. and Mrs. Howe, Mr. and Mrs. S. Toft ancl family, Mr- and Mrs. R. Copple, "Annie, Jim, Alf., Ena and Harry Woods," "Harry Jane, Joe and Jim," "Mem- bers of the Len Thomas' Fund and neighbours," Canon and Mrs. Penrhyn and family, Miss Chadwick, Mrs. Haines, Mrs. Bishop, Mrs. Thompson, Frank and Lily Milligan, and others.

div.head: BURTON WOOD.
div.p: BURTON WOOD.

The Vicar's Stipend.—The Rev. A. M. Mitchell " Excelsior," his Parish Magazine, mentions the gift from parishioners of .tlOO towards the augmentation of the stipend. It is expected that the Benefice Augmentation Fund will contribute ,t2OO and the Ecclesiastical Commissioners another .R2OO, so that the income of the benefice will be increased by .48 a year in perpetuity.

div.head: JUNE 13, 1914.
div.p: LYMM.

District Rate Increases.—At a special meeting of the Lymm District Council on Monday even- ing, it was decided that the generardistrict rate be 2s. 10d. in the X. This is an increase of 2d. upon last year.

Fewer Visitors to Lymm.—lt seems to be the general opinion that fewer people visited Lymm this last Whit-week than for many years pre- vious. Similar reports come from various places. Probably the lateness of the date has Something to do with the matter, as the school holidays are not very far away.

Congregational Pastor's Progress.—The Rev. J. A. Penaliggon, pastor of the Lymm and Buck- low Hill Congregatiowd Churches, continues to make satisfactory progress towards recovery from his recent severe illness. It is understood that he is to have a few weeks' sojourn at South- port, and probably after that he will resume his duties.

No Grant.—A special meeting of the Lymm District Council was held on Monday evening, when the Clerk read a letter from the Royal Automobile Club stating that they could not see their way to make a grant towards the cost of the re-construction and widening of Ditchfield's Canal Bridge. The Clerk (Mr. Mullard) said a similar letter had been received from the Motor Union.—Councillor Gotobed : They take all the benefits and pay nothing .towards them.—The Chairman (Mr. T. B. Warburton): It is really those people who are responsible for the danger, because they, are on you before you know where you are. They cannot expect the ratepayers of Lymm to go in for all this expense on their be- half.—The Clerk asked if the Council were going to sign the contract with the County Council or wait until a general meeting, seeing that the motor clubs had refused grants.—lt was decided to wait until the next general meeting.

New Member ,Welcomed.—At the meeting of the Lymm District Council on Monday night, Councillor G. H. Parker took his seat on the Council for the first time.—The Chairman (Councillor T. H. Warburton) said it gave him pleasure to welcome Councillor Parker amongst them. As they all knew they had had a general upset in the Council that year, and it was to be hoped that now they had got all the seats filled that they would work smoothly and in a busi- nesslike manner. He hoped Councillor Parker would like the work, and he thought he would take it as a great pleasure, considering the amount of time he had on his hands: He was the r right man in the right place.—ln reply, Councillor Parker said he thanked them very much for their remarks, and what time he had he would only be too pleased to give for the benefit of the ratepayers of Lymm and Statham Ward in particular. It had been said that he had been returned as a prominent Conserva- tive. He wanted it to be understood, and he said it straight from the shoulder, that politics would not enter into any discussion with him. They might not see eye to eye in every little discussion, but he hoped that nothing he said in the debates would be taken as a personal matter.---Councillor W. G. Groves: I hope the reporters will omit your worlds, Mr. Chairman, that we have been upset. Ido not see that we have been upset at all: The statement might be misapprehended.—Councillor Holt: The word disturbed would explain it.—The Chairman fioculorlyl: You have to be exceedingly careful. (Laughter.)

div.head: " BEERY " VISITORS. Scene in Front, of a Councillor's
div.p: THE " BEERY " VISITORS. Scene in Front, of a Councillor's
Residence.
VISITORS "DISH OUT " DRINK.

Further remarks concerning Lymm's undesir- able visitors during the summer months were made at a special meeting of the Lymm District Council on Monday evening. Councillor Ingham said that there seemed to be a feeling that the District Council had directed attention towards the publican. He was sure Mr. Cowper had no intention of doing that. They did not want unduly to harass the publicans, for they already had sufficient duties to attend to, and it was to be hoped the police would take a proper interpretation of the com- plaint. The publicans were. a respectable body of men, and he was sure they did their best to keep their houses properly conducted. ' The Clerk (Mr. Mullard) said that in his letter to the thief Constable of the County he had not drawn attention towards the publican. The Clerk was asked to read the letter he sent to the Chief Constable, and this ran: "1 am directed by my Council to call your attention to a matter which has given consider- able annoyance in this village during the last few years.

44. En the summer holiday season a great num- ber of visitors come to this district from the neighbouring towns and some of these people misbehave in a very unpleasant manner, and half-intoxicated women in particular, cause a 'considerable disturbance in the place. "In writing to you my Council do not wish to cast any aspersion on the local police adminis- tration, which is very efficient, nor do my Coun- cil blame the local hotel proprietors in any way. H you can do anything to mitigate the existing evil either by additional assistance for the police or by some other methods, I can assure you my Council will be very grateful. "Trusting you will give this matter your kind and early attention, "Your obedient servant, c' W. MIILLARD." A letter acknowledging the receipt of the ' Clerk's communication was read, in which it stated the matter would receive attention. The Chairman (Councillor Warburton) said it was not meant as a reflection upon the pub- licans at all. What was really meant was that they wanted the same behaviour in Lymm by Manchester people as Manchester would expect from Lymra people who visited the city. (Hear, hear.) If Lymm. people, when in Manchester, behaved in the same manner as some of the vil- lage's visitors, they would soon be in the hands of the police.
BEER IN FRONT OF COUNCILLOR'S HOUSE.

Councillor Cowper said he thought he made the point very clear when he raised the question. No publicans had tackled him. The Chairman: It is rather curious that a four-in-hand drew up almost opposite Councillor Cowper's house a fortnight ago. It was sug- gested that they did it as an annoyance to Councillor Cowper for bringing this matter for- ward. They had a barrel of beer, and they were " dishing " it out opposite his house. ' Councillor Gotobed said their charge was against the women who came to Lymm and brought their beer with them. He distinctly used the words that they did not blame the local publicans at all. The fault was with the people who organised the trips.

div.head: COMPOUNDING SYSTEM.
div.p: COMPOUNDING SYSTEM.
Would It Nlean Better Cottages?

Immediately after the Lymm District Council had settled upon the general district rate at the special meeting on Monday, COuncillor Holt said he thought it was an opportune time to raise the question of compounding for rates. In the towns they were able to compound for cottage property to a much higher amount than they in Lymm did; he believed their compound- ing power was only for under £lO. If they were prepared to raise that amount— The Clerk: We cannot this year. Councillor Holt said if they were, they would encourage a better class of cottage in the dis-

trict. An owner could compound under ,the £lO, but immediately he went over that amount he had to pay the full rate. In a town like Warrington they could pay ss. 6d. per week for a house whose rates were compounded, which was considerably over the £lO limit.
Councillor Groves believed that they had scores of cottages in Lymm that were com- pounded for, and the rent was 4s. to ss. 6d. per week.
The Clerk said he believed they allowed more than any other District Council round about. Councillor Ingham: Does the intending builder know that? Councillor Holt: No.
The Clerk said he would look it up, but he believed they allowed more than any other Dis- irict Council.

div.head: tinburp
div.p: tinburp
RECTOR'S WEDDING.
VILLAGERS REJOICE. Wedding Cake for the School Children. _ _ . _

The fluttering flag on Lymm's old church tower, a flag which has been unfurled on many notable occasions, served to remind the vii- lagers, if it were necessary, that Tuesday was their Rector's wedding day. The children were given a holiday, and as the veil of darkness was creeping o'er the heavens, the church bells broke the silence with a merry peal. _ .

In the afternoon ti a children from both the Lynim and Statham Schools were the guests of their Rector. They were entertained at the parochial schools, where a special wedding cake was cut and distributed. The tea was concluded in two sittings, and it is .stated that nearly 600 •were present, and all these gave vent to 'their thankful feelings when they gave cheers for the Rev. and Mrs. Thurston.

The cheers were renewed on the receipt of a telegram sent from Folkestone by Mrs. Thurs- ton, which ran: "Our thoughts are with you. Best wishes for a very happy time.—Evelyn Thurston." It was unfortunate that the weather should have been responsible for the abandonment of the after proceedings at the Lymm Hall field, but this is a treat, in store for the children. Arrangements had been made for the sports and for public dancing, but these were postponed: The Lymm Subscription Band marched round the village playing merry tunes.

Choir, Bellringers and Band Unite. In the evening the church choir, bellringers and the members of the Subscription Band sojourned to the Church Inn,- where they were entertained to supper, the chair being taken by Mr. F. E. Evans, the Vicar's churchwarden. The Chairman; in proposing the health of the Rector and Mrs. Thurston, said that was a red- letter day, not only in the life of the Rector and the bride, but also for the parish. For 16 years Mr. Thurston had laboured amongst them and the church, and the Various organisations were never in a healthier condition than at the -esent tithe, and that was mainly/ due to the Rector's untiring efforts and wondeFful organis- ing abilities. .His excellent work in connection I with the Grammar School as a governor and hon. treasurer would never be fully known, whilst as a member of the District Council he had proved himself in every way a worthy citizen of the ancient village. Ho had won and held the fullest confidence of his parishioners. On June 25th the Rector would return, bring- ing with him his wife and help-meet, when they would show their appreciation of his past ser- vices by giving him a right loyal welcome, and afterwards by extending to them both their hearty support and loyal co-operation in the important parochial duties which lay before them. (Cheers.) Songs were rendered by Messrs. George Rixon, Levi Thomass6n, J. Shaw, and H. E. Odber. Mr. W. Cook, the church organist, wits the pianist.

There were numerous telegrams despatched from Lymm to the Rector and his wife, all bear- ing good wishes for their happiness. One sent on behalf of the school children of the village contained the words. "Loyal and hearty con- gratulations from all the school," whilst one sent by the District Council ran, "On behalf of the members of the Council, I send you hearty congratulations.—T. R. Warburton, chairman."
Apologises to the_ Council as a
"Defaulter."

At a special meeting of the Lymm District Council on Monday the following letter was read from the Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston) "Dear Mr. Mullard,—l am sorry to be a de- faulter again at the meeting on Monday. "I have had my Council duties very much on my mind the past few weeks, and I should be very much obliged if you would kindly make my humble apologies to the Chairman and my brother members for my absences. They will, I hope, understand and excuse. Were it not that there have been so many changes lately, and that a resignation puts a burden on the. rates, I should have withdrawn, but under the eircumstinces I hope when I settle down to attend to the duties as punctually as I have done during the past ten years. "With many thanks for your and their patience with me, "Very sincerely yours, "G. B. THURSTON." Councillor Groves thought they must excuse the Rector and wish him, success in his under- taking. (Hear, hear.) s The Chairman (Councillor H. Warburton): I agree with that. Councillor Gotobed thought they should send some message to Mr. Thurston regarding his marriage. He was a good old colleague, and a congratulatory message should be sent to him. A Conversation on Village Changes Overheard at Lymm. .

"Hello, Jim! Wee! fancy! seeing thee here! Ha should ne'er a thowt as ha should ha' seen thee. An' how are tha geeting on like?" " Weel, Sam, ha conna grumble, tha knows; ha' bin very pooly lately, an' am not as young as ha used to be. Tha looks rare and weal, I must say. Weer ha yo' hanging out flaw?" "Just tother side a Flixthn, Yi." "Hi, that's weer I heard tha was. Ha tha comfortable theer?"

"Hi am with me dowgter. It's a long time sin I were here, an' I thowt ad may as weel see what May Queen were like. Tha knows I dunna, ex- pect to see a great many more May Queens." " Weel, lad, tha will not be the only one, for there's not many more far anybody to see. It's bin jolley hard work to get this one up. Only for a hard-working chap who lives• somewheer abowt Booth's Hill, I dunna think as tha would a bin able to see any. Of course, it's same as th' owd saying says, Wheer there's a will, method Ands a way.' Simply determination after all. Weel, anyway, what does think abowt it?"

"Weel, I think it's bin very nice. Nowt neer what thee an' me has sin in clays gone by. But they dunna do nowt now same as when me an' thee were here. But for all that, it's simply grond to see how little childer enjoy themselves. But I dunna like to see 'em eat so much of this 'ere ice cream on hot slays." div.head: WESLEY AS SCIENTIST.
div.p: WESLEY AS SCIENTIST.
His Gifts of obs2rvatloll and Power of Expression.
THOUGHTS ON "CONTINUAL MIRACLES."

GVe have before us a book, "Natural Philos6- phy," in five volumes, by John Wesley, MA., published in 1777 by J. Fry and Company, and sold at the Foundry, Upper Moorfields, and by the booksellers in town and country. This book is of interest in many ways. It gives an accurate idea of the state of knowledge of natural history and philosophy at that period, and reveals the fact that Wesley was a scientist, an accurate observer of natural phenomena, and had a power of expression and condensation which few modern or ancient writers can excel. It is remarkable as illustrating. the wonderful versatility of Wesley, considerhig the manifold calls upon his time and energy, the cares of a rapidly growing organisation, his absorption in theology and in the practical affairs of daily life. In view of these it is remarkable how he was able to master the known facts of natural science, to add to these the results of careful observation in natural history, and to gather together and condense all the then known know- ledge in regard to natural phenomena. His introduction is stately and reverent:

"1 raise myself up to the Eternal Reason; I study his laws, and I adore him. I contem- plate the. universe with a philosophic eye. I search into the relations whicß by this immense chain constitutes one whole. I stop a while to examine some links of it, and, struck with those marks of power, wisdom and goodness which I discover therein, I faintly attempt their descrip- tion."

The following extract shows the domineering spirit of the man in which he smites hip and thigh some absurd theory of a certain Mr. Hutchinson : . "But after all comes Mr. Hutchinson, calls Sir Isaac and all his followers senseless, un- philosophical blockheads, and to solve all the, difficulty in a moment, supposes the sun to be the centre of the whole universe, and to project light every way, through every point of space, to the utmost circumference of it. When this light arrives at the circumference, it is con- densed into larger masses, and I,•eturns in the form of spirit or air, through every point of space to the sun. There it is again comminuted into light by the immense fire and so issues out again to the circumference., And this double impulse of light moving outward and spirit moving inward, causes the motion of all the heavenly bodies, both round their own axles and round the sun„ But to wave that gross ab- surdity of supposing every point of space to be continually 'filled with light, and every point of it to be filled with spirit at one and the same time (which is flatly impossible, since both are material, and two particles of matter cannot co-exist in the same space),. how does this re- move the difficulty at all? How does it help us forward an hair's breadth? For what impels light outward or-spirit inward? It can be no mechanical power. It must then be the, finger of God. And if so, what have we gained? May we not as well say at once (as go thus round about), 'Gravitation can be no otherwis4 ac- counted for, than by allowing the direct, im- mediate power of God, operating through the whole universe'?"

INGENIOUS THEORY ABOUT COMETS. After rejecting the above, Wesley himself gives his support to an equally absurd theory about the use of comets. He does not think that gravitation can account for the motion of comets, and their seemingly erratic course has troubled many besides the founder of Metho- dism. After discussing the matter; he asks the question, 't Is there a continual miracle?" He gives curious, exPlanation of the use of comets by one Doctor Rogers, which appears to be that they were intended to sweep up the straying light and bring it hack to the sun. We give the matter in Wesley's own words:— "The comets, Dr. Rogers thinks, are chiefly designed to repair the quantities of light con- tinually emitted by the sun, and which are scattered and dispersed over the whole system. Their sweeping tails, which extend so many thousand miles, seem adapted to such a purpose. And as many of those particles of light are driven to a vast distance, it is necessary they should go to the utmost limits of the system, to make such a collection. "Suppose a body fit for this, detached from the neighbourhood of the sun, it should be light, porous and spongy. And such a body would be propelled by the violence of the rays, with great velocity to a great distance. The farther it goes, the fewer rats strike upon it, and their force likewise is diminished. The comet then slowly sweeps his tail over the wide expanse, beyond the orbit of Saturn. There its cells are filled with the matter it was sent to collect, but becoming heavier, the other scale begins to pre- ponderate, and he slowly returns towards his centre. His collection increases as he descends, which adds to his weight and swiftness, and he comes down if very heavy, almost in a straight line; if less so, in a larger curve, till he is near the sun, where having emptied himself, and being evenly balanced with the repelling rays, he moves round in the segment of a circle, till being continually lighter, he is no longer a balance for the repelling rays, and so is driven forward thereby, and runs the same circle as before."

There is something grand as well as comic in this idea of the comets acting as the means of replenishing the sun With light, of a comet sweeping its tail over the wide expanse, and in so doing absorbing the scattered light, and as this light adds to its weight, sweeping back to the sun with its load of light, emptying it into the sun, and, like a bee from its hive, starting again on its collecting errand. GRAVITY AND LEVITY.

_ There appears to have been amongst our fathers an idea that there was an opposite force to Gravity which they called Levity,— but as Wesley haply remarks, Gravity and Levity have always been reckoned amongst sensible qualities, but properly there is no such thing as Levity, for all bodies tend to the centre of the earth, although some are light in comparison with others.

div.head: ELEMENTS.
div.p: THE ELEMENTS.

In regard to the elements, Wesley, following Aristotle, classes them as four—Fire, Air, Water and Earth—but apparently in his day there were indications of an extension of the ele- ments. He says "The Chymists have taken another Way, en- deavouring to trace the principle of bodies, not by the ordinary use of their senses, nor by reasoning, but from experiments made by fire. And by this means they make five elements. For whatever is distilled, first emits a sapid and spirituous, vapour, Whish is by cold 'condensed into a liquor; and this they term Mercury; then an insipid liquor, which they call phlegm; after- wards an acid liquor, which is also termed Mer- cury. A thicker and oily liquor comes next, which because easily inflammable, is stiled Sul- phur. The Salt which is afterwards found is 'their fourth element, the insipid Earth, which is left, the fifth." The instances we have given indicate some a , he points where great advance has been made 1 in our knowledge since Wesley wrote. It must not be thought from these that on the subjects about which Wesley wrote he was generally so far behind. It is evident from many facts in this interesting volume that Wesley, in his journey- ings on horseback through the country, was not wholly absorbed in thoughts about his, special work. 'His references to natural phenomena chow a wonderfully accurate power of close ob- servation. The following are cases in point :
MIGRATION OF BIRDS. "Several kinds of birds change, at a stated time, their dwelling-places. We have seen
(Continua in next column.)

numerous flocks of geese, quails and crows, re- sembling thick clouds, that sometimes' darken the air. By such periodical emigrations the species are preserved, and in their long pilgrim- age Nature is their pilot and provider." "We conjecture that the emigration of birds depend principally on the winds. An exact naturalist at Malta has assured himself of this: that the same species always change their climate with particular winds. In April the south-west wind brings into that island a species of plovers, and the north-west cardinals and quails. Nearly at the same time; falcons, buz- zards, and other birds of prey come with the north-west wind, without stopping, and depart in October with the south and west. In sum- mer the easterly wind conducts the snipes to Malta, and towards the autumn the north and north-west bring thither numerous squadrons of woodcocks. These birds cannot fly, like the quails, before the wind, iince the north wind, which might carry them into Barbary, obliges them to remain in the isles. Quails, on the contrary, emigrate before the wind from one country to another. The south-east enables them to pass, in the month of March, from Bar- bary into France. They return from France in September, and go to Malta by a south-east. The winds, therefore, are the signals employed by Nature for reminding divers kinds of birds of the time of their departure. In obedience to this voice, they set out, and follow the direction it points out to them."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1914.
TABLE TALK.
The World's Tribute of Interesting
Items of News.
QUAINT AND AMUSING.

• A dozen English epicures, active members of the Gourmands' League, have decided to organ- ise a series of pilgrimages to all the towns and villages of France renowned for their cookery or whose names are enrolled on the scroll of fame by reaSon of some famous delicacy that is theirs exclusively. The first pilgrimage under- taken by the gourmands will occur in a few weeks—to the ancient town of Troyes, the home of the " andouillette " (a small sausage).

Australian Stamps. It is the intention of the Australian Post- master-General that the new' sixpenny stamp, which is to bear a representation of a kooka- burra as a main feature, shall be printed in ink which will give as near as possible the colour of the bird's plumage. It will probably be a month or two before the stamp is available for general circulation. It is estimated that for the current twelve months no fewer than 500,000,000 stamps will be required for the Commonwealth, of which about 400,000,000 will be of the penny denomination.
The American Naval Officer.

American naval officers who are " going some " just now at Vera Cruz are all graduates of the Naval Academy, which is " democratised " on the lines so dear to the Radical Press. The cadets enter after a competitive examination. But such is the effect of "democratisation," the " Carpenter" in the " Express " says, that by the time the youths receive their commissions they have become "aristocrats," a select, ex- clusive class much sought after in marriage and in social circles. There is many a cobbler's son on the quarterdeck of an American Dreadnought with the manners and aspirations of a Roman patrician.

div.head: General Huerta.
div.p: General Huerta.

General Huerta owed his first advancement in life to an accident, says the "Westminster Gazette:" He was the only Indian in a certain village who could read and write, and was con- sequently taken into the service of a general who wanted an amanuensis. The general took him with him to Mexico City, ;ind procured him a nomination to a cadetship in the military school. Diaz employed him, though he was rather jealous of him, and kept him in the back- ground. Madero placed him on half-pay, and he went into sbusiness as a contractor for the supply of building materials; but his military services were needed, and he soon had to be re- called—just as he was on the point of becoming a partner in the exploitation of a marble quarry. Captain Burnside, the Military Attache of the United States, expressed a high opinion of his organising capacity.

div.head: " In the Coils of a Python."
div.p: " In the Coils of a Python."

Actors for motion picture dramas are called on to face death in awful form in the pursuit of their profession. In a drama entitled "In the Coils of a Python," Mr. S. Bainbridge, an American actor, had a terrible experience. Mr. Bainbridge was the villain. At the close of a particularly wicked day this character tried to elude justice on horseback. A large python that had not been fed for a week was caged and carried to the centre of the road down which Mr. Bainbridge was to ride. The cage was opened, and the python slowly crawled to liberty. A few moments later the actor gal- loped up, "did a fall from horse," as the pic- ture directors phrase it, and prostrated himself before the hungry snake. The .python immedi- ately began to squeeze him, and the pain was so great that Mr. Bainbridge shouted for assist- ance. The snake was shot and killed, but it took four men half an hour to free the actor from the coils of the reptile. This picture was posed at Universal City, near Los Angeles, Cal.

div.head: Cruelty in German Army.
div.p: Cruelty in German Army.

- Almost every day fresh stories of ill-treatment and cruelty in the German Army come to hand, says the Berlin correspondent of the "Stan- dard," despite the fact that the affairs are usually kept as quiet as can be by the authori- ties. Some idea of the reputation which infan- try regiments are getting may be obtained from the fact that an apprentice named Rauch com- mitted suicide after declaring that he preferred death to doing military service in a line regi- ment, as had fallen to his lot. Recently, too, a non-commissioned officer named Wolker was sentenced by Court-martial to fifteen days' arrest fort kicking and hitting one of his men. He was brought up on the complaint of a bom- bardier who had his jaw broken by a blow. Again, it is reported from Leipzig that, mad- dened by ill-treatment he had received, a soldier named Meyer, belonging to the 100th Grenadier Regiment, attacked a non-commissioned officer with a hammer and murdered hi. The mur- derer afterwards committed sucide.
WESLEY AS SCIENTIST—continued.

div.head: BIRDS' NESTS.
div.p: BIRDS' NESTS.

" What a series of interesting ciecumstances I would not the construction of their nests also present us with! A chaffinch or goldfinch's nest I would take us up whole hours in contemplat- ing it. We should inquire where the goldfinch could furnish itself with a cotton so fine, silky, and soft, RS lines the inside of its pretty nest? After many researches we should find that by covering the seeds of certain willow's with a very fine cotton, Nature has prepared for the gold- finch the down she employs. We should never be weary of considering that kind of embroidery with which the chaffinch to agreeably adorns the outside of his nest, and, on viewiag it more narrowly, we should perceive that it is owing to an infinity of little liverworts, artfully inter- woven together, and applied with the utmost propriety-over the whole surface of the nest. The colour o,f these liverworts, which is most commonly that of the bark of the tree on which the nest is situate, would indicate that the chaffinch, seems to intend her nest should be con- founded with the branch that bears it."

div.head: "LIT. AND PHIL. "SOCIETY. AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHY.
div.p: "LIT. AND PHIL. "SOCIETY. AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHY.
Its " Proceedings" for the Last Two Years.

The "Proceedings" of the Warrington Liter- ary and Philosophical Society, 1912-14—just issued—recording the work of our premier local intellectual society, is well up to, if not above, , its usual standard of excellence. Its contents are varied—a most excellent variety of subjects dealing with science, philo- sophy and literature, the first predominating. This society has always been the medium for conveying to the Warrington public the results of the various archteological and antiquarian researches carried out in the town and the neighbouring district, and the first paper in , this volume by the Rev. H. V. Pigot—the present President of the society—is of a highly interest- jag and valuable character. Mr. Pigot gives a succincth historyfiti4reepsla°nnS of the church at differ- ent °f 'GraPPenhall Parish Church ard, and accompanying periods of its development. The latest plan fromte aoe Norman m are a of 1912 is by Mr. Arthur Down, A.R.1.8.A., of Stockton Heath. To all interested in the foundation and development of our churches those permanent monuments of man's devotion to the higher aims of existence amid the vicissi- tudes of a changing society—this paper will strongly appeal. • In her paper on "Philipßourke Marston and His Poems," Mrs. Ridgway writes with keen appreciation and enthusiasm She tells- the story of the poet's sad, short life, and gives him an important place in the realm of English poetry. There is a short but excellent summary of Professor Hobhouse's illuminating address on 'Biology and Politics." To those who had not , the privilege of listening to "one of the most brilliant of the Oxford school of philosophers," this summary will indicate the scope and nature I of the address, whose title to many may seem puzzling. The main theme of the address—and it is one which will give rise to the greatest of controversies in the near future—is the apparent antagonism between the biological and .the sociological coiceptions of • society. Professor Hobhouse recognises the importance of tne work of the biological school, especially their studies in heredity, but he is of the opinion that this work must be much extended, and rendered exact before their conclusions can be safely embodied in social legislation. He points out , that our notion of progress is not helped by the 'theory of conflict or struggle for existence, but by "the more subtle and close application of the notion of human brotherhood, freedom, and equality," Professor Hobhouse's tacit admission of the value of the Eugenist argument implies a possible reconciliation between the biological and the sociological conceptions of society. , Mr. W. Peter Rylands deals with "The Theory and Incidence of Taxation" in a very instruc- tive paper. As a student of economics, Mr. Rylands points out the importance of consider- ing the first principles of economics in all prac- tical questions •of taXation, and shows that taxation may be productive or unproductive, and that there is a limit to the burden of un- productive taxation. This paper is well worth a reflective perusal by all interested in local and national questions of finance, "Liquid Fuels" is the title of a paper on a topical isubject by an expert—Dr. Ormandy. Owing to the development of the internal com- bustion engine the problem of an adequate supply of liquid fuel at a cheap rate is becoming more and more urgent. Dr. Ormandy suggests that an almost unlimited supply of cheap alcohol could be obtained from starchy cereals grown in the tropics, and that this alcohol might be used as a substitute for the liquid fuel now obtained from sources of limited extent, and which are more and more drawn upon as the years pass by. Mr. E. T. Whitelow, F.R.A.S., of Southport, discusses learnedly on "Old World Astronomy." If theology had not already been enthroned as "the Queen of Sciences," astronomy would surely have been a strong claimant for the vacant throne. Mr. Whitelow takes us back to the beginnings of astronomical knowledge, and traces its growth onward through Egyptian, Babylonean and Grecian-times to the rise of Copernicus, in whose epoch of astronomy we now live. The present revival of the drama in Britain gives a special interest to Mr. B. S. Townroe's paper on "The Evolution of the Modern Drama." Mr. Townroe has himself made an essay in drama, and is well qualified to speak on its special place in the literature and .life of the nation. He surveys 'drama onwards from Euripides to Bernard Shaw, and discusses its tendency and influence. "The Antiquity of Man in the Light of Recent Discoveries" is the title of a paper by Dr. W. P. Gowland, of the University of Liver- pool. The antiquity of man has always had a great fascination for the workers and thinkers in the natural sciences. Structural remains preserved in the geological record point back- wards to a dark and distant part of mankind; to a period whose contemplation makes written' history seem but a day. Dr. Gowland deals lucidly with the discoveries in the various geological strata and refers in some detail to the skull or portions of a skull found at Pilt- down, in Sussex, two years ago. Five tables accompany the text, which greatly help to illus- trate the severer scientific aspects of the paper. The last paper is by the Rev. Dr. Stanley Mellor, on "The Poetry and Philosophy of Henrik Ibsen." To some the place of Ibsen in the hierarchy of the world's great writers and thinkers may be disputed, but after reading this incisive paper by Dr. Mellor no one will deny that Ibsen had a great and special message for all mankind, and that he gave it forth with the power of genius. Such, then, is a brief review of this interesting volume of over 180 pages. The book is well printed and bound. It has no preface, or, rather, there is a balance sheet as a preface. This shows that the society, in spite of its heavy expenses, has a small balance in hand. Long may it flourish. ,

div.head: SOCIETY OF FRIENDS AND NATION XL SERVICE.
div.p: THE SOCIETY OF FRIENDS AND NATION XL SERVICE.

The following has been issued by the Society of Friends:= We desire to re-affirm our sense of the respon- sibility for true national service which attaches to citizenship in a civilised state. Our convic- tion of the unlawfulness of war to the Chris- tian which prevents us from giving to our country ni any,seh omilitaryuld specially service call willingly lul isn tg 01 voluntary rendered service in other ways, even at the cost of much personal sacrifice. Those who devote them- selves with public spirit to the building of national character, the shaping of righteous policy at home or abroad, or the manifold tasks of local or central government, are doing work of high value for the Ningdoin of God. In this spirit we Must continue Ito offer strenuous opposition to the establishment in any part of the British Empire of a system of compulsory military training. The youth of the nation requires to be trained in a true con- ception of patriotism and of the duty and privi- lege of service for country and for humanity, but we maintain that this service is best pro- moted by an appeal to the highest elements of human nature rather than by associating it with warlike institutions which are out of harmony with the growing sense of inter- national brotherhood.

The ultimate defence of any nation lies in the moral qualities of its citizens, qualities which are raised to their highest power through obedience to. the Prince of Peace. It is our conviction that compulsory military training of any kind is an invasion of the rights of con- science, the right of every man to be free to follow where the Truth leads him. There is to-day no more truly national. service than the replacing of mutual suspicion between nations by mutual trust and helpfulness.

div.head: Portraits and Needlework at Warrington Museum.
div.p: Portraits and Needlework at Warrington Museum.
FLASHLIGHT HINTS.

There are at present two exhibits in our Museum, Bold-street, that will interest ama- teurs. One is a series of portraits of Warring- ton worthies of a past generation, done in the first processes known to photography. It is a singular coincidence that the first successes in photographic portraiture were in the form of a positive, of which only one copy, and that on glass, could be made. In the same way the first really successful direct colour prints of the pres- ent day, the autochromes, are made as a posi- tive, and only one original copy is possible. Already, however, the new processes by Paget, Arc., make pictures in the form of negatives, and no worker need be deterred by the great expense such as the earlier methods involved, from a patient trial of the new colour photography. The other exhibit is a portrait 'of a lady read- ing. It is an exquisite example of Japaneso skill in needlework, and it is worth the atten- tion of our lady readers also on that account. It is done in flame-coloured silk on a ground of silk material, and every stitch will bear close examination. Even the frame ie. a wonderful piece of tasteful work, and can j3e studied by would-be picture makers. The portrait is evi- dently in .the European style, but the work of, the needle does not suffer on that account.

div.head: SNAPSHOTS.
div.p: SNAPSHOTS.

A Dark Room Scrap-book.—A scrap-book with fairly large leaves, with a string so that it can be, hung up out of the way 1 when not actually required, ought to find its place in every dark room. Primarily, it should be made the receptacle for all the printed in- structions which are issued with the various plates and papers that may he used, so that one always has them at hand for reference pur- poses. To these may be added any other cut- tings likely to be useful; notes as to relative ex- posures with the enlarging lantern, in bromide or gaslight printing, and similar records.

Flash- Lighting.L-A very fine piece of night photography in last week's "Examiner" would no doubt interest many camerists. The most important point in successful work of this kind is the position of the light. It mitt be placed in such a position that no glare ricir even a reflec- tion can touch the lens. Therefore the flash Should come from behind the camera. In tak- ing groups the light should be somewhat to one ride of it, and well above the heads of the sitters, and that form of flash lamp is best where the magnesium powder can be spread out in a train parallel'with the line of the grep so that that bugbear of flashlight portraiture may be avoided, namely, heavy shadows, or " soot and whitelvash," to use a hackneyed term. • A Simple Intensifier.—For most amateur work bichromate is a convenient and very satisfactory agent, and gives permanent results. Potass Bichromate, 10 grains. Hydrochlor Acid, 20 min. Water, 1 oz: After bleaching with the above, wash, until the yellow stain is gone and then develop with amidol. Repeat several times if the first ap- plication does not give density enough. There is no need for a long washing after the plate has been originally fixed, and the redevelopment may be performed in daylight. Messrs. Burroughes and Wellcome , supply a good chromium intensifier in convenient tabloid form.

div.head: ANOTHER LOSS TO PHOTOGRAPHY.
div.p: ANOTHER LOSS TO PHOTOGRAPHY.

On May 2ith passed ;way Sir Joseph Swan, known to most people as the inventor, at the same time with Edison, of the incandescent elec- tric light. Can we imagine that it was so late as 1879 that Swan exhibited for the first time in England this Method of applying electricity to lighting our houses. For this invention be was knighted in 1904—late enough in all con- science—and death has deprived the Newcastle City Council of the long overdue pleasure of conferring the freedom of the city on her most distinguished apprentice—for he was born at Sunderland in 1828. But photographers will remember him as the inventor of the carbon process is we now know it. This was in 1864, soon after the great part- nership of Mawson and Swan had been estab- lished, as manufacturers of the collodion, so universally used at one time in the days of wet plates. It was he who introduced and patented the "transfer" process in carbon printing, and developing the tissue, after exposure, from the back. The beauty and delicacy of carbon print- ing, its exquisite range of colouring, and its absolute permanence have made it one of the most notable of photographic processes. SILVER-STREET.

This does not close 'until 27th June, so you have a; fortnight yet to write a nice, little letter. I hope to have a large number of entries.
Your loving UNCLE JACK.

SEALS AS PETS. It is rarely that one hears of a domesticated seal, except in the possession of professional animal trainers, but I am told, says a corre- spondent. that a certain Ross-shire gentleman has a pet of this sort, which comes to him like a dog when called by name. It swims after its master's boat in the bay, and comes back to land when the little craft is brought to her moorings. Only one tame seal ever came with- in my personal observation. Many years ago I stayed for some days at Port Appin, in the house of a retired sea captain.. I was much sur- prised to see a rather diminutive seal wobbling about the grounds, and making itself very much at home. I was informed that the captain hap- pened one day to take a stroll over the rocky, tangle-covered shore .at a time when the tide happened to be very low. He noticed a small seal lying at full length among the seaweed, and basking lazily in the hot summer sun. Very stealthily he advanced towards the dozing ani- mal. His caution was unnecessary. The creature soon became aware of his presence, but manifested no excitement or trepidation. Even when the captain had approached within. a couple of yards it made no attempt to retreat. A casual inspection was, however, sufficient to show that it was neither wounded nor otherwise ailing. It offered little opposition to being lifted and handled, and remained quite quies- cent while its captor carried it home. It adapted itself to its new surroundings, and be- came quite affectionate. If flung into the sea, it would speedily swim to land, and displayed' no extreme fondness for either salt or fresh water. 'Under normal conditions the common seal feeds entirely on 'fish. This specimen was distinctly omnivorous, and regaleA.elf with relish on bread, meat, cheese, ite anytliing that was offered. A small shed, well provided with straw, formed its dormitory.

div.head: AN UMBRELLA TRAGEDY.
div.p: AN UMBRELLA TRAGEDY.
" George," said a mother tq her little four- year-old, "you must take this umbrella to school with you, or you will be wet—it is rain- ing hard." - .
"I want the little one," he said, meaning a sunshade. ,
" No, my dear, that is for dry weather; you must take this and go like a good boy."
Georgie did as be was bidden, and got to school comfortably. After school, it had stopped raining, and Georgie trudged home with the remnants of the umbrella under his arm.

" Oh! Georgie, what have you been doing with my umbrella?" said his mother, when she saw the state it was in. "You should have let me have the little one, it took four of us to pull it through the school door."
OLD KING FROG. (BY STUART ROBERTSON.)

King Frog sat under his rhubarb tree, His waistcoat was speckled, his coat was brown ; And he piped a weird and wonderful glee, As he heard the rain on the leaves pour down; "Oh, I would I could bark like the butcher's dog," Was the burden chanted by old King Frog. :4! The butcher's dog was a bull-dog choice, Who adown to the brookside came each day, And cried " Wuff, Wuff !" in a deep bass voice; That frightened the ducks and the n drakes away, Each busily munching a plump young frog, Till scared by the " Wuff " of the butcher's dog.

Wise old King Frog to himself, said he, "I'll practise till I have a note like that, From the ducks and the drakes I shall then be free, And can live in peace with my froglings fat." So he squatted each night on a floating log, To practise the bark of the butcher's dog.

He practised hard, and he practised long, He puffed out his chest till his lower croak Made a growling" WO," like a Chinese gong, When its edge is cracked where the music broke; And the butcher cried to his wife, "Just hark! "Some rascal has stolen our bull-dog's bark !"

That was long ago, in the days gone by, 'Ere the stones jumped up, and the trees fell clown, And the green grass grew where you and I Now walk on the pavements of London Town; And of King Frog's kingdom, of which I speak, Nought is left but the name, which is "Barking Creek."

div.head: LATEST THING IN PINCE-NEZ.
div.p: THE LATEST THING IN PINCE-NEZ.

One of the latest things in pince-nez consists of a pocket case of the now popular rimless glasses, the bridge pieces being so fashioned that they are instantly detachable from the glass, and the wearer, from half a dozen spare glasses in his case, can select one in case of breakage and adjust it easily to the clip, like the spare blades of a safety razor. It is called the spillerflex, says the "Standard." The golfer's howl which rises on the breaking of the unprotected pince- nez miles from any succour is thus relegated to the fearsome past. Tortoiseshell rims—the rims our grandparents wore, but modernised—are all the fashion again, mainly as yet for indoor wear, though many are to be seen at the clubs and in the street. Up-to-date art has relieved the rims of the heavy appearance which caused tortoiseshell to fall into disfavour. The new rims are scarcely more apparent than gold. The smooth touch of tortoiseshell is much to be pre- ferred to that of any metal, and this fact, now that daintiness has also been secured, makes for the vogue.
Mr. D. C. Hogg, M.P. for Londonderry, who is lying seriously ill in Londonderry, is in a criti- cal condition.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
LIFE'S CRUCIBLES.
When roars the wind and beats the blast
And ceaseless wail the angry waves, And lightnings leap along the vast Above forlorn uncharted graves; When Faith shall fail, and Hope go out,
And neither God nor man seem near, When hearts at sea are sick with doubt, And hearts ashore are faint with fear: How calm is he whose goal is set Beyond the bounds of flood or fret!

When Need shall call and none shall come To brim the cup and break the crust, When Art is dead, and Song is dumb, And all the dream shall die in dust; When many fall with few to weep, When aim and deed alike decay, When eyes through gain forget to sleep, And lips through lure forget to pray : . How godlike, sure and unafraid Stands he who bath the future weighed!

When man is false and woman frail, When friend shall more than foe deceive, When Truth shall hide and Trust shall fail, And vice shall naught of virtue leave; When all of Heaven is hid above, And naught but Hell is beard below, When neither Cross, nor Ark, nor Dove Above the stricken sphere shall go: How fully God has armoured him Who strives though earth and sky be dim! —GEo. H. NETTLE.

MACHINERY AND THE HOME. The wives of working men still have to work, and work uncommonly hard. But machinery is destroying their homes, and not even giving them leisure in return. The conditions of modern industry are turning our working classes into a nomadic population. A man loses his job at Deal and hears of one at Durham. Straightway the whole family must move from one end of England to the other. Impossible to move much furniture. The solid, well-made chairs and tables which used to be a part of cottage plenishing would cost too much to move. Better bamboo tables and bentwood chairs, cheap and nasty, easy to move, easy to replace.
VIIPI

lanely responsible for the evil reputation which formerly attached to this class of work, as regards long hours and unhealthy workroom conditions, but of late years things have been greatly altered for the better, and good work- room hands can command twice the pay of shop assistants. After two years' apprenticeship a competent bodice or skirt hand can command .R. 2 a week, while a capable milliner's assistant can earn half as much or more after six months' training.

PlAeaatceodrdDioraesis)lessatainadg Ahalgseersi,aidneaSttlnylecso.me to stay, and many charming summer frocks have pleated skirts and tunics, the sleeves only being plain and rather loose. White plissé tunics over black taffetas skirts, with blouses also of plisse, are effective in voile and ninon. Frills and ruches are much in evidence, the latter so much so that they are in danger of being overdone. Plaids and stripes are a feature of linens, ging- hams and other cotton fabrics. Rather wide striped cotton gowns in striking contrasts such as black and rose, or white and mauve -- when pleated are most effective, and the wide stripe is somewhat modified. Stoles are not only graceful, but useful, for they give the necessary additional warmth that thin dresses require on chilly days. Algerian striped scarves, having some wool woven with the silk of which they are chiefly composed, are most comfortable wear just now-. They are light in weight, and can be used as sashes, should occasion arise; they therefore serve a double purpose.

This Season's Blouse. The chief feature of up-to-date blouses is their ; extreme simplicity of cut and make. Numbers are, of course, richly decorated with hand- worked and expensive embroideries, and the finest of fine lace, but the majority are made of patterned and very charming materials, cut on the Magyar lines, that require no further decoration. Or waistcoats of plain, white lawn, net, or tulle, are used to give contrast to figured fabrics. Stripes are largely employed for shirts and sports blouses, with plain collars and cuffs. In some cases the most extraordinary futurist patterned stuffs in equally extraordinary colourings are used, but when softened with tulle and net they are by no means unbecoming to the majority of their wearers. Thick silk and shantung—which is enjoying a revival—make very workmanlike shirts for morning wear, or for tennis and golf. Of all the materials shown this year, cotton crepon bears the palm for
economy, since it is easily laundered at home. Some of the new tailored shirts are cut to resemble a man's coat and have small revers, that can be worn open or closed.

Sports Coats. The Sports Coat has become an important item of the wardrobe, the cold winds of this Spring having caused it to be in great demand. Designers have, therefore, turned their attention more particularly to it, and efforts have been made, though not with much success hitherto, to evolve a combination of the fashionable cape (which is useless for games) and the coat. A shape of quite another genre, attractive in its simplicity, is tight-fitting, buttons closely down the front, and reaches almost to the knees. But it is somewhat trying to a short, stumpy figure, and should be worn only by the tall, slim, and graceful girl. The bolero coatee has invaded the domain of sport, and if not very practical is smart and novel, with its pleated basque below the waist. The new striped woven coats are warm and light, and with white roll collar and 1 cuffs, and white bpttons, are among the most useful of this season's style. Hoods appear on many of the cape-coats, but present a decidedly clumsy look, and have little to recommend them from an artistic point of view.

Hats and Veils. t Ascot is expected to settle the 'fate of the , larger hat, and nothing could be more attractive than the advance models in white and delicate ' tints, with tegal crowns and lined brims that have been prepared for this fashionable meeting. The crowns are garlanded with huge blooms of roses, pansies, or poppies, without foliage. Black hats are trimmed with bleac,hed foliage, and a natural rose, or upstanding posies of green foliage with bleached flowers. Among veils, the newest is a clear fish net. In fact, so clear are many of the nets that they are almost invisible. Short veils have deep borders of chenille, pat- terned to represent foliage or flowers, those of the harem type have borders just beneath the eye, where the net is very clear. Lace is also much worn, and for motoring there are pretty veils in washing ninon in black and white, and in champagne tints. A pretty trimming has been devised for the Panama hat that makes a welcome change to the inevitable black velvet band. This trimming consists of a flexible feather, which, like the band, surrounds the crown, and can be tied in a bow at the side with upright ends. It is in brilliant colourings and rather narrow, but very effective and novel.

div.head: COOKERY CORNER.
div.p: COOKERY CORNER.
Steamed Egg and Cheese.

Delicious for breakfast or supper. Butter breakfast cups according to the number you require, and into each put two or three pieces of butter, two tablespoonfuls breadcrumhs, and two tablespoonfuls of grated cheese. Then drop in egg, adding pinch of salt, and a good shake of pepper. Add again the same quantity of cheese, and lastly breadcrumbs, with a few tiny pieces of butter on top. Put buttered paper round top, and steam for fifteen minutes.

div.head: Sand Cake.
div.p: Sand Cake.

This cake melts in your mouth. Two ozs. butter, 40z. castor sugar, 2 eggs, 40z. corn flour, 1 tablespoon ordinary flour, 1 teaspoon baking powder. Beat butter and sugar to a cream, add 1 egg at a time, and beat; then add flour and cornflour, baking powder last. Grease and line tin. Bake half an hour in the middle of a moderate oven. VOW

By MARJORIE.

The Ball for Countess Nada Torby. One of the most brilliant and certainly the most lavish entertainment of this season will be the ball to be given by Countess Torby at the Hyde Park Hotel this month. No fewer than two thousand guests are invited, and the decora- tions will be on a princely scale. The Countess and her sister are both devoted to sport and to an outdoor life, and are well known in society, for their father—the Grand Duke Michael of Russia—has spent the greater part of his mar- ried life in this country. Countess Torby is a morganatic wife.

Women at Kew Gardens. There are no women gardeners at Kew, but several women are employed in the Herbarium and engaged in important scientific work in various branches konnected with plant life. Some of the ladies gained entrance to these posts in open competition with men. Miss E. M. Wakefield holds a special appointment in connection with plant diseases and fungi. The holder of the earliest appointment given to women is Miss M. Smith, a plant artist, who began her work in 1878. She makes coloured plates for the Botanical Magazine, first pub- lished in 1787. In addition a lady assists in the library, and another is busy on the "Index Kewensis," an important work. There are many women students in the Herbarium, and visitors interested in botany are more frequently foreigners than English—notably Americans and Japanese.

Dearth of Workroom Hands. In London, and also in the provincial towns, the dressmaking and millinery trades are com- plaining of the dearth of apprentices. Young girls on leaving school prefer to become typists, or waitresses, or anything else that offers a broader outlook in life than the dull and drab surroundings of the workroom, and it is becom- ing a serious problem for dressmakers and milliners where to look for all the skilled labour they require. div.head: MEMS. FOR MOTHERS.
div.p: MEMS. FOR MOTHERS.
The Open-air for Children.

We are now justified in expecting fine, sunny dry weather, when the children can spend every available minute out of doors. Where there are fields, grassy lanes, or a wood, the younger ones, not yet at school, should be sent off as soon after breakfast as possible with a basket of plain, wholesome food, and in charge of an older child. If there is a baby, its bottle of milk, or Mellin's (or other) Food, may be kept warm in a tea- cosy or a folded blanket.

Some Precautions. Take the precaution of strapping a waterproof and an extra shawl to the baby's carriage in the event of a shower, and your children will be safe and happy for hours. I omitted to suggest that a lemonade bottle of water—not milk—will be necessary, and also a small enamelled cup, for the convenience of drinking, may be packed up. Food taken out of doors is said to be more easily digested, and, as for the enjoyment, we all know how delightful it is to have our tea in the garden, when and where fate permits.
