And in the nomadic life you make no friends, only acquaintances. There is a certain strength and dignity of character, the endowment of people who are allowed to take root—to live in the house in which their fathers lived, to have for their friends the neighbours whose fathers were their fathers' friends, to pluck the fruit from the trees their fathers planted, and in their turn to plant trees of which their little sons, grown to manhood, shall pluck the fruit. This sterling quality must for ever be absent from a nomadic population. And the working woman imitates and always will imitate, in so far as She can, the dress, the habits and the evasions of her richer sister. She no longer cooks dinner every day. Why bother, when you can buy a tin of machine-packed meat? She no longer makes a soda-cake for Sunday. Is not the far-famed cake, dry as a Sodom apple, to be bought at the shop round tbe corner? She no longer makes her children's clothes. The ready-made things save her that trouble. And she shops, just as her richer sister shops, in the Broad-streets and the High- streets, and where the barrows line the gutters on a Saturday night. The very rich are beginning, in a vague, half- conscious way, to protest against machinery— they will have hand-carved furniture, hand- woven cloths, hand-sewn garments. But these protestants are few, and the Genie is very strong. Machinery should have been our slave and we have allowed it to become our Taster. Thous- ands of men who might have been using their eyes, hands, and brains in making something useful and beautiful are condemned to spend ten hours a day watching a machine make something ugly, and, as like as not, useless. Thousands of women with clever hands and able brains and brave hearts, who might have been making homes, are making blouses all alike at twopence-halfpenny each, or pinafores at twopence-halfpenny a dozen, or matchboxes at twopence-halfpenny a gross. And the world is steadily growing uglier and uglier and uglier.— From "Homes and Housewives of the Future," by Mrs. E. Nesbit in the "Pall Mall Magazine."

div.head: BY A LADY CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY A LADY CORRESPONDENT.

It is interesting to note what effects the en-1 franchisement of women has had in those coun- tries where it is already in operation. It has acted briefly in three ways: (1.) By decreasing intemperance, drink being one of the most powerful factors as far as' im- morality is concerned. (2.) By strengthening the position of the girl, by seeing to it that she has a living wage. (3.) By making immorality a more dangerous practice to men, in that women have succeeded in raising the age of consent, and imbued the judicial mind with a more serious view of the nature of assaults. We have also the testimony of public men to the elevating influence of women's votes. "It tends greatly to purify corruption and promote better government." (Chief Justice Fischer.) "Politically, the effect has been immeasurably uplifting and beneficial." (Governor James N. Brady.) "Women's influence has been on the side of clean government." (Hon. George Foulds, Minister of Education.) In a recent address to the Grand Jury of the Supreme Court in New Zealand, the Chief Jus- tice said he had been looking over the criminal statistics, and he found during the last three years there had been a marked decrease of crime throughout the country. The number of per- sons dealt with in the Supreme Court was 544 in 1909, and 426 in 1911, while during those years the population had steadily increased. According to the Criminal Amendment Acts (New Zealand) of 1906 and 1910, it has been made possible to detain indeterminately `moral imbeciles and degenerates of both sexes, while in Colorado, since 1901, there has been an Act for the detention and protection of the feeble- minded.

div.head: "RACE SUICIDE."
div.p: "RACE SUICIDE."

Next let us consider that bugbear of modern sociologists, the declining birth-rate. The numerical increase of the population in any country depends, of course, upon the rela- tionship between birth-rato and death-rate, i.e., on the natural increase of births over deaths. When, for instance, in New Zealand, this stood recently ae18.07 per 1,000, in England and Wales it was only 12.13. Again, New Zealand has the lowest death-rate in the world. Australia ranks next, and her birth-rate is on the increase, her marriage-rate the highest on record, and her infant mortality the lowest. For those who hanker after our old enormous birth-rate, the statistics of the colonies should bring consolation. Surely a low birth-rate, with a death-rate also low—provided of course that the natural increase is maintained —is a more ideal State of affairs. But there may be some whose bugbear, on the other hand, is the prolific increase of the working classes. Let them also take comfort. LETTERS BY AN IRISHMAN. Survey of the Facts Governing the Demand for Home Rule. V.—IRELAND UNDER THE UNION

—(continued). The answer is two forces acting together. First a party in Parliament, consisting of the ablest and most trusted men in Ireland, who in Par- liament declared war on Parliament itself; who obstructed business; who created public scan- dal; 'who outraged all traditional decorum; above all, who refused to have any responsi- bility for the government of Ireland, or accept the smallest post save in a self-governed Ireland.

To this violent agitation in Parliament was added a still more violent agitation in Ireland. A land war was declared. Continued resistance to rent was accompanied by many terrible crimes. Under these circumstances the English Government under the Union felt that it was necessary to do something. Mr. Gladstone's great Land Act of 1881 was passed, which established the principle that fair rent must be legally assessed and that famine prices for lanel should no longer be extorted; and in this way gave the fixity of tenure which had been con- ceded to Protestant farmers in Ulster a century earlier.

Mr. Gladstone's measure was bitterly opposed 1 by the Tory party; but once it passed the Tory 1 party adopted and extended its principles. Yet their principles were English ideas. Mr. Par- nell from the first desired a policy of State-aided purchase. After twenty-two years of cumbrous and costly experiment it was seen that Parnell's 1 policy was right, and the Unionist party adopted it in 1903. Only since that date has any marked improvement in Ireland set in. Yet the foun- dation was laid in 1879-80. The Land League, with Davitt as its founder, and not the English Government gave to Irish labouring farmers security for the result of their labour. And 1 the Land League was denounced by Tory States- men as a "League of Hell"; jails in Ireland were crammed with advocates of the League's Policy, including every prominent Nationalist M.P. Men were punished by every means for 1 taking the steps necessary to reform—not neces- sary under a rational and national Govern- ment, but necessary under the Union. The legislation of England for Ireland has been marked by one unfailing characteristic. One reform after another has been demanded by argument, eloquently set out by accredited speakers in Westminster, basing themselves upon expediency and justice; and every such reform has been denied until the Irish people, abandoning argument, had recourse either to open rebellion or to criminal conspiracy. make . In e 1779 the grant of Free Trade between the countries and in 1782 the concession of legisla- tive independence was made because the Volun- teers s in theirnlrelahnadnddse—mlanndleBdoo tih,ietset t.od things with the Union acceptable by promisint. aqnzlity of rights to Catholics. That promise was broken and for 29 years four-fifths of the Irish people agitated for the right to have representatives of their own religion returned to Parliament. Argument was laughed out of Court or voted down; and Catholic Emancipation was ulti- mately conceded by the Duke of Wellington on the admitted ground that the only alternative was Civil War. "LAND WAR" SINCE THE UNION. Before 1881 only one other great measure of justice to Ireland was accomplished—the dis- establishment of the Irish Church in 1889: That was avowedly clue to the Fenian Rising. From 1870 onwards Bill after Bill for the betterment of the Irish people was rejected. There was no time to discuss Irish topics—the only means of ruling Ireland was by coercion and Parliament always found time to pass Coercion Bills. Mr. A. J. Balfour, realising that the repeated intro-

duction of Coercion Bills occupied time, cele- brated the year of Queen Victoria's Jubilee by passing the Perpetual Coercion Act, which is still in force, and which can be put into opera- tion for any part of Ireland, or the whole, by the simple issuing of an Order from Dublin Castle. Some of these Coercion Acts were needed to enforce the payment of tithes by Roman Catholics to the Established Church; but the object of the vast majority has been to facilitate that process of eviction, which was distinctive of the Irish land system. Mr. Barry O'Brien says in, his "home Ruler's Manual ":

The Land Question, perhaps, affords the fair- est test of the capacity of the Imperial Parlia- ment to legislate for Ireland. There has been a land war in Ireland since the Union. The Imperial Parliament has been powerless to end it. Over and over again it has proved before Royal Commissions and Parliamentary Com- mittees that the system of land tenure was a source of evil, and even danger; but Parlia- ment did nothing to remove the evil, to avert the danger. What was the system of land tenure? The landlord let "land." The tenant improved it---built, drained, fenced, made the land a "farm." The landlord raised the rent to the enhanced value. The tenant, who had exhausted his resources in bringing the land under cultivation_ was unable to pay. The landlord evicted him, and appropriated his im- provements without allowing him a copper's compensation for them.

The right of ejection for non-payment of rent without a special clause of re-entry in the con- tract was declared by Sir Charles Russell to have no existence in England. A man who owed rent could only be proceeded against as if he owed any other bill. Yet in England if a man was put out from one farm, he could get another; failing a farm other trades were open to him. In Ireland there was nothing but the land, and for every farm there were many applicants. A sentence of ejectment was a writ of banishment, and every man whose rent was in arrears was subject to eviction. But eviction was not only undertaken for non-payment of rent. It was used as a tyrannical weapon. For instance, at Glenveagh, in Co. Donegal, because a bailiff bad been killed, Mr. Adair evicted all the families from a whole district—some five hundred families in all. But we will leave this portion of Irish history and consider briefly the results. of the Union. RESULTS UNDER THE UNION.

First, thirty years after Great Britain had assumed the complete responsibility for the government of Ireland—not being seriously im- peded by the presence of 100 Irish members in a Parliament of over 600—England had suc- ceeded in crushing out the manufacturing in- terests in Ireland, except the linen trade, in which she herself was not seriously interested; and she had converted Ireland into a farm, pro- ducing raw and unmanufactured produce for the English manufacturer and the English con- sumer. This was the object to which all the laws in restraint of Irish trade and commerce were directed during the eighteenth century, and this object, so long as Ireland had even a subservient Parliament, was never achieved. Did fifty years of the Union bring the two peoples (Irish and English) closer together? The '4B famine undoubtedly evoked great com- passion and great charity in England, but Ire- land did not ask for charity or for compassion. She asked for justice and for freedom. In the face of that sinister result of half a century's law-making and administration when the Irish people were much poorer than before the Union, could afford to buy much less of the most ordinary articles of consumption and were pay- ing a greatly increased amount of taxes upon the lessened quantities they bought—by an alien power, she demanded with greater fierceness than ever the right to manage her own affairs. (Next week: Conclusion of this Article, and "How the Union stands to-day.") •

COUNCILLOR GOUGH'S QUERIES.
A Buttermarket-street

There was a discussion at the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening Over an item whieh appeared in the private agenda. Councillor GOUGH said there was a matter which required some explanation. He noticed that Mr. Segar Owen appeared before the Street Improvement Committee and made a claim on behalf of Councillor Craik for extra payment with regard to the erection of his new shop in Buttermarket-street. He (Councillor Gough) would like to know on what ground the com- mittee refused his claim and whether it was likely to be repeated at an early date. More- over, was it a fact that the Corporation paid to Mr. Craik for his premises £2,000 in cash three years ago, Which he (Councillor Gough) consid- ered was .000 more than they were worth? The MAYOR : The Council have passed that, and you cannot re-open the question. Councillor GOUGH : I want to know whether ,! the Corporation gave him in addition 82 square yards of land? The MAYOR: Whatever was clone year; ago has been sanctioned by the Council. You have to discuss the minute now. Councillor Gomm: This is a fresh claim. The MAYOR,: • Will you kindly deal with the fresh claim? Councillor GOUGH : I was only trying to get to know whether these were facts and whether • they were the grounds for the committees refusal.

-'I;i7;97kAYOR : We cannot carry in our heads three years' work. If you give notice of that question. it will be answered by the Chairman. I cannot pretend to remember, and I don't sup- pose the others do. Councillor GOUGH : I think myself, from what I have gathered, that he has been very well paid, that this ought to settle the claim, and that no further claim ought to have been put in. The minutes were approved.

div.head: COLD-STORED EGGS.
div.p: COLD-STORED EGGS.

Many a good case has been ruined by exag- geration. It never pays to over-state, and more often than not, it does considerable damage to the cause it is meant to benefit. A statement was made a little time ago, by those who should have known better, to the effect that "the cold- storage egg is better than any fresh egg ever laid." This is truly an astonishing claim, and it would appear as though those responsible for such a pronouncement are in a somewhat tight corner, from which they hope to escape by bluff. That, however, appears to have been stated by defenders of the cold-storage interests in America, where this system is very general in- deed, partly owing to the hue size of the coun- try and the need for transporting food products over long distances. Fortunately, with us the conditions are very different and a local de- mand in many cases dispenses with the need for cold-storage on a sufficient scale to make busi- ness profitable. Whilst it is true that for shorter periods cold-storage is of the greatest value, equalising supplies and preventing slumps in prices, such does not in any way alter the fact that when eggs and chickens are held under low temperatures for a prolonged period changes take place, which, in some cases, appear to be detrimental to food value. The problem is suffi- ciently complex without the publication of claims which everyone kr ows cannot be sus- tained.

Roughley, who was beaten 21-14 by Monks, and was ruled ineligible at a meeting of the Council on Monday evening. The Conserva- tives, therefore, enter the fourth round. - In the Consolation Competition, however. Rylands' No. 2 beat Woolston by 26 points, wiping off a defeat of 20 at Gorsey-lane by a win of 46. Woolston had the best of matters in four games at home and did not lose the other three by large thajorities, but at Rylands' only one of their men won, P. div.head: 'third Round. BULL'S • HEAD_ WIN.
div.p: 'third Round. BULL'S • HEAD_ WIN.

At Church-street, against the King and Queen men, the only team in the running was the homesters, who, returning every winning card, won by 72 points, not an opponent getting more than 14 points. At Padgate-lane they did not do at all badly, for their majority was only reduced by 17 points. Here, however, the King and Queen men played in commendable style, and if the other three players had fol- lowed the example set them by the winning four, we should probably be recording the match differently. CROFT BEATEN BOTH WAYS.

Whi-tec. ross added to their successes when at Croft they beat the homesters by ten points, and at Lovely-lane won by 29 points. For quality of play the games at Croft were the better, for the homesters knew their land well and played to win with confidence, which, how- ever, was soon shattered by the victorious team. After well-fought games Warburton and Hatton only lost by two points each. It was a well-deserved victory on both matches, and we only hope the Whitecross men will go much further.

div.head: e ee
div.p: e ee
Consolation Competition.

Crosfield's were only successful in beating Hutching's Tannery by five points on the home- and-home matches, Hutching's winning by 31 points at home and Crosfield's by 36 points. Both matches were full of inten?st, and the smart- ness of style and accurate judgment of the Payers on both sides was plainly manifested. Both were good matches from every point of view. FEARNHEAD LOSE. Winning at Fearnhead and at home the Cemetery team entered the second round with a total majority of 56 points. The Fearnhead men, although they played excellently, ,were no match for their opponents, especially at the Cemetery Hotel. At , Fearnhead W. Weston returned a good card against T. Ellison, who, after having led 14-9 at the 17th end, lost by three points in 29 ends. T. Quarrie looked like winning when he led 19-14 against P. Croft, but this was his final score, Croft pulling up well, to win 21-19 in 28 ends. At the Ceme- tery Hotel J. Roberts and J. Bradshaw played the best games for the visitors, the former only losing 19-21 against F. Yarwood, and the latter winning 21-12 against R. Brobbin. The match at Fearnbead was undoubtedly the best from a spectator's point of view.

div.head: BIG WIN.
div.p: A BIG WIN.

Against Earlestown, Walker's Brewery were beaten by 91 points away, but won by 31 points at home. They had not the slightest chance at Earlestown, but in the match at Warrington some good cards were returned. J. Roberts put up a good game against J. Ogden, for after having been 5-14 in arrears, he pulled up to 17-19, but on the nest length Ogden got his winning couple in. The game between T. Savage and J. Dagnall was a very tight one, the players peeling at 9 and 18, and never being More than two points ahead of each other. On the 24th length Savage made his score into 20-19, but two successive singles gave Dagnall the winning point. Spencer, for Earlestown, and Rodgers and Bates for Warrington, re- turned splendid cards of 21-17, 21-11, and 21-12 respectively. The Liberal Club play the Stag, Walton, to- day, and their teams will be :—Away: 31. Tobin (captain), F. Walker, J. Broadhurst, jun., C. Jordan, A. Lawton, J. Middleton, and T. Drew; reserve, R. Benion; referee, George Shaw.

div.head: WORKS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WORKS' ASSOCIATION.

The matches in the second round of this com- petition were keenly contested, one of the closest matches being that in which the Assur- ance Agents beat P. and K. Boiler Yard by two points. P. and K. Rolling Mill men, however, won a glorious victory over Rylands' Wet Shop by 25 points, winning on all but four games. The Warrington Tanning Co. were just the five points better than the Corpbration team, although the handicap had a lot to do with the result. Walker's No. 1 played well to dispose of Guest Bros.' Tannery men by 14 points, for the vanquished had a large handicap start. All. the other games were full of interesting incidents, and there will be another good day's sport to-day, when the third round will be commenced.

div.head: WORKS BOWLING MAIN.
div.p: WORKS BOWLING MAIN.

- The annual bowling main in connection with Messrs. R. A. Naylor, Ltd., took place on Sat- urday, when a party of about GI) journeyed to *le Stamford Arms Hotel, Bollington. The games were four-handed, and three rounds were finished before a halt was called for tea, which was supplied by Mr. Cohen. Play was resumed after the tea interval, and the following were the principal prize-winners: Messrs. E. Caw- ley, A. Cant, J. Howarth, F. Morris, J. Bray- thing, J. P. Davenport, R. Wicks, and C. Phil- lips. `The entrants numbered 48, which formed a record, and the prizes competed for were to the value of £9. After an enjoyable day's sport the return journey was made at nine o'clock. The prizes were presented by Mr. Shakeshaft on Wednesday evening in the works' dining-room at Howley Mills.

CRICKEI.
'WARRINGTON'S UNFINISHED
GAME.

A Draw In Favour of the Local Men. It was very hard luck on Warrington that after declaring in the match with the East Cheshire Wanderers at 166 for seven wickets they could not dispose of the other side within the time limit. Time came to the Wanderers' assistance when they had lost eight wickets for 82 rims.

For Warrington, W. Richardson was not up to past form with the bat and was caught with only seven to his credit. B. Silcock was round in hitting trim and he carried out his bat with a nicely compiled 60. S. L. Partridge made a useful 31. _ _ _

S. Parid e was in equally as good form with the ball, and in seven overs, four of which were "maidens." he took three wickets at the cost of three runs, really a clever bowling feat. Hannam had three wickets for 43, W. Bennett one for 10, and B. Silcock one for 15.

div.head: RYLANDS' BEAT DIVEX.
div.p: RYLANDS' BEAT DIVEX.

Bylands'-s-ecured an easy victory over Dives by 69 runs for four wickets against a Dives total of 48. T. Barnett was the best scorer for Dives and made 25 before he was run out. J. Waywell made a nice 21 for the winners. A. Bramball knocked 19, and S. Carter 17. McGowan, for Rylands', took six wickets at the cost of 14 runs.

div.head: EMMANUEL BEAT RYLANDS' IL
div.p: EMMANUEL BEAT RYLANDS' IL

Emmanuel are to be complimented on the fine performance by beating the Rylands' second team to the tune of 63 runs. A spirit of keen rivalry was shown all through the game, but the Rylands' eleven made a very poor show against the formidable bowling of the Brothers S. and A. Hughes. A. Hughes also knocked up top score, hitting out lustily for 18. W. Knight made a good second with 17 to his credit. The fielding of the Emmanuel team was remarkably good. STOCKTON HEATH DEFEATED.

Bold-street Wesleyans, playing at Appleton, defeated Stockton Heath by five runs. The "Heathens" batted first, and although they lost five wickets for seven runs, they managed to knock up 33. It was mainly through the fine start given Bold-street by W. Cooper (13) that the Wesleyans compiled 38 before dis- missal. For Bold-street, L. W. Weaver took six wickets for 16 runs, and W. Stringer four for 11.

div.head: WORKING MEN'S MISSION STILL WINNING.
div.p: WORKING MEN'S MISSION STILL WINNING.

Cairo-street entertained Working Men's Mis- sion at Arpley on Saturday. Both teams had unbeaten certificates. The Mission have only lost one match in two seasons, and they won in an easy fashion by 47 to 24, being superior in every position. T. O'Neil and S. Lloyd batted excellently for 15 and eight respec- tively for the Mission, while S. Lloyd took eight wickets for 11 runs. This win places the Mis- sion at the head of the League table, a position they held all last season, and which they will hold at the end of this season, judging by their present form.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
W arrington Workingmen's Associa-
N.A. CENTRE.
DELEGATES' REPORT.

At an Executive Council meeting held at the Odsall Hotel, Odsall-lane, Salford, Mr. B. 0. Atherton in the chair, representatives were present from Bolton, Crewe, Preston, Oldham, Salford, Atherton, Hollinwood, Horwich, Little Lever, Plank Lane, St. Helens, Wigan, and Warringto4:

A report from the National Federation stated that the N.A.A. carried out the English cham- pionship match at Chester in a very bad way. This is the first commelit on the match that has not been satisfactory. The Press at the time said there was great improvement both in the pegging out of the land and the manage- ment. However, those who criticised the N.A.A. will soon have the arrangements in their hands, and it is hoped they will do better than the N.A.A. If so, anglers will have a treat, as there will be no difficulty in finding their pegs; as far as Warrington, they refuse to give assistance in any shape or form. THE RIVER WYE.

The Secretary read a report on the River Wye that was very interesting. He stated that 25 tons of salmon had been taken annually for several seasons, with rod and line. After the spawning 103 were found dead on top, ranging from 201 b. to 4011?. This thing occurs every year after spawning, and no alarm need be taken.

THE WEAVER. The report from Messrs. Stout and Potter was read concerning the Weaver, and a discussion followed. Mr. Stout answered all questions on the matter. After discussing the Bd. per mem- ber per annum, it was agreed that all delegates persuade their clubs to consider it and give the Northern Anglers' waters for at least one season.

TRAVELLING CARDS. The Secretary remarked on the price of the travelling cards, pointing out the advantages the angler has over other associations, by his card only costing 41. Besides his cheap travel- ling, he has more than 200 miles of fishing, including the Gowy. It was stated that if the cards were raised to Is. each there would be more than 8,000 subscribing, and the N.A.A. could then take over waters for all their mem- bers, whenever any opportunity occurred that would benefit any centre. Warrington is strongly in favour of this, as they think it is a step in the right direction. Waters could be taken over and stocked at very little expense to the angler.

CLOSE SEASON. The close season came in for sharp criticism. Warrington was brought over the coals for tak- ing pike, and several delegates alleged that eels were also included. As far as Warrington N.A. are concerned. they forbid members from taking Ilk% but td stop eels also would be about the limit. We are not to ask what other associations are doing, but we must look to our members to the best of their advantage. We think (speaking plainly) that it is about time the P.F.P.L. came to some decision over these affairs. If one society is pledged to uphold tffe Mundella Act in its entirety, others should be made to toe the line, and it is time we had INisiation regarding , pike and eels in streams where they are destruc- tive to the coarse fish. If we are out to protect coarse fish let us by all means protect them in a manner that will leave no room for coin- ; ment.

THE GOWY. Nothing great is yet weighed in from the Gowy, a trout of 9oz. 11th'. heading the list. But before the next lot of notes appear anglers will be getting ready in earnest. Up to the present the maggot and feeder are very scarce, but a few will be found for the canals, to try for the magnificent specials. Will the Northern Anglers of Warrington fish their opening event at Aintree?

BLCKLEY-sTREET P.S.A.

The monthly meeting of the above was held on Sunday, Mr. J. Urmston presiding. The speaker was Mr. Adams, of Tyldesley, his sub- ject being " The voice of God." Two solos were rendered, one by Miss E. Stanway, "Hark ! there comes a whisper," and one by Mr. J. Richardson, "Saved by grace." Mr. G. H. Cox was the accompanist.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.

The Wycliffe P.S.A. meeting was presided over by Mr. B. Farrar on Sunday, when the Rev. T. T. James, president of the society, delivered his monthly address, which was upon "The National Campaign." The speaker said that to make the work of the campaign—the rescue of the unsaved—pos- sible, it was necessary for them to get hold of the first principles of Christ. Firstly, they must share with others everything they had, and not isolate themselves from the world; in this manner they would make religion a living thing. Again, they could not give to others without themselves feeling the value of it. They would imbue their fellows with the idea that their lives were as precious as anybody else's. When a great picture or a great work was destroyed, men exclaimed "What a shame !" But how much more precious was the great temple of the human soul ! Its value was in- finite. Hut, thirdly, they could not take Christ to others unless they had Him in their own hearts. These they must surrender to God, so that He might teach them the value of their own souls; thus they might reach others. The Chairman having thanked Mr. James for his timely address, Miss Howell sang " The Nazarene" expressively, Mr. W. 11. Payton pre- siding at the organ. Mr. Wright read the lesson and the Chairman lead the prayer. One new member received a hearty welcome.

div.head: Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Sunday School Anniversary.

What Lancashire people are pleased to desig- nate the Sunday school " sermons" include usually everything else but sermons, the minis- ter merely performing the duties of a chairman, and his address being " brief, bright and brotherly." The services held in connection with the Bold- street Wesleyan Sunday school anniversary were, however, distinguished, not only by the excellence of the musical part of the programme, but also by two very powerful, practical and masterly sermons preached by the Rev. Dr. Hy. Haigh, and by able addresses from Mr. J. Gauld and Mr. T. Deakin. Dr. Haigh had pleased his hearers at he anni- versary of 1913, and the return visit was an added pleasure and a further attraction to the large circle of friends who delight to visit the mother church of Methodism upon these special occasions.

The scholars of the Sunday school, young and old, were seated in the galleries on either side of the chapel, and it was pleasing to see the bright faces and to hear the special tunes which they had rehearsed for the day. It was also very noticeable that among those who rose to take part in the "children's hymns" were tiny mites of two and three years, and " children " of a much larger growth and more mature years. The adult section of the school is very strong; and this speaks well for the work which Bold-street is endeavouring to carry on. The musical side of the service was very good, and the contributions by the choir materially added to its success.

In the morning the reverend gentleman dwelt upon the words "God thinks about me," and in the evening he chose his text from Luke xix. 10. The words of the text were, "The Son of Man is come to seek and to save that which was lost."

The 'text contained in a sentence an epitome of the Incarnation; the motive and method underlying all its teaching. The whole Bible was a boundless exposition and illustration of the text, and without the context found in the 15th chapter, it was too vast for the mind to comprehend. The word " lost " was, perhaps, the saddest word in the English language, for it conveyed the idea that the door was for ever shut. Christ, however, never used the word in the sense that there was no hope. It was employed as a word of tender regret, but not of 'repudiation. It sug- gested trouble, but never breathed despair. Dr. Haigh asked the question, " Who are the lost?" The context spoke of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. All these might ap- pear out-of-date illustrations, but on closer ex- amination it was seen that the Bible was the most up-to-date book in the world. The sheep was lost to safety. It had followed its own im- pulse without considering where it was going and what it was leaving. The modern " sheep " did not mean any harm. It merely wished to follow its own impulses, and in so doing drugged the conscience and left the will idle.

The coin was lost to service. Every person had an office to fill, a cause to battle for, and a life to influence. Most people were not doing their duty. Parents often failed in the duty of rightly training their children. The son was lost to home with its safeguards. Satisfactions and inspirations. Many "Sons" to-day were lost to the home of God, which was represented by the Christian Church. The message of the text was that Christ came to seek man, whereas the other great religions of the world made man seek God. Christ re- deemed all men from peril, and restored them to service ana to home. The afternoon gathering took the form of a flower service. Mr. T. Deakin, • who presided, spoke on the value of Sunday school work, and appealed for St more practical interest in , the school. Mr. James Gauld addressed the scholars on the proverb, "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches." The contributions by Mr. T. Bradford Barton were especially fine and much appreciated. Miss D. Caine sang "My heart ever faithful," and Miss Cotton gave recitation. " The total collections for the day were 12s. 6d. The officers and teachers of the school are very grateful to all who so generously ' assisted to achieve this success.

LANC.A.SHIRE MIDSUMMER QUARTER SESSIONS. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS OF THE PEACE for the County of Lancaster will be holden at the Castle of Lancaster on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the fore- noon; and by adjournment at the following places and times, viz.:— At the Court House. in Preston, on WEDNES- DAY, the let day of jply next, at Ten o'clock in the forenoon. At the County Sessions House, in Liverpool, on TUESDAY, the 14th day of July next, at Half-past Ten o'clock in the forenoon. At the Assize Courts, in Manchester, on MONDAY. the 27th day of July next, at Half-past Ten o'clock n the forenoon. The Solicitors engaged in Prosecutions at the said Sessions are requested to take notice that all Depositions and Instructions for indictments are required to be sent to the Clerk of the Peace's Office seven days at least before the said Sessions respec- . YHAECOURT E. CLARE, Clerk of the Peace. Clerk of the Peace's Office, Preston, 11th June, 1914.

question was or was not Cheshire cheese. He contended that any cheese made in Cheshire from Cheshire milk was Cheshire cheese. If the Bench decided otherwise he submitted that his , client acted honestly and in ignorance, and it was not a casein which a heavy penalty should be imposed. DEFENDANT FINED. I After a short, private deliberation, the Chair- man said that from the evidence they were of the opinion that Cheshire cheese must be made from practically whole milk, and that cheese from practically whole mirk could not be pro- duced with a less percentage than 24 per Cent. of fats. As that sample only contained 17 per cent. it was not, in their opinion, fine Cheshire cheese. Defendant would, therefore, be fined £1 and costs.

OUR ANNUAL REST. A Rambling Dissertation on the Holiday Problem.- - PLEASURES AT HAND. Who is not interested nowadays in the ques- tion of the annual holiday? There may be an occasional Scrooge here and there who is miser- ab'e and who refuses to acknowledge the right of anyone else to be happy; but we are essen- tially a holiday-taking, pleasure-seeking people. An unparalleled period of prosperity, during which the material conditions of the people have steadily improved, has brought this about. Half a century ago a visit to the seaside was reserved for the upper-middle classes, a trip abroad was the " finishing " of an aristocrat's "education." Free Trade, education, facilities for travelling, built up by invention quickened by increasing interest in life, have changed all that. Look at the places around our shores, places that have sprung up almost spontaneously, and compare

A West Country Holiday. THERE is a subtle charm about the beautiful West of England— The Cornish Riviera or Glorious Devon—that is felt nowhere else in the Kingdom. It is a charm that the North-countryman will 'especially appreciate because he will contrast the scenic splendour of the West with that of the North. He will enjoy the mild, equable climate of the West—its heritage. And while his health is being benefited his interest will be maintained in the shire which gave birth to the Elizabethan Sea Kings, or in the " Delectable Duchy." " Holiday Haunts." Who would not go to see where Scott laboured and Burns's genius consumed him? Blarney Castle has its special attractions, for is there not a stone, reverenced by a nation, of which it has been written : There is a stone there That whoever kisses Oh! he never misses To grow eloquent. 'Tis lie may clamber To a lady's chamber, Or become a Member Of Parliament. A clever spouter He'll sure turn out, or . An out-and-outer, To be left alone. Don't hope to hinder him Or to bewilder him: Sure he's a pilgrim From the Blarney Stone. The thing is to kiss the stone, which may become a comparatively easy task when aero- planes have become perfect machines. TOWN OR COUNTRY? It really matters very little whether one goes to a town or to a country place for one's annual rest. It is again a matter of taste. To the busy city man the ideal holiday would be in the country, away from hustling and bam- boozling methods that enslave him during the rest of the year. There is the cry of the country for all of us more potent and deep- seated even than the call of the sea. HINTS ON HEALTH. The Cure of Varts. When these are soft and flat nothing cures them quicker than a dose of Epsom Salts or any other salt of Magnesia each morning. In some way this has the power to dissolve them com- Pletely. When they are hard then nothing beats Glacial Acetic Acid. This should be applied by a match dipped into the fluid, and it is better to he done after the top has been shaVed off by a razor. Once a day is sufficient, but it should be continued for many days. A Prescription. It is a little painful, and the following is less SO: Salicylic Acid one drachm, Flexile Collo- dium one ounce. The following is still more useful: Bichloride of Mercury two grains and a half, Salicylic Acid half a drachm, Collodion to four drachms. Paint the warts with this once daily. After a few applications they peel off, leaving a small open sore, which heals quickly if dressed with Boric Ointment. • A slight scab remains thereafter for some time. Wok Nialk NotigN WO b. Wilk ISM BRAVE WARRINGTONIAN. Rescuer Recommended to Royal Humane Society. "I think he ought to be recommended to the Royal Humane Society for some recognition." So said the Chief Constable, Mr. Martin Nicholls, at the Borough Police Court on Mon- day, referring to the bravery of Mr. James Ball, a miller's labourer, of 44, Cockhedge-lane, War- rington, who, on Saturday, May 30th, rescued a girl from the River Mersey. On the day of the rescue, the girl, Mary Grady, a domestic servant, 3, Pocket-street, was brought before the magistrates on a charge of

attempting to commit suicide. She alleged she had trouble at home, and. was remanded to the Workhouse Infirmary for 14 days, with a view to ascertaining whether Mr. Laws (the police court missionary) could find a home for her. On Monday, when she again appeared in Court, the Chief Constable announced that Mr. Laws had been successful in getting a home to accept the girl, and it was suggested that the girl be sent to the home for six or twelve months. The magistrates agreed to such a course, and the case was adjourned for six months. RESCUER'S STORY. The Chief Constable said the man who went to the girl's rescue was in Court, and probably the Bench would like to hear the story. Mr. James Ball, who said he was ,employed at the Mersey Mills. then stepped into the wit- ness-box, and stated that at 6.30 on Saturday morning he was on the landing-stage opposite Mersey Mills, when he saw the girl, with her hat and coat off, come along. She jumped into the river and immediately he went to the rescue. At the spot the water was twelve feet deep, but he managed to grip her hair and with assistance he got her out, although he himself could not swim at all. The Mayor, who was in the chair, said the magistrates thought Ball's action very good indeed, especially as he could not swim very well. He deserved some recognition for the risk he ran, and it gave the magistrates great pleas- ure in recommending him to the Royal Humane Society for his very brae and gallant services.

But few people take this view, and it was with some amusement that, when the names of those appointed to sit on the Commission of Inquiry I into the declining birth-rate were published, the writer found a large number of well-known suffrage names included. It seems, despite of all the talk of women when enfranchised becoming averse to motherhood, it is those who are keen- est on seeing her with a vote, who are concerned with this birth-rate problem. The industrial and economic independence of women (likely to increase with the vote) is also a bugbear to many. But Sweden has found that the birth-rate among women engaged in indus- trial pursuits is steadily on the increase.
